# To the Kind Reader
### [He] Sends Most Hearty Greetings <note>Original: *S. P. D.*, an abbreviation for *Salutem Plurimam Dicit*, a standard formal greeting in Latin correspondence.</note>
## JOHANN LORENZ VON MOSHEIM.

Since my early youth, in addition to other branches of human learning <term>eruditio: a broad scholarly education encompassing the humanities</term>, I have greatly loved and pursued the study of Sacred History <note>Refers to *Historia Sanctior*, the study of the Church, biblical events, and divine providence in human affairs</note>; thus it happened that I devoted some diligence and labor to explaining and more fully illuminating several of its chapters. Such is the nature of people: those who dedicate themselves to a particular field of knowledge, and believe they have discovered something that might contribute to its expansion or refinement, can hardly bring themselves to keep their thoughts to themselves alone. Instead, for the most part—unless the opportunity is missing or they lack the skill to write—they commit these thoughts to the written word <gloss>original: *litteras*; literally "letters," referring here to published literature</gloss> so that they might serve the common good. I would have easily allowed these commentaries, published at various times, to fade away and be lost, for I am not so enamored of myself that I believe my labors will be of great use to future generations, nor am I so ignorant of scholarship that I do not realize how much they lack in perfection. However, certain learned men first stood in the way, by whom I have been frequently asked to [gather] these widely scattered... <note>The text breaks off here. The catchword "exi-" at the bottom of the original page likely leads to a word like *exigua* (small/slight) or *existimavi* (I have judged) on the following page.</note>

<summary>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim introduces his collected commentaries on Church History, explaining that while he is aware of his own imperfections, he was encouraged by other scholars to compile and publish his scattered writings for the benefit of the public.</summary>
<keywords>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim, Sacred History, Church History, scholarship, preface, publishing, academic modesty</keywords>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues the author’s explanation for publishing this collection. The previous page ended with Mosheim describing how learned men urged him to gather his "widely scattered" writings. This page completes that thought and introduces the specific contents of the volume, highlighting his work on Neoplatonism.</meta>

...gather these papers of small size <note>original: *exiguae molis ſchedas*</note> and include them in a single volume. Furthermore, I was moved by the affection and goodwill toward me shown by a certain book merchant <term>negotiator librarius: a publisher or bookseller who handled the physical production and sale of texts</term>, an honest and industrious man whom I have known familiarly since my youth. He was undoubtedly led by this friendship to frequently ask me for some book of mine that he might publish at his own expense. Influenced and moved by these promptings, I sought out these papers—which had been neglected for a long time—reviewed them once more, and took care to have them published together, augmented by new additions.

You have here, Friend Reader <note>original: *Amice Lector*</note>, the history of this volume, which encompasses most of my Dissertations <term>dissertatio: a formal scholarly treatise or essay</term> that I have written to illuminate the **History of the Christian Church**. There is no need for me to detain you longer at the threshold <note>A metaphorical reference to the preface or introduction of the book</note>. For the undertaking itself requires no excuse among good and fair-minded men, as it is justified by countless examples; nor does the matter demand that I offer specific remarks on each individual Dissertation. 

Almost all of them go forth more enriched and increased by various additions; yet, it was neither my wish nor was it possible to apply equal care to all of them. Thus, some have retained more of their old form, others less. One treatise stands above nearly all the others, both in the weight of its subject matter and in its usefulness: that in which I set forth the principles, teachings, and methods of the **more recent Platonic school** <note>Mosheim is referring to Neoplatonism, which he analyzed as a major intellectual rival that attempted to undermine early Christianity by blending philosophy with mystical traditions</note>, by which it sought to weaken the Christian cause. For this reason, in refining none of them... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword is "et".</note>

<summary>Mosheim explains that he was motivated to publish this collection by both scholarly requests and a persistent publisher, and he highlights his treatise on Neoplatonism as the most significant inclusion.</summary>

### THE ARGUMENT.

**T**he utility of commentaries of this kind; the occasion for this labor. § I. *The various opinions of learned men regarding the date of Tertullian's Apology <note>original: "Apologetici"; refers to Tertullian's famous defense of Christianity against paganism.</note>. § II. Others maintain it was written after the year 200: specifically, Cave <note>William Cave (1637–1713), an English church historian.</note> places it in A.D. 202. § III. Dodwell <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), a prominent Anglo-Irish scholar.</note> places it in A.D. 204, although he is inconsistent with his own views. § IV. Basnage <note>Samuel Basnage de Flottemanville (1638–1721), a French Protestant historian.</note> agrees with him. § V. Pagi <note>Antoine Pagi (1624–1699), a French chronologist and priest.</note> places it in A.D. 205. § VI. All of these men erred because they incorrectly established the start of the persecution under Emperor Severus <note>Septimius Severus, Roman Emperor from 193 to 211 AD.</note>. § VII. Therefore, it is demonstrated that the Christians were harassed under SEVERUS even before his official edicts: (1) from Tertullian's Apology itself; § VIII. (2) from his book To the Martyrs <note>original: "ad martyres"</note>; § IX. (3) from Clement of Alexandria; § IX. (4) from the Acts of the Scillitan Martyrs <note>The earliest dated record of Christian martyrdom in North Africa (180 AD).</note>; § X. (5) from Orosius and Freculphus <note>Late antique and medieval Christian historians.</note>. § XI. The arguments invented by HENRY DODWELL and BASNAGE to prove the contrary opinion are discussed. § XII. XIII. XIV. Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a foundational figure in modern chronology.</note> thinks the Apology was written after the death of Severus; § XV. as does Allix <note>Pierre Allix (1641–1717), a French Protestant pastor and author.</note>. § XVI. Others maintain it was composed before the year 200, though not all agree on the specific year. § XVII. The true opinion is explained and it is shown that: (I) the book was written during the reign of SEVERUS; § XVIII. (II) after the uprisings of Albinus <term>Clodius Albinus; a rival to Septimius Severus who was defeated in a civil war</term> were suppressed. § XIX. Since not everyone agrees on the timing of these uprisings, § XX. it is shown that they were settled in A.D. 197: (1) from the series of events conducted by Severus at that time; § XXI. (2) from the timing of the siege of Byzantium; § XXII. (3) from the time when the name Augustus was given to Caracalla <note>Severus's son and co-emperor.</note>. § XXIII. Furthermore, the reasons of those who think otherwise, especially Petavius <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a French Jesuit theologian.</note> and Pagi, are examined. § XXIV. XXV. XXVI. (III) The passage of the Apology from which its date must be extracted is explained; § XXVII. XXVIII. and having demonstrated the time of the "Caesars" <note>Referring to the remnants or supporters of the defeated Albinus.</note> of the remnants of Albinus, (IV) it is proven that the Apology was composed in A.D. 198. § XXIX. XXX. Conclusion. § XXXI.*

<image-desc>A decorative headpiece consisting of four horizontal rows of typographic ornaments. ### §. I.

If the diligent investigation of the times <note>Meaning the specific dates and chronological contexts.</note> in which the ancient doctors of the Christians committed their books to writing recommends itself by any utility, and if it had always been treated with the zeal and industry of learned men, I do not doubt that **Sacred History** <term>The study of the history of the Church and religious doctrine</term> would labor under far fewer difficulties today, and could be set forth in a more elegant and easier order. But our ancestors—men of great and excellent genius who first wiped away the filth of barbarism <note>A common Renaissance and Enlightenment reference to the perceived lack of classical learning in the Middle Ages.</note>—judged that they should focus their efforts on raising up the utterly collapsed state of letters, rather than on winning over themselves and others with those subtleties (as they thought them) which might cause disdain. 

However, a different mindset belonged to those who followed those divine restorers of the liberal arts. It is well known that they applied no small amount of diligence to these cares, with **Scaliger**, **Baronius**, **Petavius**, **Calvisius**, and others leading the way <note>These men—Joseph Justus Scaliger, Cesare Baronius, Denis Pétau, and Sethus Calvisius—were the primary architects of modern historical chronology in the 16th and 17th centuries.</note>. ### §. II.

As I looked around, as was fitting, to see what learned men before me had thought about this same matter, it immediately occurred to me that it had been entirely passed over by some writers of Sacred History, while by others it was treated not with focused effort, but only in passing <note>original: *aliud agendo*; literally "while doing something else."</note>. <meta>This page continues from the author's survey of previous scholarly opinions. The previous page ended with the observation that leading scholars disagree on the dating of Tertullian's *Apology*.</meta>

Hindered by preconceived judgments, they seemed more devoted to their own views than to the truth. Very many preferred to follow men of great name as their leaders rather than distract their minds from more important matters with the troublesome and thankless calculation of dates. Indeed, this very diversity of opinions moved and encouraged me to weigh all of them with even greater diligence and to investigate precisely the foundations upon which each one rests. And now, as candidly and clearly as the nature of the subject allows, I shall declare what I have found in them to be worthy of criticism and, conversely, what has seemed to me to align with the truth. 

Above all, to better assist the memory, I shall establish two categories of opinions. For although learned men differ greatly regarding the specific year of the *Apology* <note>original: *Apologeticus*; Tertullian's famous defense of Christianity</note> itself, some nevertheless agree that it was composed before the year 200, while others agree that it was committed to writing after this centennial year. What, therefore, prevents us from making this centennial year a boundary line and dividing the opinions into two classes: one consisting of those who believe the book in question was written before or during that very year, and the other of those who believe it was written after? 

I shall deal first with the latter group, as it is both further from the truth and more easily refuted; at the same time, I will take this opportunity to clarify from ancient records <note>original: *monumentis*; here meaning historical documents or inscriptions</note> the true beginning of the calamities that afflicted the Christians under the Emperor **SEVERUS**. The former class, which comes closer to the truth but also employs arguments whose weakness must be demonstrated from the deeper recesses of secular history <term>Historia civilis</term> <note>referring to political and administrative history as opposed to purely church history</note>, will be addressed in the second place.

### §. III.

Those who judge that this *Apology* <note>original: *Apologeticum*; Tertullian’s primary defense of the Christian faith against pagan accusations</note> was committed to writing by <term>TERTULLIAN</term> <note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155–220 AD), a prolific early Christian author from Roman Carthage</note> after the two-hundredth year from the birth of the Savior can again be divided into two classes. The second class consists of those who, going further, believe <term>TERTULLIAN</term> took up this task only after <term>SEVERUS</term> had already passed away. Among the former group, the leading opinion is voiced by <term>WILLIAM CAVE</term>, a man who, if one considers his diligence and expertise in these matters, is to be compared with few others. He convinced himself that this *Apology* was drafted in the year 202 AD: (*) *It seems more likely to me,* he says, *that it was written during the sixth persecution, around 202 AD, when the Emperor Severus forbade anyone from becoming a Christian under heavy penalty.* He indicates that the arguments for this opinion are as follows: *And indeed, it is clear from Ulpian <note>Domitius Ulpianus, a celebrated Roman jurist whose writings formed a large part of the later Justinian Code</note> that Severus ordered by a rescript <note>original: *rescripto*; a formal written reply by a Roman emperor to a legal inquiry</note> that those who were said to have joined an illegal society—should be accused before the Prefect of the city. Indeed, this Severan persecution flared up to such an extent that, as Eusebius <note>The Bishop of Caesarea and author of the first comprehensive history of the Christian Church</note> reports, throughout all the churches in every place, illustrious martyrdoms were completed by athletes <note>A common early Christian metaphor for martyrs, who were seen as "competing" for a heavenly prize in the arena of faith</note> fighting for piety. Nay, the minds of many were so violently disturbed that they even thought that famous heralded arrival of the Anti-Christ was imminent.* We can, therefore, assign the birth-year of this writing to no other epoch with a greater appearance of truth. The points which this distinguished man discusses here are correct enough; but how it is demonstrated from them that the *Apology* was drafted in the year 202 AD is exactly what escapes me. It is true that the Christians sustained a huge mass of calamities under the Emperor **SEVERUS**; however, unless everything deceives me, this does not prove the time at which the *Apology* <note>original: *Apologeticus*</note> was composed. He [William Cave] has only this one point to bolster his opinion: that in the year 202 AD, **SEVERUS** first proposed laws against the Christians. Although I do not deny this at all, I do not think it is sufficient to demonstrate that **TERTULLIAN** did not defend the Christians before that time. For if it were shown that before these decrees of **SEVERUS** against the Christians were promulgated, infinite tortures had already been inflicted on them, the entire foundation of this calculation collapses. We shall demonstrate this later, I hope, with arguments that leave no room for doubt. Furthermore, that learned man [Cave] did not sufficiently consider that even if there were significant force to his argument, the date of the book should rather be deferred to the year 203 AD. For at that time—as is clear from the entire book—**TERTULLIAN** stood forth as the protector of his sect when the Christians had already for some time felt the fury of their enemies. Therefore, it is not very credible that this defense was committed to writing at the very beginning of the calamities and in the same year in which they began.

->§. IV.<-

### §. VI.

This man <note>referring to Antoine Pagi</note>, although he spent nearly his entire life worn down by the study of chronology <note>original: *in numeris*, literally "among numbers," referring to his work on dates and calendars</note>, nevertheless frequently committed himself to opinions that no one would easily expect from a man so experienced in these matters. When he was writing his *Consular Dissertation* <note>original: *Hypaticam Dissertationem*; Pagi's 1682 work on the dates of Roman consulships</note>, no one perceived the truth more correctly than **PAGI**; for he established that the *Apology* was completed in no other year than 198 AD. (*) *Tertullian wrote the Apology in 198 AD, the year in which <term>Severus</term> celebrated his <term>Quinquennalia</term> <note>A festival marking the fifth anniversary of an emperor's reign.</note> and departed from Rome, for which reason he addressed the work to the Roman magistrates. For although no edict had yet been promulgated by the Emperor against the Christians, <term>Plautianus</term> <note>Gaius Fulvius Plautianus (c. 150–205 AD), the powerful commander of the Praetorian Guard and a close advisor to Septimius Severus.</note>, by whose authority everything was done in Rome, was already beginning to harass the Christians.*

He has excellently observed here that the Christians were already being harassed under **SEVERUS** before any law of the Emperor existed against them; and he taught no less foresightedly that the *Apology* was composed at a time when **SEVERUS’S** edicts had not yet been formally proposed. However, the remaining points he adds do not possess the same merit. For that which he took from **BARONIUS** <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), the influential author of the *Annales Ecclesiastici*.</note> is not true: (**) that **PLAUTIANUS** was in Rome in 198 AD—an opinion which he himself subsequently refuted. <meta>This page continues the critique of Antoine Pagi's shifting theories regarding the date of Tertullian’s *Apology*. This can be proven by the fact that the *Apology* appeared in 198 AD, a time when it seems to have been committed to writing while **SEVERUS** <note>Septimius Severus, Roman Emperor from 193 to 211 AD.</note> was away from Rome. If Rome had lacked the presence of the **AUGUSTUS** <note>A title for the Emperor</note> for only this one year, there would be nothing to criticize in that argument. However, since he was absent from Rome for several years, anyone can see that by the same reasoning, the *Apology* could be attributed to other years as well. 

Granted, this method of proof might not have been sufficiently accurate; nonetheless, I wish that learned man <note>Antoine Pagi (1624–1699), a French priest and historian known for his chronological critiques.</note> had persisted in that opinion, which he judged he had to abandon when he took it upon himself to correct **BARONIUS** <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a Cardinal and historian whose *Ecclesiastical Annals* were the standard of the time.</note>. At that point, he defended the view that the *Apology* was composed by **TERTULLIAN** in 205 AD. 

"*The persecution of the Christians*," he says (*) "*was not decreed before 202 AD. Therefore, since Tertullian wrote his Apology when persecution had already been raging everywhere for a long time—as is gathered from the Apology itself—that most excellent work was published much later; specifically, as one may conjecture, in the year 205, in which Antoninus <note>Caracalla, the son of Septimius Severus, who was co-emperor</note> celebrated the <term>Decennalia</term> <note>A festival celebrating the tenth year of an emperor's reign.</note> of his imperial power, and in which the persecution raged more fiercely.*" 

No one has ever changed his mind under worse omens <note>original: *deterioribus auspiciis*; an idiom meaning with more unfortunate results</note>. While he studied how to apply a remedy to **BARONIUS's** minor error, he himself fell into a far more serious one. Indeed, I am not unaware—as he bids us observe—that nations hostile to the true religion were already raging against the Christians when **TERTULLIAN** was drafting the *Apology*. But is it permitted to conclude from this that the book was written *after* the decrees against the Christians were issued by **SEVERUS**? ->§. VII.<-

We have seen that for those who determine this book was written after 202 AD, but before the death of **SEVERUS** <note>Septimius Severus, Roman Emperor from 193 to 211 AD.</note>, the primary obstacle to a more accurate judgment was their conviction that no serious injury had been inflicted on the Christians before the year 202—the year we understand laws were enacted by **SEVERUS** against them. I am quite content to except **DODWELL** <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), an influential Irish scholar known for his works on early church history and chronology.</note> from this group; because he perhaps realized that no defense could be found in that opinion, he felt he had to resort to other clever arguments. 

All the others, however, believed nothing was more solid than this line of reasoning: **SEVERUS** enacted laws against the Christians in 202 AD. Therefore, before that year, they enjoyed a period of great peace. **TERTULLIAN**, however, pleaded their cause while the cruelty of their enemies was already raging against the Christians. Thus, it is certain that the *Apology* was composed by him either in 202 AD or later. Since this is the case, to undermine the strength of all the opinions we have listed so far, nothing will be more useful than to demonstrate that a great weight of evils and miseries was thrust upon the Christians long before **SEVERUS** sanctioned public edicts against them. In this way, we might more accurately extract the first year and the beginning of what they call the "Persecution of Severus" from ancient records.

### §. VIII.

Among the witnesses of this matter, we shall first give place to our own <term>Tertullian</term> <note>A prolific early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) known for his legalistic defense of the faith.</note>, who in that very book whose date we are now investigating, supplies us with more than one passage to place this opinion beyond controversy. Everyone agrees that the *Apology* was issued at the time when Christians were already being afflicted with the most extreme punishments. If, therefore, we show that nothing had been heard at that time regarding the public edicts of <term>Severus</term> <note>Emperor Septimius Severus.</note>, we will have demonstrated what we intend. Indeed, several passages of the *Apology* indicate exactly what we have said. For now, I will omit the conjecture—which I note is not to be entirely dismissed—that because the *Apology* was written to the Governors of the provinces, it is clear that these Governors, rather than the Emperor, were the evil instigators and authors of the trouble. ### Section IX.

The *Apology* itself provides us with these points, by which we may prove that Christians were harassed under **Severus** before the Emperor's official decrees were issued; how these points could be undermined, I certainly do not understand. This is a judgment unworthy of a writer of Annals, unless I am entirely mistaken! That most illustrious man forgets the very things he was soon to defend so fiercely: that as early as 198 AD, with **Plautianus** <note>Gaius Fulvius Plautianus, a powerful commander of the Praetorian Guard under Emperor Septimius Severus. Historians of the time often portrayed him as a cruel instigator of violence.</note> fanning the flames <note>original: "faces admovente"</note>, Christians were already being harassed in shameful ways. <meta>This page continues the argument against Henry Dodwell’s claim that war prevented the persecution of Christians. ...were the laws of the Emperors passed against them? Certainly, anyone who reflects for a moment on the fact that Christians were extremely hated by both the common people and the priests, and moreover that laws sanctioned against their lives were always in force, will understand with no effort that they could have been killed and slaughtered at any time—and indeed, more so in a time of war than in a time of peace. I say nothing of the Emperor <term>Valerian</term> <note>Publius Licinius Valerianus (reigned 253–260 AD), known for his harsh persecutions of Christians despite being distracted by constant border wars.</note>, who, in the midst of the tumults of a most formidable war, afflicted the Christians with infinite hardships and injustices. And why do I dispute at such length? Does a Prince <note>The Latin *Princeps*, here referring to the Emperor.</note> need leisure to say: *I will it so, I command it so?* <note>original: "Sic volo, sic iubeo." A quote from the Roman satirist Juvenal, implying arbitrary power.</note> Or is tranquility and peace required for him to permit the common people to do what they are already doing?

Since these things are so, I truly do not understand why not only <term>Tillemont</term> <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a French ecclesiastical historian.</note> believed there was some weight to this argument of Dodwell’s, (*) but even the most learned <term>Basnage</term> <note>Samuel Basnage (1648–1691), a Protestant historian who wrote the *Annales Politico-Ecclesiastici*.</note> wished to use the same logic in this case: *Severus,* he says, (**) *did not swoop down upon the Christians any sooner, distracted as he was by various wars, both civil and foreign.*

The same value should be placed on Dodwell’s other reason, by which he denies that <term>Severus</term> <note>Septimius Severus (reigned 193–211 AD).</note> had any occasion for mistreating Christians before the year 202 AD: *Nor did any occasion at least occur which might stir the Emperor's anger against the Christians, since they were neither followers of Niger nor Albinus, as Tertullian says.* <note>Pescennius Niger and Clodius Albinus were rival claimants to the imperial throne who were defeated by Septimius Severus in civil wars. Dodwell argues that because Christians remained neutral, the Emperor had no political reason to attack them.</note> I will be brief here, since I think anyone understands that nothing more reckless could have been said. For he lays down as a foundation something that everyone knows to be completely false: that Emperors never harmed Christians unless it was because of them...

### §. XVII.

Hitherto we have dealt with the other class of those authors who contend that the *Apology* of **TERTULLIAN** was written after the year 200; now we must speak of those who [place] its birth even before this [year]—

---

—[the journal] <note>Likely completing a title like *Commentarii* from the previous page.</note> penned: <note>original: "exaravit"</note> When he was writing this book, however, he was already devoted to the faction of the Montanists, according to the opinion of all interpreters. But he wrote the *Apology* while the persecution of **SEVERUS** <note>Septimius Severus, Roman Emperor who reigned 193–211 AD.</note> was already raging, which occurred in 202 AD. Therefore, he did not compose this book before the year 202, at a time when he was already following the camp of **MONTANUS**. 

But this entire calculation rests on a very slippery foundation, and will not move anyone who has weighed the things we have said up to this point. We admit that this book was signed by **TERTULLIAN** under **SEVERUS** and while the persecution of Christians was active; however, we deny that those evils which befell Christians under **SEVERUS** first took their beginning in 202 AD. Indeed, the laws of **SEVERUS** against the Christians were not enacted before the year 202; but we have proven with testimony beyond all exception that before **SEVERUS** brought these laws, the Christians struggled under him with infinite evils, a fact which destroys this entire reasoning. 

Whether he was already devoted to the teachings of **MONTANUS** <note>A 2nd-century charismatic leader who claimed to receive new prophetic revelations; his followers were known for extreme rigor.</note> when **TERTULLIAN** composed the *Apology* on behalf of the Christians, I do not wish to explore now, but leave it undecided. Yet I cannot help but point out that it is hardly possible to judge from the precepts and dogmas of **TERTULLIAN** which books he wrote before and which after his defection to the Montanists. For this man, being exceedingly somber and stern, already cherished most of those errors which right-thinking Christians condemned in **MONTANUS**, even before **MONTANUS** began his innovations among the Christians. Evidently, **MONTANUS** taught **TERTULLIAN** very little that was new; the latter embraced that man only because he saw that he agreed with him in most matters.

There are many others whose names it is not necessary to list here. And some of these state only their opinion, omitting the reasons that led them to join it. ### §. XX.

But here, those whose authority in these matters is great—as anyone but those entirely ignorant of such things must know—will again disagree. For while some maintain that the defeat <note>original: "cladem" — referring to the Battle of Lugdunum where Albinus was finally defeated by Severus.</note> of **<term>Albinus</term>** occurred in the year **AD 197**, others nevertheless think it should be moved to **AD 198**. Therefore, since we have decided to omit nothing that pertains to both clarifying and refining this case, we shall demonstrate with evident arguments which of these sides should be supported. 

The former opinion is both older and accepted by more scholars; indeed, besides the compilers of the <term>fasti</term> <note>The *fasti* were the official chronological lists or calendars of Roman magistrates, used by historians to date events.</note> (*), **<term>Cesare Baronio</term>** (**) **<term>Francesco Mediobarbo</term>** (***) **<term>Tillemont</term>** (****) and many others have preferred it. If these men had fortified that position a little more diligently, I believe no one would have emerged to challenge it; they would undoubtedly have done so if they had imagined anyone would be so bold as to try to reject and repudiate it. Without hesitation, I profess that I consider this the better opinion. Before I dismantle the arguments of those who feel otherwise, I will demonstrate with the weightiest reasons that this choice is not made without cause. For if I clearly show the foundations upon which this calculation <note>original: "calculus" — referring to the chronological reckoning or dating system.</note> rests, then it will be far easier for anyone to judge what should be thought of the alternative opinion.

First of all, I ask you to observe that the war waged against **ALBINUS** <note>Clodius Albinus was a Roman usurper who claimed the imperial title in Gaul.</note> was not long-lasting; rather, it began in one year and was finished in the next. As soon as **SEVERUS** <note>Septimius Severus, the Roman Emperor from 193 to 211 AD.</note> had heard that Albinus was plotting a revolution in Gaul, he hurried from the East toward Gaul without delay, making great and hasty marches. **ALBINUS** did not fear the arrival of his enemy, but immediately offered himself for a struggle for the supreme power. Thus they met, and at first they decided the matter with certain skirmishes; since the outcome of these was uncertain <note>original: "ancipiti pugnaretur Marte" — literally 'fought with a two-headed Mars,' a classical idiom meaning the battle's result hung in the balance.</note>, Albinus was already beginning to hope for victory. Now, I will demonstrate with three very strong arguments why these two years of the Albinian war must be the years **AD 196** and **197**.

From this, who does not see that in the year 196 AD <term>Severus</term> set out against <term>Albinus</term>? And who does not simultaneously understand that in 197 AD, the <term>Battle of Lugdunum</term> <note>original: "Lugdunense praelium"; the decisive and bloody battle fought at modern-day Lyon, France.</note>, which brought an end to this war, took place?

Let another argument now take the stage, which, if it is less significant than the former, is certainly endowed with no less force. ### §. XXV.

Truly, **Pagi’s** arguments are remarkably disjointed; the sum of them, accurately collected, is this: The **Quinquennalia** <note>A festival celebrating the fifth anniversary of an emperor’s reign.</note> of **Severus** were, without any controversy, celebrated at Rome in 198 AD. However, **Herodian** <note>Herodian of Antioch, a Greek historian of the 3rd century who wrote about the Roman Empire.</note> narrates that immediately after the battle of **Lyon** <note>Original: *Lugdunensem*. This refers to the Battle of Lugdunum, where Severus defeated Albinus.</note>, the Emperor sought Rome with great speed, and immediately after his arrival gave the **Quinquennalia** to the people. Therefore, if **Severus** entered the city shortly after the death of **Albinus**—whom we have learned died on the nineteenth day of February—and if no delay was interposed between his arrival and the **Quinquennalia**, it must be that the year of **Albinus’s** defeat and **Severus’s** **Quinquennalia** is the same. Since the **Quinquennalia** were held in 198 AD, it would follow that **Albinus** was also slaughtered in this year.

Unless I knew that men can slip up nowhere more easily than in matters of this kind, I would be greatly amazed that such weak little arguments could proceed from a man in whom such deep learning resided. In these arguments, it must first be criticized that, contrary to the reliable testimony of all writers, he assumes the **Albinian** upheaval lasted for three years. This learned man professes that arms were taken up by both sides in 196 AD; he cannot tolerate **Petavius**, who had written that this did not happen before 197 AD—a date by which **Petavius** could have defended the same opinion as **Pagi** much more fortunately. (*) But **Pagi** does not notice that in this way he falls into far more difficult traps and snares than **Petavius**, because he protracts that war into a third year against the will of all authorities. ### §. XXVI.

In the first place, he bids us to put beyond doubt that in the year 198 AD, the **Quinquennial** games were presented by **Severus** at Rome; but those who think this postulate holds no difficulty are indeed greatly mistaken. We are, in fact, indebted to **Pagi** himself for this rule: *The Quinquennalia, decennalia, and festivals of that kind were celebrated indiscriminately, sometimes at the beginning of the fifth year, sometimes at the end.* (*) I am aware that the reason he wants us to admit this rule is not very strong—namely, the claim that Emperors presenting such games to the people always assumed the <term>Consular dignity</term> <note>The rank of Consul, the highest elected political office in the Roman Republic and an important title under the Emperors.</note>. ### §. XXVII.

Having thoroughly examined these matters, we can proceed more easily to the rest and clearly affirm that the *Apologeticus* <note>Tertullian's "Apology," a famous defense of Christianity against pagan accusations.</note> was committed to writing in the year 198 AD. Indeed, there is an excellent passage in it that teaches us this: *“But even those who are now,”* says **TERTULLIAN**, (**) *“daily being revealed as associates or supporters of the criminal factions—the leftover gleanings of the traitors <note>original: "parricidarum racematio superstes." How they used to dim their entryways with the tallest and brightest lamps! How they used to divide the forum among themselves with the most refined and proudest couches! Not to celebrate public joys, but to already declare their own secret vows during another's festival, and to inaugurate the pattern and image of their own hope, changing the name of the emperor in their hearts. These same duties are now failing those who consult Astrologers, Soothsayers, Augurs, and Magicians concerning the lives of the Caesars...”*

### §. XXVIII.

<term>Tertullian</term> <note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage and a key figure in early Western theology.</note> speaks of parricides <note>In Roman law, the term *parricidium* (parricide) originally meant the murder of a parent, but it was legally extended to include treason against the "Father of the Country," the Emperor.</note>: it is clear what sort of men they were—namely, men who were either accused of plots formed against the Emperor, or were indeed guilty of that crime. <term>Cicero</term> <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC) was Rome's most famous orator and statesman; his writings on ethics and law were highly influential in the early Church.</note> had long ago felt that (*) *such men were even more than parricides: since, as he adds, it is more atrocious to kill the father of one's country than one's own father.* Moreover, he mentions that these parricides were staying in Rome and had very recently, with great display, offered vows for the Emperor's safety while the city echoed with public applause and joy; nor were they less diligent than others in decorating for the other feast days then being celebrated. Furthermore, he reports that the greatest part of these criminals has already been removed—which he calls a "vintage" <note>original: *vindemiam*; Tertullian uses this agricultural metaphor to describe a large-scale execution or "harvest" of political enemies.</note>—but adds that a "gleaning" <note>original: *racemationem*; referring to the few remaining conspirators being gathered after the main mass execution.</note> still remains, and at that very time when he was writing, the associates of those wicked factions were being dragged daily from their hiding places. From all this, it is gathered that the <term>Apologeticus</term> <note>Tertullian's "Apology" is a legal defense of Christianity addressed to Roman governors, arguing against the persecution of Christians.</note> was written in that year when the remnants of certain conspirators were being tracked down in Rome and certain feast days were being publicly celebrated. Indeed, the life of <term>Severus</term> <note>Emperor Septimius Severus (reigned 193–211 AD), who secured his power after a series of bloody civil wars.</note> was twice in imminent danger: first from <term>Niger</term> <note>Pescennius Niger, a rival claimant to the imperial throne defeated by Severus in 194 AD.</note>, then from <term>Albinus</term> <note>Clodius Albinus, another rival for the throne who was defeated in 197 AD at the Battle of Lugdunum.</note>; and for that reason, he twice sought to destroy the remaining forces of the conspirators. Therefore, at the outset, it must be investigated whether <term>Tertullian</term> is speaking about the followers of <term>Niger</term> or those of <term>Albinus</term>? In this matter, a moderate amount of diligence will be required. For since <term>Tertullian</term> says that these plotters were dragged to punishment in Rome, and adds that shortly before...

that they were not the least part of the public joys, anyone, unless they are entirely ignorant of the events of that time, will realize that the followers of **Niger** <note>Pescennius Niger was a Roman general who claimed the imperial throne in 193 AD, primarily supported by the eastern provinces.</note> are by no means meant here. ->§. XXIX.<-

Truly, there is no doubt that **Severus**, having returned from Gaul to Rome, punished most cruelly those toward whom even the slightest suspicion of ill-will toward him pertained. This was done so that he might be free from fear once his enemies were destroyed, and might abound in money by claiming their riches for himself. No less skillfully does **Spartianus** <note>Aelius Spartianus is one of the six fictional or real authors credited with the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of biographies of Roman Emperors.</note> relate the same matter: whose testimony has this exceptional quality besides, that it elegantly corresponds to the words of **Tertullian**. (*) I wrote these things roughly ten years ago, or a bit more, when I first published this treatise <term>treatise: a formal written work on a specific subject (Latin: *commentatio*)</term>. When we first approach literature and see many things left behind by others, we are seized by a certain impulse and fire of spirit; we judge our own strengths rashly and promise that we will bring a remedy to many ills at once. Indeed, we measure the rest of our lives by the leisure we enjoy at that time, and we do not set before our eyes the turns of fortune, the shortness and troubles of life, the variety of accidents, and other things to which we are thereafter exposed. Therefore, it is no wonder if we end up providing others with the opportunity of writing the very libraries we ourselves had promised to write.

Nevertheless, there is still some room left for **diligence** <note>original: *diligentia*; careful, persistent effort</note>; and not infrequently, a **sincerity of mind** <note>original: *candor animi*; an honest or unbiased spirit</note> and a **tenacious pursuit of truth** <note>original: *pertinax veri studium*</note> are accustomed to surpass even **erudition** <note>original: *eruditio*; deep, extensive scholarship</note> itself in matters of this kind.

->§. I.<-

As I reflect quite often on why it happens that most people do not derive as much benefit from the History of the Christian commonwealth <note>original: *civitas Christiana*</note> as administrators of public affairs and leading men derive from civil History, it seems to me that the origin of this evil lies primarily in the fact that few of those who delight in the study of sacred History <note>original: *Historia sacra*</note> connect the revolutions of affairs and events with their underlying causes; indeed, many are even accustomed to neglect these causes entirely. It is certainly noble not to be ignorant of what has happened to the church <note>original: *ecclesia*</note> throughout all the centuries in which it has flourished—which errors disturbed its peace, what dogmas <note>original: *dogmata*</note> emerged, what rites <note>original: *ritus*</note> were introduced and adopted, and what other things are connected with these. Yet, all these things increase knowledge <note>original: *scientia*</note> more than wisdom <note>original: *sapientia*</note>; they overwhelm the memory, but they neither expand nor sharpen prudence <note>original: *prudentia*</note> and judgment. These qualities will be much better served if the reasons for so many changes, the production of so many and such varied rites, and the opening of the way for so many errors, are accurately explained and demonstrated at the same time. For once the causes of turmoils and evils are known, it becomes clear how the path to error must be blocked, or what must be done or avoided, so that salvation <note>Or "well-being."</note> may remain inviolate in the church <note>The text cuts off here at "ec-"; the catchword "cle-" indicates the word continues as *ecclesia* on the next page.</note>

of the church, it is more clearly understood. I will provide more copious proof of this, if it pleases the Supreme Deity <note>original: *Supremo Numini*, referring to God</note> to grant me strength and life, so that I may complete the great work <term>ON THE RITES AND CUSTOMS OF THE ANCIENT CHRISTIANS</term>, which I have had in mind for some time. this sect philosophized much more freely than most of those had done who previously wanted to be seen as professors of wisdom. For while those others had surrendered themselves to the discipline of only one master—**PLATO**, **ARISTOTLE**, **ZENO**, or others—these philosophers taught that truth should be sought from all sects <margin>(b)</margin>, and they instructed their followers to construct a certain mixed body of wisdom from the tenets of both the Greeks and the Orientals. For this very reason, **JULIAN** the Emperor not unskillfully compares them to musicians who, although the strings are endowed with various sounds, nevertheless know how to tune them so that a sweet and pleasant harmony arises from them. <margin>(c)</margin> In addition to this, they denied that the ancients were free from errors, or that they had already discovered the whole of the truth; for this reason, they not only freely criticized them whenever they judged their opinions to be far from the truth, but they even added new discoveries where they judged the ancients to be lacking.

### §. III.

But to better serve the convenience of my readers, I believe I must trace the origins of this philosophy a bit further back. There lived, during the reign of <term>AUGUSTUS</term> <note>The first Roman Emperor (r. 27 BCE – 14 CE).</note>, a certain philosopher in <term>Alexandria</term> in <term>Egypt</term> named <term>POTAMON</term> *(e)*. He entered upon a new and previously untrodden path of philosophizing, and he commanded his followers not to swear allegiance to the words of any single sect, but to gather the truth from all the schools of philosophers, and to accept nothing except after consulting reason and applying judgment. Those who were obedient to this man’s instructions, and who wished to be the arbiters of truth themselves rather than giving their names to <term>ARISTOTLE</term>, <term>PLATO</term>, or other masters, were called *Eclectics*. <meta>This page continues the discussion of how the independent, "Eclectic" mindset of Alexandrian philosophers transitioned into the early Christian church. ...bound by custom, which prevented them from seeing the truth offered to them, these men were free to pursue whatever seemed best to them. They gathered from any source those ideas that bore the shape of truth and right, incorporating them into their own discipline. Thus, when the heavenly doctrine revealed to us by our Savior was first taught in Alexandria by his disciples, some from this "family" <note>Referring to the Eclectic philosophers described on the previous page.</note> immediately joined them. These individuals later served as doctors and masters among the Christians, leading the famous school established by the Christians in Alexandria.

The first leader of this school, so far as we know, was **Athenagoras**, according to the witness of **Philip of Side** *(i)*. He joined philosophy with the profession of the Christian religion, yet he did not devote himself to a single sect. Instead, he chose from all schools what appeared better and more certain—which is to say, he was an **Eclectic**. This is made clear by his writings, which are still read today: *The Embassy for Christians* <note>original: "Legatio pro Christianis"</note> and the *Treatise on the Resurrection of the Dead* <note>original: "libellus de resurrectione mortuorum"</note>. 

After **Athenagoras**, the Christian youth in Alexandria were guided by **Pantaenus** and **Clement** (commonly called **Clement of Alexandria**). Learned men still debate which of these two succeeded the other. **Eusebius** *(k)* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the 4th-century historian often called the "Father of Church History."</note> maintains that **Clement** was appointed to replace **Pantaenus**, whereas **Philip of Side** records that **Pantaenus** only took up this office after **Clement**. We leave this dispute for others to settle, as it is outside our current focus. It is enough for us to know that both belonged to that class of philosophers...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of whether Pantaenus and Clement of Alexandria can be classified as "Eclectic" philosophers. The previous page ended with "ap-", which likely completed as "appointed" or "approved" in relation to the succession of teachers at the Alexandrian school.</meta>

...pointed successor to that class of which we are now treating. **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the foundational historian of the early Christian Church.</note> testifies that **Pantaenus** was indeed a *Stoic*, while **Philip of Side** <note>Also known as Sidetes, a 5th-century historian; only fragments of his "Christian History" survive.</note> claims he was a *Pythagorean*. But the reality of the situation prevents us from believing that these labels should be understood in an absolute sense. For if **Pantaenus** intended to be a Christian, he could not have fully approved of either the Stoic or the Pythagorean discipline. 

Thus, he undoubtedly preferred the Stoics to other philosophers in matters concerning ethics and human duties; however, regarding God and things that cannot be seen, he followed the philosophy of **Pythagoras** and **Plato**, just as his successors did. **Gottfried Olearius** *(l)* <note>Gottfried Olearius (1672–1715) was a German philologist and theologian known for his work on the Church Fathers.</note> has brought forward other reasons why it is appropriate to number **Pantaenus** among the *Eclectics*. 

Why use many words? Any of the Christian teachers who wished to be Christians without ceasing to be philosophers were compelled to follow this form of philosophizing. This was because all the sects contained many ideas that were utterly inconsistent with the religion of our Savior and could in no way be reconciled with it. **Clement of Alexandria** himself recorded that the *Eclectic* method of philosophizing was the only one that truly pleased him. After he had praised philosophy in magnificent and exquisite words—stating that it had come to men as a gift from God—he explained what kind of philosophy he meant in these very words: *(m)* 

"By philosophy I do not mean the Stoic, nor the Platonic, nor the Epicurean and Aristotelian; but whatever has been said well by each of these sects, which teaches justice along with a godly knowledge—" <note>original Greek: "Φιλοσοφίαν δὲ οὐ τὴν Στωϊκὴν λέγω, οὐδὲ τὴν Πλατωνικήν, ἢ τὴν Ἐπικούρειόν τε, καὶ Ἀριστοτελικήν· ἀλλ’ ὅσα εἴρηται παρ’ ἑκάστῃ τῶν αἱρέσεων τούτων καλῶς, δικαιοσύνην μετὰ εὐσεβοῦς ἐπιστήμης ἐκδιδάσ-"</note>

<meta>This page continues the argument for why Clement of Alexandria adopted an "Eclectic" approach. It begins with the conclusion of a quote from Clement defining what he considers true philosophy—not the dogma of a single school, but the "selected" truths found across all schools.</meta>

...teaching this whole eclectic system, I call philosophy. <note>original Greek: δάσϰοντα τοῦτο σύμπαν τὸ ἐϰλεϰτιϰόν φιλοσοφίαν φημί.</note> *Now, I do not call philosophy that of the Stoics, nor the Platonists, nor the Epicureans and Aristotelians; but rather, whatever was rightly said by these sects, which teaches justice along with pious knowledge—this whole **SELECTED** <note>original: SELECTVM</note> body of thought, I call philosophy. However, those other things which, proceeding from human reasoning, they have corrupted, I would never call divine.*

->§. V.<-

Through the influence of these and several other leaders and authors—whose names time has erased—it came to pass that some place and honor for philosophy was preserved in the Christian community <note>original: *civitate Christiana*</note>, even though many desired to see it utterly overthrown and banished from the Christian assembly. **Clement** records that there were some in his own age who claimed philosophy was the invention of an evil and infernal spirit, born for the detriment and ruin of the human race. He fights vigorously against these people, desiring that minds be "irrigated" by the decrees and writings of the Greeks before the seed of heavenly doctrine is committed to them. "Just as," he says <margin>(n)</margin> "farmers first water the earth and only then cast in the seeds, so too do we first irrigate the earthly part of people with that which is 'drinkable' from the writings of the Greeks, so that they may receive the spiritual seed being sown and be able to nourish it with ease." <note>This metaphor compares secular education to preparing the soil for the Gospel; original Greek: Καθάπερ... / Latin: *Quemadmodum terram prius rigant agricolae...*</note> This opinion of **Clement** and the other philosophers among the Christians prevailed, no matter how much those <note>The sentence ends here, continuing on the next page with the catchword "illi," (those others/those men).</note>

Truly, this form of philosophizing could in no way remain the same once it had passed over to the Christians as it had existed among those who had followed <term>Potamon</term> <note>Potamon of Alexandria (c. 1st century BC) is traditionally credited with founding the Eclectic school, which chose the best doctrines from various philosophical traditions.</note> alone and lived without knowledge of the true religion. The older *Eclectics* were free—as they obeyed only the laws of their own reason and talent—to join themselves to whichever philosopher they wished and to take from all the "families" <note>Referring to the various schools of thought, such as the Platonists or Peripatetics.</note> for their own use whatever seemed consistent with their own reason. For this reason, they had to reject many of the dogmas of the "wise" because they conflicted with the teachings of <term>Christ</term>, whereas other *Eclectics* would collect from everywhere and turn to their own use whatever pleased and delighted them.

If only the Christian philosophers had always done so as was fitting, and had not been deceived by a certain external similarity of dogmas and institutions, such that they took for Christian things which only appeared Christian in outward show. But standing in their way was partly a love for philosophy, and partly inexperience and a weakness of intellect, which prevented them from weighing all things properly. From this, it happened that they transferred many things into Christian philosophy which differ entirely in kind from Christian discipline. In the doctrine of morals, they especially approved of the <term>Stoics</term> <note>The Stoics were a school of Greek philosophy that emphasized virtue, duty, and self-control—values that early Christians found highly compatible with their own ethics.</note>, since they considered their precepts on duties to be most consistent with divine laws—a fact shown by the examples of <term>Pantaenus</term>, <term>Clement</term> <note>Pantaenus and his student Clement of Alexandria were prominent 2nd-century Christian teachers who famously blended Greek learning with the Gospel.</note>, and others...

### §. VI.

Whoever observes these things will, with little effort, settle that dispute which, in our age, <term>François Baltus</term> <note>original: Franciscvs Baltvs; a French Jesuit theologian (1667–1743) who defended the Church Fathers against charges of corrupting Christianity with pagan philosophy.</note>, a Jesuit of no small learning and well-versed in the records of the ancient teachers of the Christian state, stirred up concerning the *Platonism of the Fathers*. There is an old complaint among learned men that the *Fathers*—the teachers of the earlier church—were more inclined toward the doctrine of <term>Plato</term> than was proper, and that they recklessly confused the precepts of this philosopher with the dogmas of <term>Christ</term>, our Savior; from which followed a great corruption of heavenly doctrine and a disturbance of truth. 

But this Baltus whom I mentioned vigorously attacked this opinion in a specific volume <margin>(p) *Defense of the Holy Fathers accused of Platonism, Paris, 1711. in quarto.*</margin>, in which he disputes with a great abundance of both oratory and erudition that the Fathers were not devoted to one single sect—and therefore not to <term>Plato</term> alone—but selected the better and safer things from all schools. <margin>(q) *See especially Book I, Chapters III and IV, page 18 and following.*</margin> In a certain way, <term>Pierre-Daniel Huet</term> <note>original: Petrvs Dan Hvetivs; a prominent French scholar and Bishop of Avranches (1630–1721).</note> had preceded him; after he had discussed the erudition and studies of <term>Origen</term>, he concluded that Origen should be called a *Potamonist* rather than a *Platonist*, as is commonly done: <margin>(r) *On Origen [Origenianor.], Book II, Chapter I, §. IV, page 27.*</margin> *For this reason, he was not so much addicted to any one sect, but was a student of all of them, and from them he plucked whatever was more useful and more likely to be true; and <term>Gregory Thaumaturgus</term> <note>a 3rd-century bishop and student of Origen.</note> left it written that he cautiously instructed his disciples to do the same: so that he should be called not so much a Platonist or a Pythagorean, as a Potamonist, after that Potamon of Alexandria, who was the author of the <term>Eclectic sect</term>.* <note>The Eclectic school, founded by Potamon, sought to select the best "flowers" of truth from various philosophical systems rather than adhering to one dogma.</note> Truly, either that good Jesuit did not know in what sense the ancient teachers of the church are called <term>Platonists</term>,

...or perhaps he did not wish to know it, and thus he confirmed the common opinion rather than refuting it. Those who accuse the *Fathers* <note>The "Church Fathers," early influential Christian theologians and bishops.</note> of an excessive inclination toward the teachings of **PLATO** do not mean to suggest that the ancient leaders of the Christians approved of the entire Platonic philosophy—which, indeed, they were in no way permitted to do. Nor do they deny that those teachers sharply attacked certain doctrines of **PLATO** which were plainly opposed to Christian decrees, or that they convicted this philosopher of various errors. Finally, they do not deny that Christian teachers took something from every sect; rather, they say only this: that the *Fathers* studied **PLATO** more than all other philosophers and sought more from him alone than from all the others combined. This was because they convinced themselves that no one taught better or more seriously about the nature and perfections of God, about the soul, and about heavenly matters.

If <term>Baltus</term> <note>original: Baltvs; the Jesuit scholar mentioned on the previous page.</note> wishes to call them *Eclectics* <note>Philosophers who do not follow one school but select the best parts of various systems.</note> or *Potamonians* <note>original: Potamonicos; followers of Potamon of Alexandria, who is credited with starting the Eclectic school.</note>, we will hardly fight over the word; yet they do not, for that reason, cease to be Platonists. They are *Eclectics* because they sample something from all sects; they are *Platonists* because they borrow more from **PLATO** than from others, and they diligently follow his footsteps in the most important part of divine wisdom—that which deals with God, the soul, and simple natures. Could it have escaped so great a man, who wishes to seem ignorant of nothing regarding ancient matters, that those very people who are called the *Later Platonists* <note>original: Platonici iuniores; often referred to today as Neoplatonists.</note> and wished to be seen as the genuine disciples of **PLATO**, were at the same time *Eclectics* and transferred something from every sect into their own schools?

...by his [arguments], he might open a way for the Christians to triumph over all [others] at once. Therefore, to meet such great dangers, he first assumed a principle that the followers of **POTAMO** <note>Potamo of Alexandria was the founder of the Eclectic school, which chose the best doctrines from various philosophies.</note> had approved and the Christians had similarly adopted: that the whole truth had not turned aside to any one family of philosophers, but was to be sought from all sects. For that reason, he held that those who wished to find the truth must use reason and intellect, rather than the authority of masters.

To this he added another point, which he had received from the Christians: that **PLATO** was, as it were, the prince and leader <note>original: "coryphaeum"</note> of all philosophers. This was because he had treated the most excellent part of philosophy—which deals with God and matters removed from human sight, and with the healing of the soul—more wisely and purely than all others. Not indeed that even this philosopher was free from every error, nor was universal wisdom so exhausted by him that nothing more could be added; but his failings were very slight if compared with those things he spoke well, and the greatest and most weighty matters were explained by him in a manner altogether divine.

Perhaps the man’s own disposition <note>original: "ingenium"</note>, which many of his precepts and dogmas show to have been largely fanatical, drove him into this love for **PLATO**; yet it is at the same time certain that, since he wished to resist the Christians, he could not fail to have an extraordinary devotion toward **PLATO**. For since the Christians themselves preferred **PLATO** to other philosophers, and maintained that he agreed with them in many great matters, it was possible for him [Ammonius] to conclude from this that the disciples of **CHRIST** had brought nothing new into the world that had not been said before, and that those things which seemed better and more holy among the Christians had long ago been handed down by the **Academy** <note>The school of philosophy founded by Plato in Athens.</note>...

->§. IX.<-

To these ideas, which **AMMONIUS** owed more to the **Eclectics** <note>The Eclectics were philosophers who did not adhere to a single school, but picked what they considered the best doctrines from many sources.</note> and the Christians than to himself, he added certain other things of his own. He perceived that his plan for defeating the Christians could not succeed without these additions. The Christians indeed admitted that **PLATO** had come closer to the truth than other philosophers; yet they contended that he had borrowed <note>original: "mutuatum esse"</note> whatever sound and useful ideas he possessed from **MOSES** and the **Hebrews**. There was not so much knowledge of literature and ancient erudition in this man <note>Ammonius Saccas</note> that he could refute this opinion by historical reasoning; therefore, he attacked it by another method.

Specifically, he determined that the ancient philosophers—both the Orientals and the Greeks—had taught the same things as **PLATO**. He concluded that those who thought there were as many disputes and battles among philosophers as were commonly reported were greatly mistaken. And since no one among the philosophers was more famous after **PLATO** than **ARISTOTLE**—who nevertheless seemed entirely opposed to **PLATO**—all his effort was spent in showing that these philosophers did not disagree with each other on the more serious and weighty matters. 

Once this was accomplished, he hoped that no one would believe the Christians when they claimed that **PLATO** had stolen <note>original: "suffuratum esse," literally "pilfered"</note> his teachings from **MOSES** and the writers of the **Hebrews**. For if all the philosophers, separated by such great intervals of place and time, held the same dogmas as **PLATO**, it is evident that it was not necessary for **PLATO** to visit the Jews to learn his wisdom; rather, he found it either with reason as his guide, or from other philosophical...

The Platonists took under their wing every form of religion found across the entire world. Furthermore, they maintained that the poets' myths about the Gods should be interpreted in a manner quite different from what the literal words seemed to suggest: the outer **bark** <note>original: *corticem*; referring to the literal or surface meaning of a text.</note> was to be discarded and the inner **kernel** <note>original: *nucleum*; the hidden, spiritual, or philosophical truth.</note> extracted. For they believed that beneath these humble coverings, profound metaphysical, physical, and moral truths were hidden—meanings which the wise man ought to draw forth and bring into the light. I am relating these things in summary here, but I will explain them in detail later and support them with specific evidence.

It is now clear what kind of philosophy this is—the school commonly referred to as **"Junior" Platonism** <note>Now known to history as Neoplatonism, a mystical form of Platonic philosophy that flourished from the 3rd century AD.</note>. It is a specific type of doctrine, blended and tempered from the tenets of the ancient <term>Eclectics</term> <note>Philosophers who did not adhere to a single school but selected what they judged best from various systems.</note> and Christians, along with the original ideas of <term>Ammonius</term> <note>Ammonius Saccas (c. 175–242 AD), the influential teacher in Alexandria regarded as the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> himself. This school insists that <term>Plato</term> <note>The 4th-century BC Greek philosopher whose works on the soul and the realm of Ideas formed the foundation of this school.</note> must be heard above all others, and it attempts to reconcile all other philosophers to his teachings. Yet at the same time, it teaches that whatever is missing in Plato must either be freely adopted from other sects or discovered through one's own reason and intellect. Indeed, it was established with the primary goal of saving the fading traditions of the Gods from total ruin, blunting the weapons used by Christians against the old superstitions, and, if possible, uprooting the Christian religion itself.

These philosophers could have been called **Eclectics** because of the careful selection of opinions they required of their followers; or they might have been called **Conciliators** because of their dedication to establishing harmony among all philosophers...

### §. XI.

In a short space of time, <term>AMMONIUS</term> <note>Ammonius Saccas (c. 175–242 AD), often considered the founder of Neoplatonism in Alexandria.</note> gathered a numerous company of disciples through his eloquence and the subtlety of his mind. Among these, some contributed more to the embellishment, organization, and propagation of this doctrine than the master himself, who never left Alexandria. The most noble of all these is <term>PLOTINUS</term>, whose life was recorded by <term>PORPHYRY</term>, his student and a most bitter enemy of the Christian community. *(h)* What kind of man this <term>PLOTINUS</term> was can be learned no better than from his own surviving books; from these it is clear that he was a man of certainly sharp intellect and endowed with no common insight, but at the same time a fanatic, intensely superstitious, and—through an excessive zeal for subtlety—frequently delirious. Furthermore, his speech and diction were extremely obscure and hampered, and filled everywhere with poetic figures. And yet this man, when he opened a school in Rome, infected almost all of Italy with the doctrine of <term>AMMONIUS</term>, and emerged as the leader and authority for the most outstanding minds of both the city and the provinces to adopt it. *(i)* Among his disciples, <term>PORPHYRY</term> stands out—a man otherwise learned, but fickle, changeable, and suffering from an abundance of black bile <note>A reference to the "four humors" of ancient medicine; "black bile" was thought to cause melancholy or erratic behavior.</note>: he [went to] Sicily... <note>The sentence ends abruptly as the text continues on the next page.</note>

### §. XIV.

I will now demonstrate this more clearly and at greater length. But so that the discussion may proceed in a certain way and order, I will first categorize the **evils** <note>original: "mala"</note> which I am certain were brought upon Christian affairs by this sect <note>Referring to the Neoplatonists or later Platonists mentioned on the previous page.</note>; then I will discuss each type in detail, as far as the scope of my project allows. Whatever calamities flowed from these philosophers into the **Christian community** <note>original: "civitatem Christianam"</note> can be conveniently divided into *external* and *internal* ones. I call those **external** evils which afflicted the kingdom of our Savior from the outside, or those obstacles which were placed by this faction against the spread and growth of Christian doctrine. To me, **internal** evils are those vices which grew within the Christian community itself from the reckless and imprudent coupling and conjunction of this philosophy with the most holy precepts and dogmas of CHRIST. 

To the external evils I have named, I again assign three types. First, these philosophers structured their teaching in such a way that it was suited to undermining those arguments by which Christian teachers used to demonstrate the vanity and madness of the old religions—or rather, **superstitions**. Second, they worked to ensure that the arguments by which Christian leaders and teachers were accustomed to placing the divinity and excellence of the Christian religion beyond controversy were shattered and undermined by new inventions. From these two things flowed the third: that some people defected from the Christians and returned to the **ancient filth** <note>original: "veteres sordes"; a disparaging reference to pagan practices.</note>, while others fashioned for themselves a new kind of religion, forged and composed from both Christian precepts and ancient superstitions.

<term>External evils (mala externa)</term>: Pressures or intellectual obstacles applied by philosophers from outside the Church to stop its growth. 
<term>Internal evils (mala intestina)</term>: The corruption of Christian theology caused by mixing it with Platonic philosophy.
<term>Superstition (superstitio)</term>: In this context, the author uses this to refer to traditional Roman and Greek pagan religions.

<summary>The author categorizes the negative impacts of Neoplatonism on early Christianity into external harms (attacks on Christian arguments) and internal harms (the corruption of pure doctrine through philosophical blending).</summary>
<keywords>Neoplatonism, external evils, internal evils, Christian doctrine, paganism, religious syncretism, theological corruption</keywords>

### §. XV.

First, therefore, the **Platonic school** <note>original: "Platonica natio"; a term used here to describe the community of Neoplatonist philosophers</note>, when they saw that the worship of the Gods and whatever religions then existed in the world were being attacked by the Christians with the weightiest arguments and reasons, and yet understood that there was no one else capable of standing against such powerful adversaries, they believed they had to undertake a new approach to repel the weapons the Christians aimed at the Gods and the ancient religions. The Christians were engaged in a struggle either with the **Philosophers**, who claimed to follow a wisdom better and purer than that of the common people, or with the remaining less-educated worshippers of the Gods—namely the priests and their associates. The Christians constrained these opponents so effectively—as is clear from the writings of <term>TERTULLIAN</term> <note>A prolific early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) known for his apologetics.</note>, <term>ARNOBIUS</term> <note>A North African apologist (d. c. 330 AD) who wrote "Against the Heathen."</note>, <term>TATIAN</term> <note>An Assyrian believer and student of Justin Martyr.</note>, <term>ATHENAGORAS</term> <note>A 2nd-century Christian philosopher who addressed the emperors in defense of the faith.</note>, and almost all those who wrote in defense of the Christian religion—that they were able to uncover the shame and the most serious errors of philosophy by examining every sect. They stirred up and mocked the contentions and brawls of the philosophers, by which those thinkers wore each other out; and finally, they complained that the most excellent part of all human knowledge—that concerning God and the duties of men—had been set aside and neglected by the philosophers, while they exhausted themselves in useless contemplations. These philosophers strove to wash away all these accusations. Since **nothing can be said or thought so absurdly that it has not been said by some philosopher** <note>original: "Quum nihil tam absurde dici vel cogitari possit, quin ab aliquo dictum sit philosophorum"; a famous observation originally attributed to Cicero</note>, it was possible for the Christians, with the slightest effort, to collect an incredible number of follies and outrages from each individual sect which the philosophers had handed down to their followers as examples of singular wisdom. Nor could those devoted to philosophy find anything to oppose to such numerous examples and clear proofs.

Nothing more elegant can be read on this matter than the third book of the *Institutes* by <term>LACTANTIUS</term> <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325 AD) was an early Christian advisor to Constantine I, often called the "Christian Cicero" for his polished Latin style.</note>, which he titled *On False Wisdom*. (x) The followers of this new philosophy <note>The Neoplatonists</note> freed themselves from this entirely troublesome dispute by establishing this principle among the very foundations of their knowledge: that truth is to be sought not in one sect alone, but in all of them, and that it has not been so perfectly refined that nothing more can be discovered. By the benefit of this dogma, they were able to reject as false and empty whatever vices or outrages were charged against this or that school <note>original: "familiae"; literally 'family,' used here to refer to a specific philosophical lineage or school of thought</note> of thought.

And here, indeed, the Christians themselves came to their aid. When the Christians perceived that some of the philosophers' tenets were not inconsistent with their own teachings, they clearly affirmed that *almost the entire truth*—these are the very words of LACTANTIUS (y)—*is divided among the sects of philosophers, and that no philosopher was so empty that he did not see something of the truth.* <note>original: "veritatem pene univerſam... per philoſophorum ſectas eſſe diviſam, nec ullum philoſophum tam fuiſſe inanem, qui non viderit ex vero aliquid"</note> This can be more fully proven by many sayings of <term>CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA</term> <note>A 2nd-century theologian who argued that Greek philosophy was a "preparatory training" for Christianity.</note>, <term>JUSTIN MARTYR</term> <note>An early apologist who famously used the concept of the "Logos" to bridge the gap between faith and reason.</note>, <term>ORIGEN</term> <note>A major scholar of the early Church known for his massive output and allegorical interpretations.</note>, and others, some of which we have already cited above.

Therefore, whenever Christians criticized something <term>Stoic</term> <note>A school emphasizing endurance, logic, and living in accordance with nature.</note>, <term>Cyrenaic</term> <note>A school that focused on immediate physical pleasure as the ultimate good.</note>, or <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>The school of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note> that was clearly flawed or ridiculous, they [the Neoplatonists] would freely admit that there were indeed things in all sects that could be condemned and rightfully rejected. But they also argued that certain "sparks" and "seeds" of truth lay hidden in each, which it was the task of the wise man to collect—while discarding the rest—and adapt for his own purposes. They claimed that the ancient philosophers had sometimes erred, being only human, and had even left some matters untouched, which they would undoubtedly have clarified and explained if they had been able to fulfill their duty properly... <note>The sentence continues onto the next page; the catchword "care" suggests the next word is a form of the Latin "carere" (to lack) or "curare" (to care for).</note>

They sometimes abandoned his footsteps even in that part of wisdom where they had otherwise chosen him as their leader—concerning God, the soul, and divine spirits <note>original: "geniis"; in Neoplatonism, these are intermediary beings between gods and humans</note>—whenever the matter required it. **AUGUSTINE** noticed this several times in **PORPHYRY** <note>Porphyry (c. 234 – c. 305 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who edited the works of Plotinus and was a significant critic of early Christianity.</note>, the most famous master of this sect: *“If,”* he says in one place (z), *“after Plato it is considered unworthy to correct anything, why did Porphyry himself correct several things—and no small things at that? ### §. XVI.

With no less vigor, the Christians criticized the arguments and brawls of the philosophers. Among them, the followers of Aristotle raged against the Platonists, and these in turn against the Aristotelians; the Stoics <note>a school of philosophy emphasizing virtue and endurance</note> against the Peripatetics <note>the "walkers," or followers of Aristotle</note>, and against these the Platonists and Pythagoreans <note>followers of the mystical and mathematical teachings of Pythagoras</note>—to say nothing of the remaining sects—fought with both voice and writings. It can scarcely be described how much zeal has produced forced and perverse interpretations of the ancient philosophers. It was therefore claimed that so many philosophical contentions arose through the fault of men who failed to grasp the minds of the wise, rather than from the philosophers themselves, who were said to agree wonderfully on matters of greater importance. To most, **PLATO** and **ARISTOTLE** seemed to be the leaders of the philosophers; and yet, no others were thought to conflict with one another more than these very two. 

And so the Christians, in their disputations against the pagans <note>original: "gentes"; literally "the nations," a common term for non-Christians or "Gentiles" in early Church writings</note>, especially emphasized this discord between these two philosophers. They did this to demonstrate that nothing sound or certain could be expected from philosophy, and that the Christian religion was superior to all human wisdom. This can indeed be shown in many passages from **JUSTIN MARTYR** <note>an early Christian apologist (c. 100–165 AD) who sought to reconcile faith and reason</note>, **HERMIAS**, **CLEMENT**, and others. 

The Platonists <note>specifically the Neoplatonists of late antiquity</note>, on the other hand, exerted all the powers of their intellect to put some limit to these controversies between **PLATO** and **ARISTOTLE**. ### XVII.

(e) It was very pleasing for me to learn that the same thing I have related here had already occurred to a man especially knowledgeable in ancient sacred and philosophical history, <term>Jakob Thomasius</term> <note>1622–1684; a influential German philosopher and rector at Leipzig who taught Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz</note>.
