These philosophers therefore began to brush this accusation away from themselves and cast it back upon our people. — — — Thus, naturally, just as when Christ was to be condemned, it was necessary for Pilate and Herod to be turned from enemies into friends, so Aristotle had to return to favor with Plato, so that it might go hard for the Christians.* <note>original: "ut Christianis aegre fieret"; meaning to create difficulties or trouble for the Christian cause</note> Truly, long before him, the same thing had been perceived by <term>Benedict Pererius</term> <note>1535–1610; a Spanish Jesuit known for his commentaries on science and scripture</note>, a very learned Jesuit. When he mentioned <term>Simplicius</term> <note>a 6th-century Neoplatonist who wrote extensive commentaries attempting to harmonize Aristotle and Plato</note> attempting to remove the discord of the philosophers in his *Commentary on Aristotle's Books of Physics*—according to the custom of his sect—Pererius adds these words in his book *On the Common Principles and Affections of All Natural Things, Book IV, ch. 10, p. 238*: *With these words he [Simplicius] correctly, if I am not mistaken, targets the ancient doctors of the church—I mean Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Origen, Justin Martyr, Lactantius, Eusebius of Caesarea, and many others. To refute the philosophers (who were puffed up by their reputation for wisdom and held Christian doctrine, which relies on faith and simplicity, in mockery), they concentrated on demonstrating and refuting their errors and the discord that was always greatest among them...*

### §. XVII.

Finally, the Christians complained that the most excellent part of all knowledge had been neglected by the "professors of wisdom" <note>A sarcastic reference to pagan philosophers</note>—namely, the science of God, of the soul needing to be purged of its impurities, and of the duties to be performed for God and others. They argued that the philosophers' commentaries were filled with empty and vain questions and disputes about the nature of things: the causes and origins of the natural world, lightning, stars, water, and air, as well as syllogisms and <term>sophisms</term> <note>Clever but fallacious arguments used to deceive</note>. These were matters that either human minds could not untangle, or they offered nothing of value to the human race...

---

...to declare <note>This text continues a footnote from the previous page</note> them, they labored greatly. In our own time, **FRANÇOIS BALTUS** <note>1667–1743; a French Jesuit scholar and librarian who defended the early Church Fathers against the claim that they were too influenced by Plato</note>, a member of the same society, arrived at the same conclusion. After stating that almost all the doctors of the early church had challenged the pagans with the disagreements between all their philosophers—and especially between **PLATO** and **ARISTOTLE**, philosophers seen as hostile to the Christian religion—he adds that he has no doubt that this was why the Platonists spent so much effort trying to resolve the contradictions between these two philosophers. He writes in his *Defense of the Holy Fathers Accused of Platonism*, Book II, chapter III, p. 115: <note>original in French: "Defense des SS. Peres accuséz de Platonisme"</note> *“I have no doubt at all that it was to answer this invincible argument of the Holy Fathers that the Platonists who came after the rise of Christianity strove to show, through several works, that the philosophy of Plato and that of Aristotle was absolutely the same, and that these two philosophers agreed perfectly in their sentiments. ... It was a miserable resource for a desperate cause. But it was of the utmost importance to these philosophers, the protectors of **Paganism** <note>original: "Panagisme," likely a typographical error for "Paganisme"</note>, to reunite their two most famous theologians. They did this to oppose the Christians more successfully, or at least to parry the blows that the Christians dealt them by pointing out the perpetual dissensions between their leaders and masters.”* If everything handed down by **BALTUS** were as certain and well-considered as this point is, nothing would be better than his book.

### §. XIX.

Thus, while they defended the cause of philosophy and strove to destroy the resources that Christians had gathered within it, they nevertheless believed they should defend the religion of the common people from the insults and mockery of the Christians with no less vigor. That multitude of deities—whose public rites were fortified by state authority—and the deeds of the gods—which had been handed down primarily through the songs of poets—had so thoroughly occupied and miserably corrupted the minds of the common people that they provided the Christians with inexhaustible material. This material allowed Christians to demonstrate the filthiness of popular religions and, in contrast, to reveal the truth of the Christian religion, which commands belief in one God in three persons. If one reads even the discourse of a single man, <term>Arnobius</term> <note>Arnobius of Sicca (c. 255–330 AD) was a North African convert to Christianity who wrote "Adversus Gentes" (Against the Heathen) to defend his new faith by attacking the absurdities of pagan mythology.</note>, regarding these gods and their history, it will be more than sufficiently clear that the eloquence of those who had undertaken the protection of the Christian religion triumphed in this argument. <margin>(t) <note>original: "Add. CLEMENTINA Homil. IV. & XV. f. p. 659. quorum auctor nervoſe docet, quam pernicioſae fuerint hae fabulae de Diis."</note> See also the *Clementine Homilies* IV and XV, p. 659, whose author vigorously teaches how destructive these myths about the gods were.</margin> Most of the older philosophers had despised the absurd religion of the common people; while they publicly put on a show of piety toward the gods, in their private conversations and formal speeches they had thoroughly demolished the cause of the gods. This is made clear by <term>Cicero’s</term> <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman statesman and philosopher. His work "On the Nature of the Gods" summarizes the views of different philosophical schools, often showing deep skepticism toward traditional myths.</note> books *On the Nature of the Gods*, among many other sources. This recent sect <note>The "recent sect" refers to the Neoplatonists, such as Porphyry or Iamblichus, who lived centuries after Cicero.</note> acted differently. Whether they were driven toward superstition by their hatred of the Christians, or because they took superstition as their guide to any manner of absurdity, they decided to bring aid to the almost ruined systems of the gods. They set out to provide a legal defense not just for the gods of a single nation, but for the gods of the entire world—

Nor was the opinion of the other wise men of this sort any different. We have heard that many of them traveled through a great part of the world and took care to be initiated into the mysteries and sacred ceremonies of whatever deities they found, so that they might make all the gods favorable to them and wash away the branded stains of the soul by the power of "holier waters" <note>A reference to the lustral waters used in pagan purification rites, which Neoplatonists interpreted as symbols of spiritual cleansing.</note>. 

First, therefore, they decreed this: that nothing from the ancient opinions and views should be rashly rejected. If, however, anything in these views seemed absurd or contrary to reason, it must be skillfully and suitably interpreted and explained. For they argued it could not be denied that those things which had been nobly handed down by the ancestors long ago had contracted some flaw through the faults of men and the ravages of time—a condition which it is the duty of the wise man to heal with his intellect and reason. Hence, you will find nothing so ridiculous or mythical, whether chanted by poets or passed down by the word of the ancients, that they do not adorn, anoint, polish, and bring back into conformity with the laws of their own philosophy. I have cited examples of this custom here and there in my *Observations on Ralph Cudworth’s Intellectual System* <note>Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688) was an English philosopher; the author of this text likely refers to the Latin edition of Cudworth's work "The True Intellectual System of the Universe," which was heavily annotated by the historian Johann Lorenz von Mosheim.</note>, which there is no need for me to repeat here.

->§. XX.<-

Since these seekers of wisdom <note>referring to the Neoplatonic philosophers</note> were not so blind and dull that they failed to see that religion—at least as it was commonly presented by priests and believed by the masses—could in no way be defended by them, they decided they had to set the stage a little differently so that they might better avoid the attacks of the Christians. Almost all nations before the birth of the Savior <note>original: *Servatorem*; a common title for Jesus Christ in Latin academic texts.</note> had spoken of their gods as if there were no order among them, and as if no one Deity obeyed the commands and orders of another, but rather that all possessed equal right and power among themselves. ### §. XXI.

Nothing stood more in the way of this goal of defending the superstitions of the people than the stories told by the ancients—especially the poets—about the gods and their deeds. It also notes how philosophers found it difficult to flatly deny these points.</meta>

<unclear>P</unclear>rimary arguments were usually sought from two places. For they either bore witness to the deeds and the history of our Savior, or they proclaimed the utility, sanctity, and excellence of the doctrine itself handed down by Him. This is known especially from the books of <term>Origen</term> <note>A prolific 3rd-century Christian scholar and theologian from Alexandria.</note> *Against <term>Celsus</term>* <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher who wrote the first comprehensive intellectual attack on Christianity.</note> and from the first book of <term>Arnobius</term> <note>An early Christian apologist who wrote 'Adversus Nationes' around 300 AD.</note> *Against the Heathen*. And this was indeed a great and unconquerable argument: Whichever religion is handed down by a man born in a wondrous manner, renowned for infinite portents and miracles, and finally endowed with a chastity of life and an incomparable holiness of character—and which is itself entirely divine, healing, and most useful to the human race—that religion is undoubtedly true and placed above all suspicion of fraud and deception.

What then did our subtle and sharp masters <note>Referring to the pagan philosophers.</note> say to these things? Did they deny that the deeds, history, and miracles of Christ had occurred? This they were by no means able to do, unless they wished to be deranged and to reject those things which were much more certain than all other history, and which were furthermore confirmed by the daily miracles of the Christians. Did they then try to tear down the sanctity and majesty of His doctrine? How indeed could they have done this, when they were day by day arranging their own discipline more and more according to its form? These men were philosophers who, although they were for the most part fanatics bound by superstitions, had nonetheless not so completely abandoned reason <note>original: "rationi nuntium miserant," literally "sent a message to reason," an idiom meaning to bid farewell to or renounce reason.</note> that they were entirely unable to distinguish the crooked from the straight <note>original: "obliquum pravo," referring to the ability to distinguish truth from error.</note> and dared to "lie against the sun" <note>An ancient idiom for denying an obvious, undeniable truth.</note>. 

Therefore, there was need of greater cunning to break the force of the Christian argument and keep the affairs of the Gods safe against it. Regarding the latter point, taken from the very sanctity and excellence of Christian doctrine, how they met... <note>original: "occurre-", likely followed by "rint" on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how Neoplatonic philosophers responded to the rapid spread of Christianity. The previous page established that these philosophers could not easily deny Christ’s miracles or the moral purity of his teachings. This page explores their strategy of "appropriation"—claiming that Christian virtues were actually stolen from philosophy—and their nuanced view of Christ as a wise man rather than a god.</meta>

...as we have already shown above, when we taught that they [the philosophers] attempted to perfect their moral system and their doctrine concerning God and divine matters with all their effort, borrowing from the Christians themselves what seemed good and useful in this regard. The purpose of this strategy was to persuade people that the excellent and outstanding things found among the Christians were also taught and approved by the philosophers, and therefore it was not necessary to go to the Christians to learn these things. It remains, therefore, for us to explain how they attempted to refute those things which were sought from the deeds and history of our Savior to demonstrate the excellence of the religion brought by Him.

### §. XXIII.

At first, they did not deny that <term>Christ</term> <note>Jesus of Nazareth, the central figure of Christianity.</note>, our Savior, was a great, divine, and most wise man who had taught things that were plainly outstanding and divine, and that after he had been killed by the Jews through a most unjust punishment, he had passed into heaven to the Gods. That great teacher of this Platonic school, <term>Porphyry</term> <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonic philosopher and one of the most sophisticated intellectual opponents of early Christianity.</note>, the same one who wrote a massive volume against the Christians, honors <term>Christ</term> himself with the most ample praises; indeed, he even reports that the Gods proclaimed his virtue and wisdom. He also says—I quote the words of <term>Augustine</term> <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), an influential Christian theologian who quotes Porphyry in his own works to refute him.</note> (q)—good things, this philosopher [Porphyry], says about Christ; finally, as if about to bring forth something wonderful and incredible, he says (r): *“It would surely seem beyond expectation to some, what we are about to say. For the Gods have pronounced Christ to be most pious and immortal...”*

I) Augustine, whom we have followed, asserts that this oracle was issued by Hecate. However, Eusebius, who indicates he is reciting Porphyry’s exact words, attributes it generally to "the Gods." I believe this discord can be easily resolved. For anyone carefully comparing Augustine and Eusebius, it will immediately become clear that Eusebius, for the sake of brevity, omitted certain things in Porphyry’s speech that are provided in Latin by Augustine. And in those words which Eusebius omitted, the oracle is specifically attributed to Hecate. II) Augustine reads this oracle differently than it is read today in the manuscripts of Eusebius, as is evident from his Latin version: "*Since indeed you know how the immortal soul proceeds after the body, yet cut off from wisdom it always wanders; that soul belongs to a man most excellent in piety.*" <note>original Latin: "Quoniam quidem immortalis anima post corpus ut incedit, nosti, a sapientia autem abscissa semper errat, viri pietate praestantissimi est illa anima."</note> In my opinion, there is some flaw in this passage of Augustine’s; nevertheless, this does not prevent everyone from seeing that this interpretation does not correspond to the Greek words found in Eusebius. Let the critics look into this; for it matters little to our current purpose which of the two possessed the better reading.

### §. XXV.

In order to more strongly support these claims—which they were chattering about without witnesses or evidence—they called History to their aid. By citing examples from historical records, they attempted to prove that there had existed others besides <term>CHRIST</term> <note>original: "Christvm"</note> who were famous for the same miracles and wonders as he, yet who nevertheless continued to worship the Gods in a holy manner. They believed two points could be achieved by this. First: that a person should not immediately be considered a God simply because they performed many stupendous works beyond the power of other mortals, and therefore <term>CHRIST</term> should not be viewed as such. Second: that the worship of the Gods was being wrongly cast aside by the Christians (as if it had been rejected by <term>CHRIST</term> himself), since the most religious ministers of the Gods had been in no way inferior to <term>CHRIST</term> in their ability to perform miracles. 

When this way of philosophizing <note>Referring to Neoplatonism, a school of thought that often competed with early Christianity.</note> first arose, its followers were little concerned with ancient History and devoted themselves solely to contemplation. Later, however, when they saw that the biographies of our Savior were not only being read greedily, but were even strongly driving many people to adopt his teaching, they decided that this branch of learning would also be necessary and useful for themselves. And so, in the third century <note>original: "saeculo tertio"</note>, they applied their minds to composing the lives of philosophers, both ancient and modern. In these works—as is clear from those that survive—they had one single aim: to make those whose deeds they were reporting appear as similar as possible to our Savior. There exists a work by <term>PHILOSTRATUS</term>, a rhetorician of no small learning, concerning the life of <term>APOLLONIUS OF TYANA</term> <note>A 1st-century philosopher and teacher often compared to Jesus by early pagan critics.</note>, a Pythagorean philosopher; learned men have long since demonstrated that this work was written for that sole purpose...

...wherefore these things tend <note>original: "quorsum spectent," meaning what their ultimate goal or aim was.</note> cannot be unknown to those who are well-versed in the life and history <note>original: "vitam & Historiam"</note> of our Savior. Their aim, clearly, was to persuade those unlearned in such matters that nothing so miraculous had happened to our Savior, and nothing so divine or unique had been performed by Him, that certain philosophers of their own school had not also experienced or accomplished the same.

### §. XXVII.

I cannot, indeed, refrain from adding to these points that, although the Platonists <note>Specifically the Neoplatonists of late antiquity who competed with early Christianity.</note> agreed with Christians on the reality of the matter—contending not only that miracles are possible, but that they have been performed by many—a great difference nevertheless appeared between the two groups when they came to explain the doctrine of miracles more precisely. Christians asserted that it was not within the power of any man to acquire this ability for himself, but rather that the Supreme Deity <note>original: "supremum Numen"</note> bestowed it upon certain men whom He had freely chosen as administrators of His will. They held that God is not lavish with this gift, but only for the wisest of reasons—to prove and confirm truths necessary for the whole human race—does He typically equip certain individuals who are better and holier than the rest. These boastful "wise men" of ours, who wished to be called Platonists, disagreed entirely with these views. For first, they contended that there was no need for the help of the Supreme Deity for one who wished to either terrify or comfort mortals with wonders. They claimed there was a certain arcane and secret art; whoever took the trouble to learn it could, through words and other means, compel the lesser gods and spirits <note>original: "genios"</note> to obey his commands and disturb the laws of nature. With this same art as a mistress, they believed one could attain to conversations with the gods and the contemplation of things known to no mortal...

This highlights the intellectual conflict between late pagan philosophy and early Christian doctrine regarding the nature of the supernatural.</summary>

...any person might reach contemplation. They called this art <term>Theurgy</term> <note>From the Greek "theourgia," meaning "god-working"; a system of white magic practiced by later Neoplatonists to communicate with or evoke the presence of deities.</note>: concerning which, besides others, <term>PORPHYRY</term> *(m)* <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Phoenician Neoplatonist philosopher who was a prominent opponent of early Christianity.</note> and, following him, <term>AUGUSTINE</term> *(n)* <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), who critiqued Neoplatonic theurgy in his writings.</note> may be consulted. Finally, they maintained that a great and weighty cause was not always required for miracles to happen; rather, they claimed this entire matter depended on the will and judgment of the wise man, who, if he so wished, had the power to compel the lesser gods to be at his service. It is clear that men could conveniently abuse these doctrines to weaken the conclusions <note>original: "consectaria," meaning the logical consequences or inferences.</note> that the disciples of our Savior drew from His miracles. For if Christians had conceded that this doctrine of miracles was true, they would have been able neither to demonstrate His divine origin from the magnitude of the deeds performed by Him, nor to show the supreme majesty and dignity of the Master from the miracles performed by His disciples, nor finally to teach through His wonders that a new and heavenly wisdom—which no mortal could do without—had been delivered by Him.

### §. XXVIII.

It is beyond all controversy that this effort to establish a new philosophy and a religion at the same time—one that would not be exposed to the arguments of the Christians—brought much harm to our most holy religion. This movement stood as the cause for many either to turn back and return to their ancient outrages, or to persist in the superstition of their ancestors.

<margin>(x)</margin> [I see that] **EZECHIEL SPANHEIM** <note>Ezechiel Spanheim (1629–1710) was a prominent Prussian diplomat and scholar of ancient history and numismatics.</note> <margin>(y)</margin> and others group this **MAXIMUS** with the Cynics <note>The Cynics were a school of ancient Greek philosophers who rejected social conventions in favor of a simple, ascetic life.</note>. When I had seen him from a distance, I thought it was no one else but you.”* <note>original Greek: "ταύτης πλησίον τῆς πόλεως ἀπηντήσει κυνικός τίς ἀνήρ, ἐχών τρίβωνα καὶ βακτηρίαν τοῦτον πόρρωθεν θεασάμενος, οὐδὲν ἄλλὸ ὑπέλαβον ἢ σέ." But from this saying, it seems to me that nothing else can be concluded than this: that **MAXIMUS** was similar to the Cynics in external appearance and dress, and that he carried a pouch and a staff no differently than they did. This is hardly proof that he also loved the discipline of the Cynics or approved the dogmas of this sect. But though this **MAXIMUS** may have been a Cynic in certain habits and practices, it cannot be doubted that in doctrine and opinions he remained a Platonist. To say nothing of his writings, enumerated by **SUIDAS** <note>The Suda is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world.</note> and others, which clearly taste of the spirit of this "family" <note>original: "familia," here referring to a philosophical school or lineage.</note> [of thought], his early education first proves that this is the case. 

For he was not only a relative, but also the principal disciple of **AEDESIUS**, a most noble Platonist, who was so powerful in this kind of doctrine that he adorned the chair of **IAMBLICHUS**—the supreme teacher of the Platonic school—with extraordinary praise after his death, as **EUNAPIUS** testifies.

<margin>(a)</margin> Who would believe that **MAXIMUS** <note>Maximus of Ephesus (c. 310–372 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and a key advisor to the Emperor Julian.</note>, educated in the Platonic schools under such a great teacher, was anything other than a Platonist? There is also the fact—which in my judgment settles the matter—of the remarkable zeal he possessed for those arts which were called <term>MAGIC</term> <note>In this context, "magic" refers to theurgy, a Neoplatonic practice of rituals intended to invoke the presence of gods or spirits.</note>, and the ability to prophesy and predict future events which he claimed for himself. For there was a certain Maximus, says **THEODORETUS** <margin>(b)</margin> <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 AD) was an influential bishop and historian of the early Christian church.</note>, around that time, who wore the cloak of philosophy but practiced sorcery, and boasted of foretelling the future. <note>original Greek: Μάξιμος γὰρ τις ἦν... προλέγειν τὰ μέλλοντα σεμνυνόμενος.</note> *In those times there was a certain Maximus, a philosopher by profession, but devoted to magic arts, and who boasted that he himself predicted future things.* He was present with **JULIAN** <note>Emperor Julian (r. 361–363 AD), often called "the Apostate" for his rejection of Christianity in favor of Hellenistic paganism.</note> as he set out against the Persians, and by his false divinations, he ensured that the Emperor had not the slightest doubt regarding the success and victory of the war. Therefore, when matters later turned out far differently than **MAXIMUS** had prophesied, and **JULIAN** had perished miserably, the people of Antioch <note>Antioch was a major Roman city in Syria where Julian had spent a difficult winter facing public ridicule.</note>, as **THEODORETUS** reports <margin>(c)</margin>, cried out: *Where are your prophecies now, foolish Maximus?* <note>original Greek: πȣ͂ σȣ τὰ μαντεῖα, Μάξιμε μωρέ?; original Latin: Vbinam sunt vaticinia tua, Maxime stulte?</note> Not long after, he was publicly accused along with **PRISCUS** <note>Priscus of Epirus, another philosopher and friend of Julian who survived the transition to Christian rule.</note> of attempting to do away with the Emperors **VALENS** and **VALENTINIAN** <note>Valens and Valentinian I were brothers who ruled the Eastern and Western halves of the Empire after the brief reign of Jovian.</note> through magic arts. For this crime, whether true or invented, he would undoubtedly have paid the ultimate penalty <note>The Latin phrase "poenas capitales" refers to the death penalty.</note>, had he not been saved by the help of **SALLUSTIUS** <note>Saturninius Secundus Salutius, a high-ranking official who managed to maintain influence under several emperors.</note>, the Praetorian Prefect, and other friends. <margin>(d)</margin> However, he did not enjoy this good fortune for long.

I see that **EZEKIEL SPANHEIM** <margin>(x)</margin> <note>Ezekiel Spanheim (1629–1710) was a distinguished Prussian diplomat and scholar known for his work on ancient coins and his editions of Julian the Apostate.</note> and others group this great **MAXIMUS** <note>Maximus of Ephesus (c. 310–372 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher and advisor to Emperor Julian.</note> with the **Cynics** <margin>(y)</margin> <note>The Cynics were a school of ancient Greek philosophers who rejected social conventions and lived in ascetic poverty, often identified by their coarse cloaks and staves.</note>; but in my judgment, this opinion rests on a very weak foundation. Even if this **MAXIMUS** was a **Cynic** in some of his customs and practices, it cannot be doubted that in his doctrine and opinions he stood out as a **Platonist**. ->§. XXX.<-

Others, who were blessed with a more temperate disposition, were led by this kind of wisdom to strive to reconcile both religions—the Christian and the Pagan <note>original Latin: "ethnicam," referring to the ancestral polytheistic religions of the Greeks and Romans.</note>—though they were entirely different in nature. They forged a kind of mixed religion from the dogmas of the Christians and of other peoples, so that while they did not generally reject Christian rites, they nevertheless joined them with the worship of the Gods as explained by these philosophers. One might not unskillfully call this kind of sacred practice the *religion of the prudent* of that age. Unless I am entirely mistaken, most of those whose religion seems doubtful and uncertain to learned men were such reconcilers of religions; some counting them among the Christians, others among the Pagans...

However, after diligently weighing the arguments, I am convinced that one must take a middle ground and adhere to neither opinion. For while I frankly admit that in many places **CHALCIDIUS** speaks about several Christian dogmas <note>original: "dogmatibus," referring here to established doctrines or articles of faith</note> in such a way that he seems to value them highly, nor do I deny that he had read the holy books <note>meaning the Bible</note>, as he indeed testifies throughout his work; yet I see nowhere any clear evidence of a man who approves of the Christian religion in its entirety or considers it the only true and divine path. On the contrary, I see that he admits many things that sharply disagree with Christian sacred teachings, demonstrating a mind bound by the most shameful pagan <note>original: "ethnicorum," meaning Gentile or non-Christian</note> superstition. Among other things, he approves of the divinations of the nations, and teaches that *men are forewarned either by the flight of birds, by entrails, or by oracles, through the prediction of some well-disposed spirit <term>daemon: in Neoplatonism, this refers to an intermediary spirit between gods and humans, not necessarily an evil "demon" in the modern sense</term> who knows all things that follow in sequence.* <margin>(z)</margin> Indeed, I do not know what could be more opposed to Christian affairs, or more beneficial to the interests of the priests who presided over auguries, oracles, and sacrifices. For whoever attributes the power of prophecy to oracles admits the existence of Jupiter Ammon <note>An Egyptian-Libyan deity equated with the Roman Jupiter</note> or the Pythian Apollo <note>The god associated with the Oracle at Delphi</note>, albeit perhaps in a different way than the common people do; nor can someone who praises divination by entrails <note>extispicy, the practice of inspecting animal organs to discern the future</note> completely reject sacrifices and their rituals. Furthermore, he clearly defends **ARISTOTLE'S** opinion on the eternity of the world <note>The belief that the universe has no beginning or end, which contradicts the Christian doctrine of a creation "in the beginning"</note>, a noble...

### §. XXXII.

In a certain sense, one may join **SYMMACHUS** and **THEMISTIUS** to these—the latter being the most excellent orator and philosopher of his age. For both, although they worshiped many gods and vehemently opposed the abolition of ancient religions, did not do so in a way that suggested the Christian religion should be destroyed or abolished. Instead, they believed that there was no dispute between Christians and the "servants of the Gods" <note>original: "Deorum servos," referring to pagans</note> concerning the essence of religion, and that the inquiry was solely about the manner and method of divine worship. 

**SYMMACHUS**, when speaking to the Emperors on behalf of the Altar of Victory <note>The Altar of Victory was a traditional symbol of Roman state religion; Symmachus famously petitioned Emperor Valentinian II to restore it to the Senate House in 384 AD</note>, openly professes that it matters not by which rite one reveres the supreme Deity—the ancient Roman way, or the Christian way? He claimed that the questions debated between Christians and the worshipers of the Gods regarding the truth of religion were merely "the questions of idle men." He held that the supreme God had assigned to each nation its own guardians and guardian spirits <term>genios: protective spirits or tutelary deities associated with a specific person or place</term>, whom it is proper to honor with specific rites. This view is, indeed, entirely Platonic. 

*“Each,”* he says, *(f)* *“has their own custom, each their own rite. The divine mind has distributed various guardians to all cities. Just as souls are given to those being born, so fatal guardian spirits are divided among peoples. — — — What does it matter by what wisdom each person seeks the truth? One cannot arrive at so great a secret by a single path. But this is the DISPUTE OF IDLE MEN.”* <note>original: "OTIOSORVM DISPVTATIO." Symmachus is arguing that the underlying truth of the divine is so vast that no single religion can claim a monopoly on it.</note> Yet the Christian leaders could not be ignorant of how much ruin to the human race and the be-

Yet this philosopher had not devoted himself to the Gods in the manner of the common people, nor was he so hostile to Christian rites that he believed them to be entirely devoid of truth and hateful to the Gods. On the contrary, he believed there was no conflict between Christians and the "friends of the Gods" <note>A term often used for the practitioners of traditional Greco-Roman religion</note> regarding the foundations of religion: both worship one God and can please Him if they live chastely and honorably. He argued that God is not offended by a variety of rites and ceremonies, but rather takes delight in them. Therefore, both groups would act wisely if they bore and tolerated one another mutually, and if they worshipped and approached the supreme **Deity** <term>Numen: a Latin term for a divinity's divine power or presiding spirit</term> with equal sincerity of heart, even if their customs differed. ### §. XXXIII.

But these evils were only external; although they were harmful to the most holy religion and delayed its course, they did not corrupt its intimate nature, nor did they infect its very marrow, so to speak. But far more deadly diseases afflicted the Christian cause <note>original: *rem Christianam*</note> once this philosophy crossed the very boundaries of the sacred city <note>The "sacred city" here refers to the community of the Church</note> and made a home for itself in the minds of those to whom the instruction of the unlearned had been entrusted. For we have nothing so holy that has not been violated since that time, losing no small part of its ancient and natural form. From the innumerable examples with which this might be illustrated, it will suffice to pluck out a few. I would therefore wish this first to be held: that many of those who transferred themselves from this philosophy to Christian rites fashioned for themselves by their own wit a new and unique religion, which had not entirely lost the appearance of the philosophy they had professed before they [turned] themselves to the Christians...

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the Pseudo-Clementine Homilies, specifically focusing on the author's unique theological justification for baptism. <margin>(l)</margin> Our author no doubt felt great gratitude toward philosophy, which provided him with a defense against this very <term>cavillation</term><note>A formal word for a petty or deceptive objection; here referring to those who questioned the necessity of baptism.</note>, as he himself believed. However, with water, from the very beginning, the Spirit of God was joined—a fact that <term>MOSES</term><note>Referring to Genesis 1:2, "And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters."</note> himself testifies. And that this is so is proven by the fact that nothing is produced or grows, and nothing bears fruit, unless it is irrigated. Therefore, to extinguish and gradually diminish the "natural heat" by which men are carried headlong into vice, nothing is more effective than water; nor is anything more fruitful for the soul than frequent washings in the sea. In <term>baptism</term>, however, the invocation of the Supreme Deity and the recitation of the names of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit moves and drives the Spirit hidden in the waves to emit its power more effectively. This Spirit, therefore, along with the water with which a person is sprinkled, penetrates his very marrow and soul, and utterly and radically destroys all the fire of lust. <margin>(m)</margin> Here we have a very subtle demonstration of the efficacy of baptism; it is not too far removed from the decrees of the philosophers, many of whom we know held that water was the <term>first principle</term><note>original: "principio"; referring to Thales of Miletus and other Pre-Socratic philosophers who believed water was the fundamental substance of the universe.</note> of all things.

I have not yet mentioned the reasons by <unclear>which</unclear> he was led to publish these disputations under the venerable name of Clement, and to adorn the entire production with a story—<unclear>pleas</unclear>ant enough indeed, though in itself absurd—as if with a decorative garment. I am speaking here of men who possess mind and reason: for I do not deny that perhaps one or two from the flock of fanatics might have fallen into such a plan.

Therefore, whatever **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who defended the divine origin of these texts.</note> may say, the Egyptian priests seem to have prefixed the name of **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Egyptian wisdom.</note> to the books they themselves wrote for no other reason than to gain greater respect for their dogmas and precepts among the unlearned. Whether they meant it in this sense—that **Hermes** himself composed them—or in this way—that the books were completed by the priests under the inspiration of **Hermes**, whom they proclaimed to be a God—it is all the same as far as this matter is concerned: in either case, the Egyptian leaders appear guilty of fallacy and <term>pious fraud</term> <note>original: "pii doli." Deception used for a supposedly "good" or religious purpose.</note>. 

The example of **Mnevis**, their most ancient King, sufficiently declares that this custom flourished among the Egyptians in the most ancient times: namely, to attribute to **Hermes** things they wished to have great authority in the state. **Diodorus Siculus** (y) records that when Mnevis wished to commend his laws to the Egyptians, he inscribed them with the name of **Hermes**, *pretending that Hermes had given these to him, as they were destined to be the cause of great benefits.* <note>original Greek: "προσποιηθῆναι δὲ αὐτῷ τὸν ἑρμῆν δεδωκέναι τούτους, ὡς μεγάλων ἀγαθῶν αἰτίους ἐσομένους."</note> He feigned that the laws had been delivered to him by Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes, often used interchangeably by Latin authors.</note>,

### §. XLII.

**Pythagoras**, who we are told eagerly followed the customs of the **Egyptians**, did not want to distance himself from this practice either. As his entire life demonstrates, he did not consider it forbidden to manipulate and mislead the common people. We need only consider the accounts that **Diogenes Laertius** <note>A 3rd-century biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> relates from **Hieronymus** and **Hermippus**; no further evidence is required. <margin>(z)</margin> These authors recorded that **Pythagoras**, seeking to reform the morals of the most corrupt commoners, hid himself away in a cave for a long time. Upon hearing this, the crowd abandoned their more serious vices. ### §. XLIV.

Where these things we have discussed so far are headed, no one, I think, is so dull that they do not already perceive. The philosophers whose cause is dealt with here, having received from the Egyptians, <term>Plato</term> <note>The famous Athenian philosopher and student of Socrates.</note> and <term>Pythagoras</term> <note>An earlier Greek philosopher who influenced Plato; he was often associated with mysticism and secret teachings.</note> that part of their wisdom which they themselves considered more sublime and excellent, also shaped their own character according to their masters' disposition in this matter. I believe that anyone who reads the Holy Scriptures and understands what it truly means to mislead and deceive will immediately notice that these examples taken from <term>PAUL</term> do not fit the matter at hand very well. My purpose here is not so much to refute <term>CHRYSOSTOM</term> as it is to reveal what he thought about "pious frauds" and where he sought the foundation for his opinion. *The power of deception is indeed great, provided it is not done with a deceitful intent. *Therefore, he would be worthy of the name of a true mocker and deceiver—whoever, in the thing itself, misuses it with an unfair and harmful mind—not he who performs it with right counsel. Furthermore, for the man who always walks the straight path, never deviating from it, it often happens that he becomes the author of many evils and inconveniences, even for the person for whom he did not intend any trickery.*

# THE SUBJECT MATTER.

§. I. The reasons why so many forged <note>original: "suppositorum"; referring to books falsely attributed to famous authors to gain credibility.</note> books appeared among the early Christians have not yet been sufficiently investigated.

§. II. Such books did not exist among the Christians until philosophers began to join their ranks.

§. III. Around the time of our Savior's birth, there existed a certain fanatical kind of philosophy in the provinces of the East.

§. IV. All those heretics who are called <term>Gnostics</term> <note>From the Greek word for "knowledge" (gnosis); these groups claimed to possess a secret, mystical knowledge necessary for salvation.</note> were devoted to this philosophy, and they are said to have had <term>Simon Magus</term> <note>A figure mentioned in the biblical Book of Acts who was traditionally viewed by early church writers as the first heretic and the father of Gnosticism.</note> as their father and founder.

§. V. For although these groups disagreed among themselves on various matters, they nevertheless shared common principles.

§. VI. Therefore, anyone who wishes to shed light on the history of the ancient heretics must, above all else, acquire a knowledge of <term>Oriental philosophy</term> <note>A term used by historical scholars to describe a blend of Persian, Babylonian, and Platonic ideas that permeated the Near East.</note>.

§. VII. These ancient heretics fabricated many books under the names of great men, partly to gain dignity and authority for their own philosophy.

§. VIII. They did this also to persuade the unlearned <note>original: "imperitis," meaning those without formal education or theological training.</note> that they were presenting nothing foreign to the teachings of Christ.

§. IX. The causes of this wickedness should be sought first in the defects of both their intellect and their will, but most especially in the decrees and dogmas of these sects.

§. X. The moral teaching of these men was clearly perverse and corrupted.

§. XI. This is evident from the very starting points of the discipline they followed.

§. XII. From these principles, wicked consequences could not help but follow.

§. XIII. They established that there were two kinds of human beings: one "animal" <note>original: "animale," referring to the natural or soul-led person who lacks higher spiritual insight.</note> and the other "spiritual."

§. XIV. The testimony of <term>Plotinus</term> <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who wrote a famous critique of Gnostic teachings.</note> regarding their wickedness.

§. XV. Certain observations are provided here to help investigate the remaining reasons that moved the Gnostics to forge books.

§. XVI. The older philosophers used to present one doctrine publicly to everyone, and another privately to a few chosen followers.

### §. I.

I intend to show briefly, as far as the obscurity of that age allows, the reasons why such a vast multitude of coarse <note>original: "inficetorum"; literally "unwitty" or "clumsy," referring here to the poor literary quality or obvious nature of these forgeries.</note> books appeared in the early centuries of the Christian era—works to which authors attached the names of great men, and even the name of **Christ** himself and his companions. We know generally that this "plague" <note>The author uses the strong Latin term "pestis" to describe the widespread distribution of forged writings.</note> arose because Christians—including those with sound views as well as those with misguided ones—believed they could gain greater authority for their opinions and attract more followers if they could demonstrate that the holiest of men, and even the founder of the Christian religion himself, favored their cause. *(a)* However, since the Christian religion embraced by these men utterly abhors wicked lies of that kind and has no need for such defenders, there is no doubt that there was something in their circumstances that led them to believe they were doing nothing contrary to truth and piety by crafting so many fictitious writings. And so <note>The Latin text ends with "Atque," which corresponds to the catchword "que" at the bottom of the page, indicating the sentence continues on the next leaf.</note>

->§. II.<-

As long as Christian doctrine remained within the limits of simplicity, and unrefined people lacking in formal education joined it, there was no place for such fabrications within the Christian community. ->§. V.<-

There is no reason for anyone to object that there is a significant difference between these sects in many matters—a fact that would be obvious to anyone who compared their various teachings. While I do not deny this at all, I completely reject the idea that my argument is weakened by these disagreements. I am not claiming that these sects were so much in agreement that no differences existed between them; rather, I only assert that the fundamental principles and beginnings—upon which each "family" built the rest of their complex systems of belief—were shared by all of them. I am not at all surprised that these people disagreed with each other so strikingly on other matters. 

First, I am convinced that among the Eastern philosophers who taught them, there were different schools of thought, just as there were among the Greeks. Furthermore, anyone who considers the great variety of human intellect will not easily deny that their methods of teaching varied; for some they were clearer, and for others more obscure. Moreover, when these philosophers converted to Christianity, they were not all of the same background or mindset. Some had previously been devoted to the Jewish religion, while others, rejecting Jewish customs, revered only the name and words of **Christ**. Because of this, a great deal of difference was bound to arise in many of their opinions—and indeed it did. I will demonstrate this further elsewhere, though any perceptive reader can see it for themselves. On the contrary, I would readily grant that these good men were sometimes deceived and occasionally attributed meanings or powers to the words of the heretics that the heretics themselves, if they were alive today, would reject. 

However, I can hardly forgive those who, despite lacking the deep learning necessary to judge this matter skillfully, nevertheless throw everything into confusion with insane shouts about the ignorance, malice, and greed for honor and profit of the *Fathers*. They cry out that nothing the Fathers did or said was in good faith, but that everything was done with evil deceit and treachery to stir up hatred against the heretics. 

As if we today could truly judge the motives of men who lived so many centuries ago—men otherwise distinguished by many virtues! Have we received permission from God to judge the internal thoughts of people long dead? What would happen if someone decided to repay these modern critics in kind, and judged their own words and deeds by the same harsh standard they use for the ancient teachers? 

But perhaps I will speak of this at another time. ...I shrink from accusations, nor do I feel that the **Church Fathers** <note>The influential bishops and theologians of the early Christian church, such as Irenaeus or Augustine, whose writings established orthodox doctrine.</note>, as they are called, always judged all matters fairly; on the contrary, I feel they frequently stained themselves with great errors. ...[for they believe] that because of their impious and filthy life, the **Gnostics** <note>A term for various early religious groups who emphasized secret knowledge as the path to salvation; they were often accused of extreme behavior by mainstream Christian writers.</note> were worthy of those insults with which we know they were attacked by ancient authors: <note>original French: "Ils ont été souverainement odieux: & les Peres les ont accablez d'outrages, que l' IMPVRETE DE LEVR VIE MERITOIT."</note> *They were supremely hateful; and the Fathers overwhelmed them with outrages that the IMPURITY OF THEIR LIFE DESERVED.* Others, however, either leave the dogmas—which these men considered necessary to believe—in their original contexts, or despise them as foolish and fanatical. Meanwhile, they labor greatly to prove that the Gnostics' moral teaching was purer than is commonly thought, and that their lives were not stained by as many crimes and disgraces as the Fathers blamed on them. 

There is, however, some difference of opinion among those who take this matter upon themselves. Some contend that these sects were not entirely free from every crime; yet they think those foul disgraces and horrific practices that are said to have flourished among them—such as holding women in common, sleeping promiscuously with anyone, and other even worse things—were unjustly charged against them and were fabricated by perversely religious men out of hatred for them.

**DESIDERIUS HERALDUS** <note>Didier Hérault (1579–1649), a French jurist and classical scholar known for his critiques of early Christian history.</note>, a most learned man, teaches this same point when he illustrates that passage of **MINUCIUS** <note>Marcus Minucius Felix, an early Christian apologist. The author refers to a passage in his dialogue "Octavius" where he defends Christians against false rumors of ritual murder.</note> in which those who slandered the Christians—claiming they were initiated into their rites with the blood of an infant—are refuted. Heraldus argues that the same mark of infamy was unjustly and rashly branded upon the heretics.

### §. XVI.

Since this wicked and perverse faction <note>Referring to the Gnostic sects discussed in previous sections.</note> perceived that **Christ's** discipline differed entirely from their own—even though they held nothing to be truer than their own views—they suspected that **Christ** and his messengers had taught something far different to their private, close associates and more intimate friends than what they had publicly proposed to the people and the disordered multitude. It was a custom for the greatest part of the Philosophers, especially those from the East, to set forth one far different doctrine publicly to whoever flocked to them without distinction, but to instill another privately to selected listeners, in whom they saw gifts of either the soul or the intellect, such as <term>discretion<note>original: *taciturnitatem*. This refers to the ability to keep secrets, a vital trait for the "secret discipline" (*disciplina arcani*) of ancient mystery schools.</note></term>. From this very method of teaching—which some judge praiseworthy while others condemn—the distinction between the *exoteric* <note>original: *exotericos*—public books intended for a general audience.</note> and *esoteric* <note>original: *esotericos*—internal or secret books meant only for the initiated.</note> or *acroamatic* <note>original: *acroamaticos*—teachings intended only for the ears of advanced students.</note> books of the Philosophers arose, as the learned **Ottavio Ferrari** <margin>(y)</margin> has taught. **Pythagoras**, who is known to have received many of his own ideas from the Egyptians and Chaldeans, spoke far differently among those he called *listeners*, differently among his *disciples*, and differently "inside the curtain" <note>original: *intra sindonem*. Pythagoras famously lectured from behind a curtain to his junior students, while senior initiates were allowed to see him.</note> versus "outside the curtain": a similar discipline flourished among other Philosophers, which the most learned men, **Melchior Goldast** <margin>(z)</margin> and **Johannes Scheffer**, <margin>(a)</margin> have most abundant- <meta>catchword: ube- (uberrime)</meta>

# TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED AND LEARNED YOUNG MAN, JOHANN CASPAR STRUVE, (*)
->SENDS HEARTIEST GREETINGS<-
# JOHANN LORENZ MOSHEIM!

Most distinguished STRUVE, you who have until now given many private proofs of your virtue, talent, and diligence, now demonstrate by a public example how much the teachings of those you listened to so attentively and constantly have mattered to you. Besides the study of <term>sacred letters</term> <note>original: "litterarum sacrarum"; a term for the study of the Bible and theology.</note>, which you have deservedly preferred above all else, History—especially sacred and literary history—has always greatly pleased you. For this reason, you wished to test the strength of your intellect on a subject drawn from the most ancient history of the Christian community—a subject that is indeed obscure and, like most ancient things, shrouded in darkness, yet most useful and worthy of a man who has devoted himself entirely to sacred wisdom. 

There are those who boldly assert that the Christians of the first centuries were equipped with every kind of fraud and evil art, and that they looked not so much to the truth as to their own convenience. There are others who say that the ancient teachers were covered "with the hide of an elephant, not their own," <note>original: "elephanti corio, non suo"; a metaphor for being thick-skinned or insensitive to moral truth.</note> as that character in **Plautus** <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC), a Roman playwright known for his comedies; his works were often quoted by early modern scholars to show off their classical education.</note> puts it...

I do not doubt that it could be done even more clearly if we weighed the records of that ancient age left to us with greater care and, following the example of wise men, joined deep meditation to our labor. 

What distinguished men complain about regarding the extreme obscurity of ancient <term>Christian History</term> is true. But perhaps it is also true that a greater light would be lit for it if those who approach the task of illustrating it would spend more time exploring the decrees of the **Philosophers** of that age—which, by some evil fate, were almost always coupled with religion—and would not rashly reject things simply because they do not harmonize with the customs and opinions of our own age. 

Consider those common arguments: 
*This is utterly absurd; therefore it is false.* 
*This man was endowed with mediocre talent; therefore he lied.* 
*This exists in only one writer; therefore it belongs to the realm of fables.* 
*None of his contemporaries mention it; therefore it never happened.* 
*A writer of meager wisdom narrates it; therefore it is a lie.* 
*It is repugnant to our customs and cannot be read without horror; therefore it ought not be believed.* 

These arguments, I say, which possess nothing solid except for their appearance, [have been used] more than...

# THE SUBJECT MATTER.

The approach to the treatise and its division. § I. The first part of the inquiry begins regarding the Emperors to whom the *Embassy* <note>original: "legatio"; this refers to the *Legatio pro Christianis* or *A Plea for the Christians*, the primary work by the 2nd-century writer Athenagoras.</note> was dedicated; the first argument in favor of Commodus <note>The son of Marcus Aurelius, who served as co-emperor with his father.</note> is presented in § II and defended against objections in § III and IV. A second argument taken from the book itself is proposed in § V and further explained in § VI. The argument made by Tillemont <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a French ecclesiastical historian noted for his rigorous use of primary sources.</note>, based on the mention of a certain Alexander in Athenagoras’s *Apologia*, is weighed in § VII. The objections of those who disagree—specifically those of Suffridus Petrus <note>A 16th-century Dutch scholar known for his work on ancient history.</note>—are refuted in § VIII. The argument based on the use of the term "philosopher" is examined in § IX, where a specific passage from Marcus Antoninus <note>Commonly known today as the Emperor Marcus Aurelius.</note> is also corrected. Three passages from the *Apologia* cited by opposing parties are discussed in § X, XI, and XII. From this, it is concluded in § XIII that everyone who claimed this book was written before the year 176 was mistaken. The second part of the inquiry, which proves this *Apologia* was written in the year 177, begins in § XIV. This view is supported by: (I) the fact that the world was at peace when ATHENAGORAS was writing (§ XV); (II) the passage where he states that slaves never testified against Christians (§ XVI); and (III) the passage where he addresses the Emperors as residing together in the palace (§ XVII). The conclusion follows in § XVIII.

### Section I.

Since knowledge of the date when **ATHENAGORAS** <note>A Christian apologist of the 2nd century AD, likely from Athens, who wrote a defense of Christianity addressed to the Roman Emperors.</note> presented his little book <note>original: "libellum"; referring to the *Legatio pro Christianis* (A Plea for the Christians).</note> on behalf of the Christians to the Roman Emperors can greatly assist those who wish to shed light on and explain the history of the Christians in the second century, I have decided to devote some effort to establishing the year this book was written. Indeed, a long controversy has flourished regarding this question among experts in these matters and those skilled in ancient history. As far as I know, no one has yet appeared who could settle the matter so clearly that it becomes obvious which side possesses the truth. I certainly do not approve of the reasoning of that most ingenious man, **PIERRE BAYLE** <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a French philosopher and author of the famous *Dictionaire Historique et Critique*, known for his skeptical approach to history and religion.</note>, who concludes that because this controversy has not yet been resolved, neither of the dissenting parties has produced anything clear or evident. *(a)* For who is unaware of the character of men, who, even when everything shines with its own light, would nevertheless prefer to remain in error than to admit they have been wrong? Rather, I confess that certain arguments have been brought forward by some which, if rightly applied—

...if they are applied and proposed, they could successfully resolve the matter for the most part. Therefore, I say only this: not all the arguments in this case have yet been set forth; and those that have been set forth are neither sufficiently fortified nor so free from the objections of those who disagree that no doubt remains at all. I also add this: only more general matters have been thoroughly treated, and there has been less discussion about the specific year of this little book than about the Emperors to whom it is inscribed. Why this was done is easily understood when one considers that the conclusion of the former controversy depends on the latter, and unless the Emperors are certain, the year of the book dedicated to them cannot be certain.

My purpose now is to collect and weigh whatever has been said on this matter by learned men, so that it can be clearly judged which side truth favors. But I will also add certain new points, by virtue of which fairer judges will perhaps decide that the case has been fully pleaded. For this reason, I have instituted a twofold investigation. First, I shall inquire concerning the Emperors to whom this **Embassy** <term>original: *Legatio*; the title of Athenagoras's defense of the Christians</term> belongs, and I will show that those who think it was dedicated not to **Commodus** but to **Verus** <note>Lucius Verus, who co-ruled with Marcus Aurelius until 169 AD. Once this is done, all their conflicting opinions—those who contend it was written before 177 AD—will be displaced and overturned. Next, I will speak more diligently about the year, showing it to be 177 AD, the very same year in which the Gallic persecution <note>original: *Gallica vexatio*; a famous period of state-sponsored violence against Christians in Lyons and Vienne, Roman Gaul.</note> of the Christians took place, (*b*)

I will clearly show. The first investigation, although the footsteps of others are not lacking <note>i.e., others have attempted this path before</note>, will involve more difficulty. In both, I will conduct myself in such a way that light and clarity will not be found wanting, even in an especially thorny matter. There is one thing which I think should be mentioned for the sake of the inexperienced, who are accustomed to judge the skill of an author by the sheer number of books and writers they cite. I have examined almost all who have worked on this argument, but I will not name them all—only those who brought forward actual arguments or clarified this matter with their observations. My case will be no better if I weave together an ambitious list of those who agree with me. Nor will it be any worse if I show that many people were moved by the authority of those who disagree, or by other causes, to judge differently. I do not want names to be the focus, but reasons.

### §. IV.

But even if the name itself could not remove all our doubts, the titles that are attached to it certainly place this case beyond any uncertainty. The Emperors addressed by <term>Athenagoras</term> <note>A 2nd-century Christian philosopher and apologist from Athens.</note> are hailed as **Armeniacus** and **Sarmaticus**. ### §. VII.

To these arguments—by which it is established that, besides **Marcus Antoninus**, the *Apology* was offered to **Commodus** by **Athenagoras**—another reason is joined by that most learned and diligent man, **Sebastianus** 

<column-break/>

[Sebastian Le Nain de Tillemont], as well as those points which the most learned men, **Samuel Basnage** and **Wilhelm Ernst Tenzel**, have pointed out to confirm what we have said and to refute the overly clever interpretation of **Pagi**. Tenzel, in the passage cited from his *Exercises*, p. 450, observes that no passage from any writer can be produced in which **Verus** is called the son of **Antoninus**. Indeed, Pagi will provide no example where Lucius was called the son of Marcus; rather, he was always known as the "brother." Therefore, the same son is understood here who is called <term>pais</term> <note>original: παῖς — a Greek word meaning child or son, often used for a prince</note> at the end of the *Apology*: namely, Commodus. Basnage, in the cited passage of his *Annals*, Section VIII, p. 162, chastises **Pagi's** subtlety with more words and arguments: "Pagi's sharp wit," he says, "is of no assistance. — — To be sure, in a most elegant speech, Athenagoras transformed a brother into a son just to set up a comparison? By doing so, he would have made himself a laughingstock to his audience [he meant to say 'readers,' for **Athenagoras's** *Apology* was not recited publicly]. Therefore, for the comparison to fit, Athenagoras must mean the son who was born of Marcus, just as Christ is the proper Son of God. Furthermore, if the *Apology* of Athenagoras had been offered to Marcus and Lucius [Verus], the title of the *Apology* would have commemorated Commodus and Verus, the sons of Marcus who were already Caesars, just as the first *Apology* of Justin, which was addressed to [Antoninus] Pius, mentions Marcus and Verus. [There is less strength and clarity in this argument than in the former.] To these points is added the fact that these words of Athenagoras—*we pray that the son may one day succeed the parent in the kingdom* (we shall speak of these words below in Section IX)—are a most certain argument that Marcus had only one son at that time: specifically Commodus, since his brother, Verus Caesar, had already departed to the many <note>original: *ad plures abierat* — a Latin idiom meaning he had died.</note> after the death of Lucius Verus Augustus." This reasoning seems to me by no means negligible.

<meta>This page continues the author's argument regarding the historical context and dedication of Athenagoras’s "Apology." ### §. VIII.

No one who has duly weighed these matters will fail to admit that the case for **Commodus** <note>Marcus Aurelius’s son and successor, who reigned from 180 to 192 AD.</note> has been pleaded with more words than were perhaps necessary, and that the dispute has been settled. Now I shall make it my business to dismantle the arguments of those who defend the opposite side and favor **Verus** <note>Lucius Verus (reigned 161–169 AD), the co-emperor with Marcus Aurelius.</note>. **Suffridus Petrus** <note>A 16th-century Dutch scholar and historian known for his philological notes on early Christian texts.</note> long ago brought forward two reasons (*n*) which might persuade one that this Apology was perhaps dedicated to **Verus**. The first is this: it is very likely that at the very beginning of the calamities which the Christians suffered under **Marcus** [Aurelius], **Athenagoras** undertook their defense; and it is certain that these calamities had already begun while **Verus** was still alive. The second reason is drawn from the fact that **Verus**, while the Parthian War <note>A conflict between the Roman and Parthian Empires (161–166 AD); Lucius Verus oversaw the campaign from the East.</note> was raging, stayed in Athens for some time. From this, he concludes that because **Verus** was present, the Christians who were in Athens were harassed by far more severe miseries. If this were certain, he also thinks it would not be far from the truth that these distresses prompted **Athenagoras**—whom he believes lived in Athens—to record his little book in writing and present it to **Verus**.

You see here a heap of dry and weak suspicions, which I have nevertheless arranged in such a way that they might appear to have some value, however slight. If I wished to subject them to the laws of sound reason, they would vanish into smoke without delay. But the father of these ideas has spared me the trouble, as he himself confesses they are not very strong. Therefore, I will not waste time in examining them, which can be better spent elsewhere.

### §. VIII.

No one who has properly considered these points will fail to admit that I have argued more than enough in favor of **Commodus** <note>Emperor of Rome from 180 to 192 AD</note> and that the case has been fully pleaded. Now, I shall turn my efforts toward dismantling the arguments of those who take the opposing side and favor **Verus** <note>Lucius Verus, who co-ruled with Marcus Aurelius until 169 AD</note>. **Suffridus Petrus** <note>A 16th-century Dutch scholar and historian known for his philological work</note> long ago put forward two reasons *(n)* that might perhaps persuade one that this *Apology* was dedicated to **Verus**. The first is this: it is highly likely that **Athenagoras** undertook the defense of the Christians at the very beginning of the calamities they suffered under **Marcus** <note>Marcus Aurelius, known for his Stoic philosophy but also for the persecution of Christians during his reign</note>; and there is no doubt that these calamities had already begun while **Verus** was still alive.

The second reason is drawn from the fact that **Verus** stayed in **Athens** for some time while the Parthian War <note>A conflict between the Roman Empire and the Parthian Empire in the mid-2nd century</note> was raging. From this, he concludes that in **Verus's** presence, the Christians who lived in Athens were harassed by far more severe miseries. If this is indeed certain, he believes it is also quite plausible that these hardships stirred **Athenagoras**—whom he assumes lived in Athens—to commit his short work to writing and present it to **Verus**. 

You see here a collection of dry and weak suspicions; nevertheless, I have arranged them so that they might appear to have some value, however slight. If I were to hold them up to the standards of sound reason, they would vanish into smoke immediately. However, the author of these arguments himself has saved me the trouble, as he admits they are not particularly strong. Therefore, I will not waste time scrutinizing them when that time could be better spent elsewhere.

I shall now move on to those arguments brought forward by others who are somewhat more refined in their learning. <margin>(r) There is a very troubled passage in **Marcus Aurelius**'s *Meditations* <note>original: "ad se ipsum" (To Himself)</note>, Book 1, § XIV, p. 16 of **Gataker**’s edition, which has exercised the wits of many scholars. In it, the Emperor praises "his brother Severus" <note>original Greek: "τον αδελφον ου Σεβηρον" (*ton adelphon ou Seberon*)</note> among his teachers and declares that he learned much from him. If we were to rely solely on the corrections of great men such as **Scaliger**, **Salmasius**, **Baronius**, **Casaubon**, and others, this statement by **Aurelius** would result in our **Verus** being assigned a certain rank and place among the philosophers. Indeed, since Marcus had no other brother, they advise that one should undoubtedly read "Verus" <note>original Greek: "Ουηρος" (*Oueros*), as the name Verus is commonly written by the Greeks</note> instead of "Severus." But, as **Gataker** <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), an English scholar and theologian known for his critical edition of Marcus Aurelius</note> correctly pointed out, it is highly unlikely that any of the qualities the Emperor praises in that passage could be said of this man of most shameful life; furthermore, there is no clear reason why Marcus would place a brother in the middle of a list of his teachers. Philosophers whom he studied under precede the mention, and others follow. Who could be persuaded that Marcus would inappropriately group an adopted brother into such a choir? Therefore, I believe a different remedy must be sought for this "unhealthy" passage. My opinion is that the words "the brother," which I suspect were written in the margin by some unskillful person and later crept into the actual text, should be struck out entirely. It should simply read "from Severus" <note>original Greek: "παρα Σεβηρου" (*para Seberou*)</note>, as Marcus is accustomed to speaking. Many examples show that the Greeks and other ancients frequently confused the names of **Severus** and **Verus**, as the great **Scaliger** <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a foundational figure in modern textual chronology and philology</note> among others demonstrated. Therefore, when someone not very skilled in history encountered the name "Severus" in his manuscript, he fell into the common error of thinking it meant this **Verus**...</margin>

These words were added later to the text itself quite carelessly, as has often happened. Nor do I doubt that if we had more handwritten manuscripts, this error and its source would be even more evident.

Furthermore, that **SEVERUS** is none other than **CLAUDIUS SEVERUS**, the **Peripatetic** <term>A follower of the philosophy of Aristotle</term>, whom **JULIUS CAPITOLINUS** recorded as being among the teachers of **MARCUS** (*in his Life, chapter III, page 58*). **GATAKER** <note>Thomas Gataker, the 17th-century English critic mentioned on the previous page</note> had already considered this, but he was troubled by the words "of my brother"; he understood that if these words were to fit any of this Emperor’s teachers, they would suit **JUNIUS RUSTICUS** far better than this man, with whom he was not particularly intimate.

Our correction removes this difficulty. Indeed, it gains no small strength from the fact that while **MARCUS** reviews all the philosophers he listened to in this book of his commentaries <note>referring to the first book of the *Meditations*</note>, and diligently explains what he drew from each one, he does not make even a single mention of this **CLAUDIUS SEVERUS**, even though it is certain he was among them.

I once thought that the Emperor, whose style of speaking is quite concise, might have implied the word "teacher" <note>original Greek: διδασκάλου (*didaskalou*)</note>, so that the full sentence would flow thus: "from the teacher of my brother Severus" <note>original Greek: παρὰ τοῦ διδασκάλου τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ μου Σεουήρου (*para tou didaskalou tou adelphou mou Seouērou*)</note>, which he would have expressed more briefly as: "from my brother’s [teacher]." In this way, this **SEVERUS** would be called the teacher of both **VERUS** and **MARCUS** at the same time. However, even if I set aside the fact that **SEVERUS** does not appear among the teachers of **VERUS** whom **CAPITOLINUS** lists (*in his Life, chapter II, page 91*), anyone will easily see that what I wrote earlier is more probable.

<summary>The author argues that a confusing reference to "my brother Severus" in Marcus Aurelius’s writings is a scribal error, identifying the person instead as the philosopher Claudius Severus. This textual criticism is used to support the broader argument that titles and names in ancient manuscripts were often incorrectly interpolated.</summary>

### §. X.

Learned men proceed to the book itself and present three primary arguments drawn from it, by which they hope to prove that it was not dedicated to **Commodus**. The first is the argument that the philosopher <note>Athenagoras</note> attempted to instruct the Christians. *Lampridius* writes in the *Life of Commodus*, chapter I: <note>original: "Quanquam tot disciplinarum magistri nil Commodo profuerint: at neque etiam Lucio fratri Marci emolumento fuit ea disciplina, qua educatus; cum mores imbiberit a sapientia alienissimos."</note> "Although many masters of various disciplines were of no use to Commodus: that same education was also of no benefit to Lucius, the brother of Marcus, for he absorbed habits that were utterly foreign to wisdom." Since **Commodus** was a "philosopher" by his formal education and was born to a philosopher father <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>, why would Athenagoras not have honored him with this noble and beautiful title? This would be especially likely at a time when the vices of Commodus were not yet known, and in a speech where this man—a Greek and an Athenian—was heaping on much praise to win the favor of the princes. As he wrote in that very *Apology*: "But what need is there to examine either the songs of poets or the opinions of others in your presence, you who have scrutinized every kind of literature?" 

Even if these words were applied to Lucius Verus <note>The co-emperor with Marcus Aurelius from 161–169 AD</note>, the speech is exaggerated beyond measure: "For I know that as much as you surpass all in intelligence and the power of the empire, so much you also excel in the exquisite knowledge of the sciences, being so well-versed in individual parts of wisdom that you are in no way inferior to those who have chosen only one particular thing to cultivate." Therefore, the Christians could, by the best right, pray to God that he might fortunately obtain power not only while his parent was living, but also after his death. For the word *to succeed* <note>original: 'διαδέχεσθαι' (diadechesthai)</note>, which Athenagoras uses, properly signifies succession in an inheritance after the death of another. In this, there is a pursuit of singular goodwill, since senior Princes desire nothing more in their prayers than that their sons should eventually succeed them—well aware that their children could be snatched away by the force of fate before the parents, even if they are already designated successors or colleagues. [Peregri]nus <note>The text begins mid-word, referring to Peregrinus Proteus, a Cynic philosopher who famously immolated himself.</note> threw himself onto the funeral pyre before the death of **Lucius Commodus** <note>Also known as Lucius Verus, co-emperor with Marcus Aurelius.</note>. Therefore, in the same Olympiad <note>A four-year period used in Greek dating; Peregrinus died in 165 AD, during the 236th Olympiad.</note>, **Peregrinus** threw himself into the fire, and the *Apology* of **Athenagoras** was presented to the Emperors. But, in order to prove that this burning was then a very recent event, he summons another defense for his position: namely, the inscription <note>The formal dedication at the beginning of the manuscript.</note> of the book. He places at the very start of his argument that point which has already been dismantled by us: that the work was dedicated to **VERUS** in addition to **MARCUS**. He reasons as follows:

Yet **VERUS** passed away <note>original Latin: "ad plures abiit," a classical idiom meaning "went to join the many," i.e., died.</note> in the year 169 AD, three years after this man’s death. Therefore, at the time when **ATHENAGORAS** was writing, the fate of **PROTEUS** <note>Another name for Peregrinus.</note> was recent. Therefore, he defended the Christians in the same Olympiad in which the philosopher burned himself. 

This reasoning would indeed be entirely correct if the first premise from which it is drawn were certain—namely, that this *Apology* actually pertains to **VERUS**. However, the learned men with whom we are dealing are far from accepting this; they want these very words to serve as proof in themselves, and they claim the words were phrased in such a way as to establish that the event he speaks of had been carried out just a little while before. Next, it should also be noted that **SCALIGER** did not accurately establish the year of our *Apology*, an opinion I see held by certain others besides **BAYLE** (*h*).

The first leaders of the Christian churches *imitated the customs and institutions of the pagans in many matters. § I.
