### §. I.

The ancient teachers and the first founders of the Christian community <note>Often referred to as the "Church Fathers," these were the influential theologians and bishops of the first few centuries of Christianity.</note> frequently encounter criticism because they adapted many of the rituals and institutions of that most pure worship—which they performed for God with a sincere mind—to the profane decrees and ceremonies of the pagans, doing so more than was appropriate. That this blame is not entirely unjust is testified and shown by so many choice authorities of grave and wise men. But while these most learned men were diligent and vigorous in pointing out the faults of the Christians and demonstrating their zeal for imitating the pagans <note>original: *ethnici*; literally "the nations," used here to mean non-Christians or polytheists.</note>, I do not know why they have been much more sluggish and remiss in identifying the institutions of the pagans that were derived from an imitation of Christian discipline. ...[it seems] that the pagans worked with even greater zeal to ensure they were not unlike the Christians, than the Christians did in adapting profane pomp and display to their own purposes. Nor do the pagan writers themselves sometimes conceal this fact—as we shall see shortly—nor do they fear that it will be held against them as a fault. What of the fact that the Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (ruled 361–363 AD), the last pagan emperor, who attempted to revive traditional Roman religion to counter the spread of Christianity.</note>, than whom the Christian cause had no more bitter enemy, did not hesitate—as will later be made clear—to exhort his followers to imitate the Christians and to entice them with refined words? I believe this entire matter has been treated rather negligently by very learned men and handled by almost no one, because the discipline of the pagans after the birth of Christ is more obscure today than that of the Christians. Added to this is the fact that the writings of the Platonic philosophers <term>Platonic philosophers: specifically the Neoplatonists like Plotinus or Porphyry, whose complex metaphysical works often reacted to or incorporated Christian thought.</term>, from which we must primarily draw here, do not recommend themselves either by the pleasantness of their style or the order and choice of their subjects, nor are they as commonly known as the books of the Christians. (*b*)

(*b*) These things are not to be understood as if no learned men before me had perceived that the pagans took many things from the Christians to adorn their own religion. ### §. IV.

Therefore, as I am about to depart from this illustrious **seat of learning** <note>original: *literarum sede*; a common academic reference to a university or academy</note>, and since I have decided to render an account of the time I have spent here through a public demonstration of my studies, I have determined in my mind to touch upon some part of this argument in a special commentary. I do not consider myself to be the kind of person who is capable of exhausting this subject or treating it according to the true excellence of the matter. Rather, this plan is intended to rouse others, who are more learned than I and more practiced in reading the ancient authors, to devote more leisure and industry to this topic than has been done thus far.

I would not want anyone to expect from me everything that could possibly be said on this cause. Neither do these thin pages contain the vastness of the subject, nor have I yet been able to cultivate such a close familiarity with the ancient authors as someone ought to possess who intends to explain this entire matter in full. I will provide only a very small specimen, of the sort common among those who, having just entered the first stages of their studies, possess more will and zeal than they do strength.

The path I have decided to follow will be this:
1. First, I will show that the Christians' style of speaking was pleasing to foreign <note>original: *exteris*; referring to non-Christian or pagan authors</note> writers.
2. Next, I will demonstrate that the philosophers made certain **doctrines** <term>dogmata: the foundational and authoritative principles of the Christian faith</term> with which the Christians were imbued almost their own.
3. In the third place, I will add that the very facts and actions upon which the Christian religion rests served as an example for the **pagans** <term>ethnici: a term for those practicing traditional Greco-Roman religions rather than Christianity or Judaism</term> to imitate.
4. Having done this, I will take it upon myself to indicate the agreement between the two in terms of external discipline, rites, and ceremonies, by providing a certain specimen.

Grant, O most kind Divinity of God, that from this labor—though it be meager and thin—some benefit may remain for the city of **Jesus Christ** <note>This refers to the "City of God" or the collective body of the Christian Church</note>.

### §. V.

A comparison of the style of writing, as I promised, will form the beginning of this exercise. For after the Lord added a greater number every day to the community of those who professed faith in **Jesus Christ**, the method of teaching and writing used by unbelievers took on a clearly different form than it had held before the birth of the Savior. No one can easily deny this, unless they have completely failed to examine the works of more recent philosophers, specifically the followers of **Plato**. For those who, during that span of time, expressed their thoughts on religious matters as worshippers of God—though an unknown God <note>original: *ignoti cultoribus*; a reference to the "Unknown God" mentioned by St. Paul in Acts 17:23</note>—seem to have almost stripped away their ancient ways of speaking.

On the contrary, the terms they use regarding God, the nature of the soul, the purification of the soul, the wretched state of corrupt man, and other matters, are of such a kind that it is clear they were borrowed from the divine writers of the New Covenant <note>The New Testament</note>, rather than being born in the schools of the ancient philosophers. I call as witnesses all those who are of the greatest renown among the pagans: the philosophers <term>Plotinus</term>, <term>Iamblichus</term>, <term>Hierocles</term>, <term>Simplicius</term>, and others. However, I contend that these later writers must be consulted and employed much more cautiously than the earlier ones, lest we rashly take these "apes of the Christians" <note>A common polemical term for Pagan philosophers who were accused of mimicking Christian ideas without having the faith.</note> as the true interpreters of the sacred books. But I note these things in passing; I return now to the point from which I digressed a little.

->§. X.<-

Before I demonstrate with specific examples in the second part of this work that the philosophers and the wiser individuals among the ancient worshippers of the Gods plundered the desks <note>original Latin: "scrinia compilasse," a metaphor for intellectual theft or plagiarism.</note> of the Christians to form certain of their doctrines, it will be helpful to note in general that the seeds of this accusation are found everywhere among the ancient Church Fathers. **Theodoret** *(e)* strives to show in many ways that those who wished to appear as masters of wisdom among the outsiders <note>A term often used for those outside the Christian faith, i.e., Pagans.</note> were actually followers of the Christians. He also compares **Porphyry** *(f)* to an ape, because just as an ape imitates human gestures and manners, so did this man emulate the Christians. **Basil the Great** *(g)*, **Eusebius** *(h)*, and—

The opinion of the man who not long ago took great pains, with an impressive display of learning, to free the Church Fathers from the charge of Platonism is quite close to this; he is a most erudite man from the Jesuit family, **François Baltus**. <gloss>(l)</gloss> I, however, believe that one must judge cautiously and with foresight. For if anything was common and customary among the early leaders of the church, it was that they rashly saw the footprints of Holy Scripture wherever they perceived even the slightest appearance of a relationship between the Savior's teaching and the beliefs of the pagans. To bring forward one example out of many, **Augustine**, <gloss>(m)</gloss> asserts that he found everything in the books of the Platonists that the divine man **John** teaches regarding the *substantial word of God* <note>original: "substantiali Dei verbo," referring to the "Logos" or the Word mentioned in the opening of the Gospel of John.</note>. If this were true, there would be no doubt that they had stolen these things from Sacred Scripture. But the most learned man, **Jean Le Clerc** <note>A prominent Genevan theologian and scholar.</note>, writing under the name of **Joannes Phereponus**, has already wisely and skillfully observed that the empty sound and similarity of words cast a kind of cataract <note>original: "glaucoma," a medical term used here metaphorically to describe a blurring of vision or a deceptive veil.</note> over the eyes of **Augustine**. *“Deceived by the similarity of some words and sentences,”* he says, <gloss>(n)</gloss> *“Augustine, like many Greek writers, mixed Platonism with Christian doctrine.”* Therefore, not everything that the Fathers left in writing concerning these matters should be believed; however, as far as the heart of the matter is concerned, there is no doubt that these pagans diverted many things into their own gardens from the streams of the Christians. We shall now confirm this with several examples.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the history of religious thought, moving from the specific critiques of the Church Fathers to a broader comparison between ancient "heathen" polytheism and the shift toward clearer theological concepts following the advent of Christianity. ->§. XI.<-

In general, from the time of our **Savior’s** <note>original: "salutaris redemtoris" (saving redeemer)</note> arrival, the ancient beliefs of the nations regarding the religious worship of deities underwent various changes, and under **Christian** guidance, they took on a much more honorable and better form. Before **CHRIST**, none of the people sitting in darkness <note>A common biblical metaphor for those living without the knowledge of the Gospel.</note>—neither the high-born nor the lowly—clearly and distinctly understood how they should think about the multitude of Gods they professed to follow. Instead, they nourished their minds with portents and nonsense, which were more harmful the further they were removed from all reason. 

Most believed that the Gods were of the same kind, rank, and nature, and they did not consider one better or more excellent than another. They established that the first Gods were born from **Chaos** <note>In Greek mythology, the void state preceding the creation of the universe.</note>, and the rest were born from the marriages of the primary Gods, especially from the union of **Saturn** and **Rhea**; any reader of **HESIOD’S** *Theogony* <note>A poem by the Greek poet Hesiod (8th century BCE) describing the origins and genealogies of the Greek gods.</note> will learn this. Moreover, they thought that **Jupiter** <note>original: "Iovem"</note>, the younger son of **Saturn**, held power over the rest of the Gods and men, not by natural law, but by the favor of the other Gods, whom he was believed to have freed from **Saturn’s** belly through trickery and cunning <note>Referring to the myth where Saturn/Cronus swallowed his children and Jupiter later forced him to disgorge them.</note>. For this reason, they called him the *Parent of Gods and Men* <note>original: "Parentem Divum hominumque"</note>. (o) 

Others, wishing to far surpass these in wisdom, named one certain and supreme God, who would use the labor of many spirits <note>original: "geniorum"</note> of an inferior nature in governing the world. But remarkably, these same people did not exempt the Lord of laws from the laws themselves, but bound him to a certain order of fate and nature. It suffices for this one

<term>RALPH CUDWORTH</term> <note>A 17th-century English philosopher and leading figure of the Cambridge Platonists, known for his work "The True Intellectual System of the Universe"</note> (*q*) and <term>JEAN LE CLERC</term> <note>A prominent Swiss theologian and scholar of the Enlightenment</note> (*r*) and others have debated this; no one would easily call it into doubt. ### §. XIV.

What we have said shines forth even more clearly from those who wrote from a Pagan <note>original: *Ethnicis*</note> perspective after the controversies regarding the Trinity were stirred up among Christians by **ARIUS**, a Priest of Alexandria. ### §. XV.

It is very well attested among those who are skilled in ancient history and opinions that almost all the ancient philosophers who acknowledged a God associated eternal matter with this supreme Divinity <term>Numen</term> <note>original: "Numini". In this context, "Numen" refers to the divine power or essence of the supreme deity.</note>. Indeed, there were already long ago some among the Church Fathers who... <note>original: "prae-". The text breaks here to accommodate a long footnote, continuing the thought from the previous page.</note>

---

...observations <note>original: "vationibus", the conclusion of "observationibus" from the previous page</note> on this passage, Volume II, *Works*, page 534. He says: "What the Holy Scriptures and the early Church Fathers handed down concerning the true and only Son of God, **ARISTIDES** <note>Aelius Aristides (117–181 AD), a famous Greek orator who wrote a celebrated hymn to Minerva (Athena).</note> clearly distorts these in favor of **MINERVA**. The dogmas regarding the production of the goddess from the very substance of her father, her perpetual coexistence with him, and her work and counsel employed in the creation of things—all these he adapts to the Christian mindset." The same opinion is held by that most learned man, **JACOB ELSNER** <note>Jakob Elsner (1692–1750), a German theologian and philologist.</note> in his *Sacred Observations on the Books of the New Covenant*, Volume I, page 308. There he says: "Namely, so that the pagans might more strongly oppose burgeoning Christianity, they applied a mystical sense to their fables about the Gods—something I remember **TERTULLIAN** <note>An influential early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–240 AD).</note> also observed somewhere—and they attributed those things to their Gods, and especially to Minerva, which Christians preached about Christ." And this distinguished man pursues this very point at length in that passage, where he compares the words of **ARISTIDES** with the sayings of the sacred books regarding **CHRIST**. Add also what **EZEKIEL SPANHEIM** <note>Ezekiel Spanheim (1629–1710), a prominent Swiss-Prussian diplomat and scholar of ancient coins and texts.</note> brought to illustrate the same passage in his *Commentary on Callimachus’ Hymn to Pallas*, page 643. This opinion does not lack a great appearance of truth. It is, of course, incredible that the divine writers took from the older Greek authors (who are now lost) the formulas and modes of speaking by which they expressed the nature and glory of our **SAVIOR**; therefore, it remains for us to conclude that these praisers of the Gods drew their own ideas from the Christians.

The more recent scholars, however—if I may be permitted to judge—did not always correctly understand the sayings of the ancients. On one hand, they included among the proponents of creation out of nothing those who devised some sort of eternal **emanation** <term>emanatio</term> <note>The philosophical concept that the world flows out from the divine essence, like light from a sun, rather than being a distinct act of creation from nothing.</note> of matter from God. On the other hand, they misinterpreted what is read in **PLATO** and others concerning the composition and arrangement of matter, wrongly taking these descriptions to mean this type of creation.

If I wished to be more extensive and demonstrate through a specific example how eager the pagans <note>original: "ethnici"</note> were in imitating the moral precepts of the Christians, I would select their prayers above all others. ->§. I.<-

I call upon YOU as judge, most learned man, in a controversy that requires YOUR particular expertise. The matter concerns sacred antiquities and the events that occurred in the early times of the community of our Savior <note>original: "Servatoris"; a common Latin term for Jesus Christ</note>, a subject in which there is hardly anyone more skilled than YOU. You know there are very many today who, relying on the reasoning of most learned men, favor the former opinion [the denial]. The other [assertion] pleases me, for significant reasons, which I intend to lay out to YOU with the hope that they might not be immediately approved, but carefully weighed by anyone—and especially by YOU, most distinguished man.

### §. V.

The existence of this sect rests on the consensus of all antiquity, which no one denies should not be rejected rashly or without the greatest force of reason. However, unless my mind deceives me, it seems to me that these most learned men <note>The skeptics mentioned on the previous page</note> wish to argue that this sect is not actually proven by as many testimonies of the ancients as is commonly believed. They suggest that <term>Irenaeus</term> <note>A 2nd-century Bishop of Lyon and one of the most important early Christian theologians</note>—a man not entirely free from errors (*g*)—is the only one who first introduced the group to the public, having been led astray by misunderstood passages of the divine Revelation of <term>John</term> <note>The Apostle John, author of the Book of Revelation, which mentions the Nicolaitans in chapters 2:6 and 2:15</note>. Indeed, this was the view of the most learned man who reviewed <term>René Massuet’s</term> <note>A Benedictine scholar (1666–1716) known for his edition of Irenaeus's works</note> edition of <term>Irenaeus</term> in the *Leipzig Acts of the Learned* (*h*) <note>original: "Actis Eruditorum Lipſienſibus," the first German scholarly journal</note>. For, by accusing this Church Father of bad faith <note>original: "malae fidei"</note>, he transfers any blame for the fabrication of this sect to that holy man and his negligence. Therefore, before I proceed to the heart of the matter, we must examine what testimonies exist and how firmly the whole case rests upon them.

Following <term>Oecumenius</term> <note>A 10th-century commentator often called the "Father of Greek Catenae"</note>, they believe that the <term>Nicolaitans</term> are quietly criticized in 2 Peter 2:10–15 and the Epistle of Jude, verses 4, 8, and 12 (*m*). Indeed, even <term>John Lightfoot</term> <note>A 17th-century English clergyman and Hebraist</note> has been found to contend—based on a certain conjecture drawn from the vocabulary used—that Saint **Paul** had these people in mind (*n*). However, since there is no room for these suspicions unless it is first proven that heretics of this name actually existed at that time, it is clear that nothing can be settled by these arguments.

I will hold the same view regarding the evidence usually sought from <term>Ignatius</term> <note>Ignatius of Antioch (c. 35–107 AD), an early Christian martyr</note> on this matter. He mentions the <term>Nicolaitans</term> in two places, but only in those letters which the common consensus of scholars has declared to have been corrupted by the shameful efforts of an impostor (*o*). Therefore, these testimonies may depart along with their true author.

Yet, I am not unaware that a fairly ancient witness, <term>Stephanus Gobarus</term> <note>A 6th-century writer known for his work "Conflicting Opinions of the Fathers"</note>, includes <term>Ignatius</term> among those who, through their writings, brought the <term>Nicolaitans</term> to heel. For he says: (*p*) "<term>Ignatius</term> the God-bearer, <term>Clement</term> the Author of the *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Stromateus"</note>, and **Eusebius**..."

This is stated splendidly enough, if only it were true. It is claimed without basis that everyone held **IRENAEUS** <note>c. 130–202 AD, an early Christian theorist and bishop</note> as their sole source, until this can be proven by suitable reasons. Those who have once been imbued with a certain opinion tend to be fertile in conjectures; however, no value is assigned to these unless they rest upon their own supports. Did everyone perhaps believe **IRENAEUS** alone? What if they did not? I would believe it, if learned men could demonstrate that those writers wrote nothing except what they were able to draw from the revelation of **JOHN** <note>The Book of Revelation/the Apocalypse, where the Nicolaitans are first mentioned</note> and the books of **IRENAEUS**.

But how will that be accomplished? **IRENAEUS** is sparing with his words, for which I will soon give a reason. The other writers narrate far more. He explains their doctrine in only a few words. These others report the customs and opinions of the men much more fully and at greater length. Therefore, they must have been informed from somewhere other than from **IRENAEUS** alone, since they are far more detailed than he is. But these details are trifles, some say, which they added to the words of **IRENAEUS** according to their own whim. Again, proof is needed here. It is hardly credible that someone would lie in a matter of this kind without any cause. While the so-called <term>heresies</term> <note>From the Greek 'hairesis', meaning a choice or a sect; used here to denote groups deemed unorthodox by the early Church</note> are flourishing and in full bloom, they are frequently burdened with lies and insults. And there are some to whom this custom seems to be a matter of prudence—that is, a way to deter people so they do not rush headlong into the detours of wicked dogmas. But what cause could the good **Fathers** <note>The 'Church Fathers', the influential early Christian theologians and writers</note> have had to invent so many hateful crimes against the sect of the **NICOLAITANS**, or to devise so many monstrous opinions, long after the sect had been put to rest (as they indeed thought), and when there could hardly be any suspicion of danger or seduction? How much this shrinks from all truth, I ask you, most honorable Sir, that men, otherwise not foolish nor unlearned...

...learned men—I will not mention **EPIPHANIUS** <note>c. 310–403 AD, known for his work against heresies</note>, or **PHILASTRIUS** <note>died c. 397 AD, Bishop of Brescia</note>, and those like them, whom I would not deny may have given some weight to empty rumors—but **AUGUSTINE**, **EUSEBIUS**, **THEODORET**, and the rest? Indeed, I would easily grant that these excellent men may have mixed the <term>teachings</term> <note>original: 'placita'</note> of other wicked doctors with the errors of the **NICOLAITANS**, attributing to them things that ought to have been assigned to others. But the real question is: did they do this in every instance? And does everything they hand down belong to the realm of fiction? This will never be confirmed by sufficient arguments. For this line of reasoning suffers from an obvious flaw: "The Church Fathers did not distinguish the sect of the **NICOLAITANS** clearly enough from others which perhaps held similar views in some respects; therefore, nothing they record about the **NICOLAITANS** is true." Many things are blamed upon **SIMON MAGUS** <note>A figure from the Book of Acts often called the "Father of Heresies"</note> which might have been more rightly charged to others. Does it then follow that the man never existed, or that he taught none of the things he is said to have taught? Heaven forbid! This at least is manifest from these testimonies: that no one among the followers of Christ in former times ever doubted that certain **NICOLAITANS** truly caused disturbances at some point.

...they wish. At that very time, we encounter a most serious witness who, besides that, makes mention of the **NICOLAITANS** <note>An early Christian group mentioned in the New Testament (Revelation 2:6, 15), later accused by Church Fathers of promoting licentious lifestyles.</note>; I mean **CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA**, a man who, as everyone knows, was circumspect and learned. There are two passages in his writings where he mentions this sect so clearly that anyone who claims these details were merely copied from **IRENAEUS** <note>A 2nd-century bishop and influential theologian whose work *Against Heresies* is a primary source for early Christian history.</note> must be far from the truth.

Indeed, even if he were the only witness, I would consider it almost a sin to doubt the matter, for he is a man who can be shown by many examples not to have lent his ears lightly to idle gossip. For he teaches not only that such men survived even into his own age, and explains what their mindset was regarding sexual lust, but he even brings forward a saying of the holy man **NICOLAUS**: "that one must abuse the flesh," <note>Original Greek: *ὅτι παραχρήσασθαι τῇ σαρκὶ δεῖ*. What, I ask, most learned sir, can be justly raised against the testimony of this most upright man? One would have to say either that he copied Irenaeus, or that he fabricated everything according to his own whim, or finally, that he imprudently gave credit to uncertain and false rumors. However, any of these claims is so hostile to the truth and so difficult to assert that I believe they could not prove acceptable to learned men. That CLEMENT had read the books of IRENAEUS—

...that he had read them, I grant. Who, indeed, would dare to maintain that the good **CLEMENT** drew all these things out of his own imagination? <note>Original Latin: *ex suo cerebro deprompsisse*, literally "brought forth from his own brain."</note> Such a shameful attempt is so foreign to the character of this most learned man—as is clearly evident from his books—that anyone who has read them could hardly imagine such a thing even in a dream. On the contrary, the nature of his narrative itself is such that by its very simplicity, it can sufficiently repel this insult from its author. 

But some might say he was credulous, and drank in the rumors of men with greedy ears. Perhaps he was, perhaps not. We want arguments, not conjectures. But even suppose he was. The things **CLEMENT** narrates were being circulated among the people of that time. This at the very least is evident: that this sect was not unknown in those days. 

Did they know of them, as some say, only from the revelation of **JOHN**? <note>Referring to the Book of Revelation (the Apocalypse) in the New Testament, where the Nicolaitans are condemned in the letters to the seven churches.</note> But it is not likely that—while they were ignorant of everything else—they would have painted this specific sect, which could bring them no personal harm, in such dark colors. To this testimony, I add the words of that man who wrongly composed the *Apostolic Constitutions* <note>Apostolic Constitutions: A 4th-century collection of ecclesiastical law, falsely attributed to the 1st-century Clement of Rome.</note> under the name of **Clement of Rome**, in *Book VI, chapter VIII, page 339, Volume I of the Apostolic Fathers:* "Others loathe certain foods; but others now shamelessly commit fornication, such as those now falsely called Nicolaitans." <note>original Greek: ἄλλοι δὲ τινα τῶν βρωμάτων βδελύσσονται. οἱ δὲ νῦν ἀναιδην ἐκπορνεύουσι, οἷοι οἱ νῦν ψευδώνυμοι Νικολαΐται.</note> *Other heretics...*

<meta>The author continues to defend the structural integrity of Irenaeus's work "Against Heresies." Having previously noted that the sequence of heretics seems disordered, he now proposes a theory as to why: Irenaeus was following a list of questions sent to him by a friend, rather than creating a chronological history from scratch.</meta>

Therefore, the questions he was answering had been proposed to **IRENAEUS** <note>Saint Irenaeus (c. 130–202 AD), Bishop of Lyons and a key figure in early Christian theology.</note> by a friend. I believe that this holy man kept these questions before his eyes while he committed his work to writing. However, because these questions came from a man who was completely inexperienced in such matters, they did not follow a chronological logic; instead, they were written down just as they had occurred to the man’s mind. Consequently, **IRENAEUS**—who did not wish to change the order—produced a work that suffered from some confusion. This will likely not seem like a fabrication to those who have consulted the work itself, or at least the summaries of the chapters in the first Book, which are almost entirely made up of "Questions." I confess I am almost convinced that those very inquiries which the friend had presented to **IRENAEUS** were used as headings for various parts of his work, serving as the "answers." This is particularly true for the chapter on the **NICOLAITANS** <note>A sect mentioned in the Book of Revelation whose practices were condemned by the early Church.</note>, where the summary title asks: *What are the works of the NICOLAITANS?* In Greek, using words drawn from **JOHN** <note>The author of the Book of Revelation.</note>, that friend had phrased it this way: *What are the works of the Nicolaitans?* <note>original: "ἅτινα τὰ ἔργα τῶν Νικολαϊτῶν;"</note> Let these things be said in defense of **IRENAEUS**, as the occasion allows, even if they provide little direct help to our own argument. (c).

### §. XVIII.

Thus far, Most Distinguished Sir, I believe I have handled this matter in such a way that, having set aside the lighter and more recent arguments, I have established the existence of the **Nicolaitans** with certain arguments—specifically those which are usually considered the strongest in historical proofs of this kind. Indeed, in matters of fact such as this, if they contain nothing contrary to human reason, no greater proof can be demanded than to show that the witnesses were closest to the time when the events occurred, and were as far removed as possible from any suspicion of deception or carelessness. If, in addition, other reasons are added by which a matter called into doubt can be made clearer, then surely a man would be forgetful of his own judgment—to say nothing more severe—if he refused to accept them. 

And since I have not only used this method of proving, but have also removed the obstacles that presented themselves, I have achieved this much: unless I am mistaken, unless equal or even greater arguments are brought against mine, the victory is already established on our side. Therefore, I believe I must now look into these counter-arguments and weigh the reasons that moved far more famous men to adopt the opposite opinion.

While I do this, I would wish you to believe, Most Learned Man, most honored patron, and may everyone believe with **you**,

But on this point he clearly agrees with **Irenaeus**: that this impure crowd boasted of him as their "father." Clement says, however, that in his view, they wrongly claim him as their leader, since they have utterly perverted his righteous words and deeds. Thus, **Clement** is not at odds with **Irenaeus**:

Being challenged for this reason, he demonstrated publicly that he had fully restrained the movements of his soul. He showed that he clung not so much to his wife, as was suspected, but to the Lord. To better reveal these inner feelings of his mind to everyone, he granted his wife the opportunity to marry another, while he consecrated himself to perpetual **chastity** <note>original: *continentiae*; the practice of self-restraint, particularly regarding sexual relations.</note>. Suppose a pious man enacted for himself a law more severe than was just, following a plan that is not necessarily to be praised: is he therefore wicked because he was too pious? And who, I pray, is unaware that it was a most accepted custom among the early disciples of Christ to vow, by mutual consent, perpetual abstinence from the marital act? (t)

Once these facts are admitted, what could be easier than for men inflamed by wickedness and lust to pervert these actions—especially after **Nicolaus** had passed away—and adapt them to their own unspeakable crimes? That era was certainly filled with men who, though they had been initiated into Christian rites, wanted to be granted the license to commit fornication safely and to join in the profane feasts of the pagans. When their madness was restrained by the **Apostolic decree in Acts 15** <note>The Council of Jerusalem (c. 50 AD), which prohibited believers from sexual immorality and food sacrificed to idols; the author argues the Nicolaitans were looking for a way around these rules.</note>, and they were thus left without any defense, do you not think they searched for other loopholes to escape? It is a constant and widespread tradition among the ancients that **JOHN**, the disciple of the Savior, composed his Gospel <note>original: "Historiam suam," literally "his history," referring here to the Gospel of John</note> to oppose the deceitful traps of a certain madman—be it **CERINTHUS**, **EBION**, or someone else (**IRENAEUS** also mentions the **NICOLAITANS**) —who attempted to undermine the divinity of the Savior. Nowhere. 

Must we therefore conclude that there was no such adversary for **JOHN** to contend with; that all the ancient writers who recorded this were wrong; and that this divine man wrote his volume for no particular reason? Far be it from us to entertain such a thought. There are further points that could be answered, but for now, lest I become more wordy than is proper, they must be omitted. I add only this: No one can be certain whether the name of the **NICOLAITANS** did not emerge only after the *Acts* written by Saint **LUKE** and the *Epistles of the Apostles*. Among the sacred writers, **JOHN** was the last, all of whose works, as Chronology shows, were written as the first century was already coming to a close. All of them (if you except **JUDE**, whose age is quite uncertain) preceded him in writing by many years. In short: whatever learned men may attempt, there are so many things to be resolved before they can fight with these weapons that their arguments ought rightly to be regarded as slight and useless.

### §. XXIX.

I have conducted the case of the **NICOLAITANS** to the best of my strength. With what skill I have done so, You, Most Distinguished Sir, and all the more prudent men with You, shall judge. There are perhaps some points still brought forward by those who think otherwise: but I have found these to be of such a nature that they can hardly enter the conflict due to their weakness. I preferred, therefore, to approach only those things which seemed of greater weight, rather than being a burden to the readers with every little detail. If, after the manner of some, I had wished to show off an infinite amount of reading, I could have set against myself a countless crowd of very famous men—especially the **Belgians** <note>original: "Belgarum." In the scholarly Latin of this period, this often refers to the people of the Low Countries, including the Dutch and Flemish</note>—and appealed to no few books. But let those who are led by such delights forgive me for not favoring their opinion, as I am not accustomed to increasing the number of witnesses where there is no need.

Let this custom be valid only when the truth of rituals or of **History** <note>original: "Historiae"</note> must be established. It is the mark of a prudent man, when a matter is disputed, to have regard for the arguments themselves rather than for the writers or some empty scrap of personal glory. It is the mark of a fickle mind to judge the nobility of a fight by the sheer multitude of those who disagree. I have taken these opponents for myself, as reason demanded, because they were particularly at hand, they had written most recently, they had gathered the most important points, and they flourish today in the praise of their erudition. I do not believe this will be turned into a fault against me—not by those most celebrated men themselves, whose learning I venerate, nor by **YOU**, most distinguished Sir, nor by any wise person.

For the rest, **Most Honored Patron** <term>Fautor: A patron or supporter of scholarly work</term>, I know that I am capable of error, and perhaps I have erred not lightly. For who of sound mind would take offense at such criticism? Its purpose is to pursue truth everywhere, to spare no mental infirmities, and to grant nothing to hatred or to favoritism.

Neither my salvation nor that of **Greece** <note>likely referring to the collective body of Greek scholarship or the Greek Church</note> depends on defending them. ### Section I.

What I wrote about the **Nicolaitans** <note>A group mentioned in the Book of Revelation, traditionally viewed as an early heretical sect</note> nearly fifteen years ago as a young man—written primarily to prove to the followers and disciples of **Johannes Cocceius** <note>1603–1669; a Dutch theologian whose "Federal Theology" influenced many scholars to see the Nicolaitans as a symbolic rather than historical group</note> that a sect of this name truly existed in the past—has been so far from displeasing to those experts in these matters that it has instead led several of those who previously agreed with **Cocceius** to change their opinion. As a representative of them all, I shall name a most learned man and a name of the highest rank among Reformed theologians, **Friedrich Adolph Lamp** <note>1683–1729; a prominent theologian and professor at Utrecht and Bremen</note>, who publicly declared that my arguments carried such weight with him that he no longer doubted that this group of Nicolaitans should be numbered among the other sects of the most ancient church. (a) From the theologians of our own circle <note>The author refers to his fellow Lutherans</note>, I could point out many who judged this youthful little study not unworthy of praise and considered it strong enough to blunt the arguments of those who thought otherwise. ### §. III.

And with these, I think I should also associate the once most famous and highly learned theologian of the University of Wittenberg, **JOHANN WILHELM JANUS**, although he wished to follow a somewhat new and singular *opinion concerning the Nicolaitans*. He published a specific *Dissertation on removing the Nicolaitans from the Catalog of Heretics* <note>original: "Dissertationem de Nicolaïtis ex haereticorum Catalogo expungendis"</note>: (k) in which he approves the opinion of those who believe that the name of the **NICOLAITANS** in **JOHN** <note>The Apostle John, in the Book of Revelation</note> is figurative. He refutes those who trace the name back to a specific man named **NICOLAS**, yet he does not contend—as do the followers of **COCCEII** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a theologian who interpreted the Seven Churches of Revelation as representing seven distinct periods of church history</note>—that the meaning of the letters which precede **JOHN’S** revelation is entirely mystical. Instead, he concedes that there existed in **JOHN’S** time certain wicked and criminal men to whom the holy man gave this name to show that they were similar to **BALAAM** <note>A biblical figure who led the Israelites into sin; the name "Balaam" in Hebrew can be interpreted as "swallower of the people," similar to the Greek "Nicolas" or "conqueror of the people"</note>. Thus far, he maintains the same view as **VITRINGA** <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a famous commentator on Revelation</note> and others. However, he has this point as his own and peculiar: he denies that these nefarious men, whom **JOHN** calls **NICOLAITANS**, were heretics <note>In this context, meaning a formal sect with specific false doctrines</note>. On the contrary, he judges them to have been impious and profane men who, although they professed our Savior with their mouths, nevertheless retained the ancient customs of the pagans. They did not consider it a sin to eat food consecrated to gods <note>Sacrificial meat offered to idols</note> or to engage in sexual immorality.

> For both, he says, (l) in the Apostolic age just as in the Mosaic age, were familiar to the pagans, and the latter was considered no less lawful than the former by the common people—indeed, it was even regarded as a part of religion. Hence many of the Gentiles, especially those from the East, having converted to the Christian religion, [found it] difficult [to turn away] from their long-established custom—

...way they were receding, and the more this flattered their **carnal desires**, the more they were inclined to excuse it. To be sure, this most learned man <note>referring to Johann Wilhelm Janus</note>—as he himself indicates at the very beginning of his Dissertation—attacks those especially who, in our age, have judged that the crime of heresy should more truly be placed in an immoral and wicked life than in opinions and beliefs turned away from true religion. Alternatively, he addresses those who decree that there are two kinds of heresy: one **theoretical** <note>heresy of belief or doctrine</note> and the other **practical** <note>heresy of conduct or lifestyle</note>. For since these people strive to confirm their opinion primarily by the example of the **Nicolaitans**—who, although they are held as heretics by everyone, are accused by **ST. JOHN** not so much for errors in religion as for an immoral life—he therefore thought he must act to completely expel the **Nicolaitans** from the order and number of heretics.

He therefore considers them to have been degenerate Christians living impiously, who were separated from other Christians not so much by their beliefs and opinions as by their morals and customs. Indeed, I would not want to make that controversy over **practical heresy** my own—which many wise men judge ultimately boils down to a dispute over the definition of the word *heretic*. Yet, I cannot help but indicate in a few words that I neither agree with those who think they have found an example of **practical heresy** in the **Nicolaitans**, nor do I entirely take the side of the learned man who attacked this view. I do not favor those who think the **Nicolaitans** were purely **practical** heretics. For even if I set aside the fact that **ST. JOHN** expressly attributes a certain *teaching* <note>original: διδαχὴν (didachēn)</note> or **doctrine** to the **Nicolaitans** in **Revelation 2:15**, nor what the ancients wrote concerning the perverse dogmas and opinions of the **Nicolaitans**...

<meta>This page continues the critique of Johann Wilhelm Janus’s view on the Nicolaitans. ...writers report, I might mention, it is well known that those who once considered it lawful to commit fornication and eat food sacrificed to idols, defended their practices by the help of "knowledge"—which they boasted had been granted to them, or **gnōseōs** <note>original Greek: $\gamma \nu \omega \sigma \epsilon \omega \varsigma$ (gnōseōs). This refers to Gnosticism, a movement that claimed "secret knowledge" excused them from traditional moral laws.</note>—*1. Cor. VIII. 1. etc.* and used certain dogmas as a pretext for their outrages and crimes.

Therefore, they were men infected with perverse and false opinions about God and religion, who allowed themselves to be led away into an impious life by these decrees of theirs. If distinguished men wish for those whom they call **practical** heretics <note>those whose "heresy" is found in their actions rather than their words</note> to be of this sort, there will be no reason for anyone to think they must dispute with them. For I do not think, I believe, that anyone would deny that wicked and perverse dogmas usually produce a life that is likewise contrary to God and religion.

And from this it is now clear why I do not entirely agree with that person <note>Janus</note> who denies that the **Nicolaitans** were heretics for the reason that they are rebuked by our most holy Savior in **John** <note>referring to the Book of Revelation, traditionally attributed to the Apostle John, where the Nicolaitans are condemned (Rev 2:6, 15)</note> primarily on account of their impious life. For I do not see what prevents a person from being called a heretic in the true and proper sense if they adopt and defend perverse and false dogmas with the intention of being able to live according to their own will and securely indulge their lusts—especially if, after being warned many times, they nevertheless persevere in their purpose. To me, indeed, such a heretic seems even greater and more detestable—one who joins wickedness of life with manifest and capital errors—than the one who, although living honestly, is nonetheless bound by great errors regarding divine matters.

### §. IV.

Those who deny that the **NICOLAITANS** received their name from a specific man <note>referring to Nicolas, one of the seven deacons mentioned in Acts 6:5, who was traditionally but controversially linked to this sect</note> and that they deserve a place among the ancient sects, nevertheless disagree among themselves regarding the origins of this word. **John Lightfoot** <note>1602–1675, an English churchman and Hebrew scholar known for using Rabbinical literature to explain the New Testament</note> suspects that this name was derived from the Hebrew word **nichola**. A very learned man, **JOHANN WILHELM JAN** <note>Johann Wilhelm Jan (1684–1726), a German theologian and historian</note>, thinks differently; he believes this name was given to this wicked "family" because it obeyed its own depraved and perverse desires and allowed itself to be conquered by them.

### §. VI.

...[they] had willingly hidden it, lest they incur public condemnation. It follows fourthly from these words that this group had a certain definite **teaching** <note>original: διδαχὴν (didachēn)</note> or doctrine, undoubtedly designed to defend the crimes and outrages they loved. To be sure, although their impiety was situated primarily in the fact that they considered it permissible to participate in the feasts usually celebrated in the temples of the Gods and to pursue prostitutes, there is no doubt—as I have already shown above from **1 Corinthians 8**—that they attempted to teach through theological or philosophical arguments and decrees that these two things were not at all opposed to the Christian religion. 

It appears fifthly from these passages that their morals and doctrine are compared with the morals and doctrine of **Balaam**, who is known to have been the one who prompted the Israelites to feast with the worshipers of the Gods and to contaminate themselves through fornication. From this, it is sixthly evident that this "family" was particularly hateful to God for two reasons: because it considered it lawful (and tried to persuade others) to participate in profane banquets and to enjoy the shameful company of lustful women. 

Finally, seventhly, I think it is worth observing that although the doctrine of this faction is compared with the doctrine of **Balaam**, the Holy Spirit nevertheless does not say that those who lived among the **Pergamenes** from this corrupt rabble <note>original: "colluvies," meaning a collection of filth or dregs</note> followed the doctrine of a certain man **"of Nicolaus"** <note>original: τοῦ Νικολάου (tou Nikolaou)</note>, but rather of a certain family, **"of the Nicolaitans"** <note>original: τῶν Νικολαιτῶν (tōn Nikolaitōn)</note>. From this I believe I understand that this sect rashly took its name from **Nicolaus** and falsely asserted that a certain good and holy man had stood as their master and the leader of their crimes.

### §. VI.

Anyone who diligently and without partisan bias compares and weighs all these points will, I have no doubt, admit that the words of **St. John** cannot be understood in any other way than this: that there flourished at that time a certain sect among the **Christians** known as the **Nicolaitans** (regardless of where they eventually derived that name). This group, while it spread certain other errors harmful to the Christian religion, was especially unafraid to maintain that no sin was committed by those who reclined <note>The author refers to the Roman and Greek practice of reclining on couches during formal banquets</note> in the temples of the Gods and indulged in the crimes that usually accompanied these profane feasts. 

This interpretation, which is the simplest and most fitting to the words of the holy man [St. John], is strengthened by the common consensus of all the learned teachers <note>original: "doctorum," referring here to the early Church Fathers</note> who lived closest to those times. These figures not only report that a **heresy** of this kind existed, but they even attacked and opposed it in their own written books—a matter we discussed more fully in the preceding **Dissertation**. 

The interpretations of historical passages within the sacred text <note>original: "sacri codicis," the Bible</note> cannot be fortified with stronger or more valid supports than these. For if a certain explanation of a passage containing **historical** elements is perfectly consistent with the words themselves, and the most ancient authors support it with harmonious testimonies, I truly do not see what more could be required to establish its truth and stability. To undermine interpretations so well-fortified and strengthened by using mere conjectures and suspicions is something I would consider neither reasonable nor safe. To do so would open a path toward calling everything into doubt that rests upon the good faith and authority <note>original: "auctoritate." The final syllable "tate" appears as a catchword to ensure the reader transitions correctly to the next page</note> of ancient authors...

### Section VIII.

The third point that these distinguished men bring forward to claim **ST. JOHN** for themselves and their cause is, if I am not mistaken, of even less weight than the previous ones. ...must be grouped with the heretics <note>original: "haereticis esse aggregandos"</note>. If the **Balaamites** and **Nicolaitans** are the same, how can it be said that either both, or neither, should be counted among the heretics? Whatever the case may be, a few words will be needed to untie this knot. I grant that those who, in the writings of **JOHN**, are said to follow the doctrine of **BALAAM**, and those who are called **Nicolaitans** shortly thereafter, do not differ from one another by any distinction, but are people of the same kind. From this, it is correctly concluded that if the **BALAAMITES** were not heretics, then the **Nicolaitans** were not heretics either. But as for what follows from that—meant to push back against those who group the **Nicolaitans** among the sects <term>sectis: factions or schools of thought, here referring to early heretical groups</term> that arose among the first Christians—I, for my part, hardly see it. "*Either both*," says the most learned man, "*or neither should be accepted among the heretics of the Apostolic age.*" Since this distinguished man demands one of these options from us, we accept both; but we add that they differ from each other only in vocabulary and name. In all other respects, in their dogmas <term>dogmatibus: established religious doctrines</term> and practices, they constitute a single family. Unless perhaps the weakness of my own intellect stands in the way of my desire to understand the mind of this most learned man, his reasoning would be as follows: The **Balaamites** and **Nicolaitans** are the same. But the **Balaamite** heretics are a fiction <note>original: "commentitii," meaning invented or imaginary</note>. Therefore, the **Nicolaitans** are also a fiction. We reject this second proposition, which is called the minor premise. For the **Balaamite** heretics are not false or fictitious; rather, they are the same as the **Nicolaitans**, whom we—along with the most ancient writers—maintain truly existed.

...I have discussed <note>original: "tavi," likely the conclusion of "disputavi" (disputed) or "notavi" (noted) from the previous page.</note>, nevertheless, because **JOHANN WILHELM JANUS** <note>Johann Wilhelm Janus (1674–1727) was a noted German theologian and historian at the University of Wittenberg.</note> arranged these arguments in a different manner and equipped them with new strengths—even augmenting them with several additional resources—it is pleasing to briefly survey and dissolve <term>diluere: to wash away or refute an argument</term> them once again. First, this most celebrated man thinks it hinders the weight of our witnesses <note>The "witnesses" are the early Church Fathers like Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria who wrote about the Nicolaitans.</note> (x) because they all speak of that heresy as a thing of the past and report nothing except what has been handed down to them. But I believe that if he were alive today, he would himself disapprove of this reasoning: that "he who speaks of a certain thing as a past matter deserves no credit." It would be all over for by far the greatest part of both ancient and modern History if no credit were granted to any witnesses except those who were present at the events themselves and who personally saw and spoke to the men of whom they write.

Secondly, this most excellent man objects to those witnesses because they indicate neither a specific place nor a time when they began to disseminate <term>disseminare: to scatter like seeds; the spreading of ideas</term> their errors; he argues they can name no followers and no books from which, or through which, those destructive dogmas were handed down and propagated. Indeed, I am also little moved by this argument. For who would immediately pronounce someone unworthy of trust simply because they do not narrate every single detail pertaining to a matter? We know that ancient writers—to say nothing now of sacred and divine matters—narrate many things in a universal and general way, omitting specific notes of place, time, and other circumstances; yet no one judges any of them to be utterly contemptible for that reason, provided they suffer from no other faults. It can happen for various reasons that a writer does not report everything necessary to know the whole matter; who, truly, would think that their entire testimony should be rejected because of it?

### §. XI.

This distinguished man <note>referring to Johann Wilhelm Janus</note> continues, and for his third point adds that these witnesses regarding the **Nicolaitans** <term>Nicolaitans: a group mentioned in the Book of Revelation, often accused of moral laxity and heresy by early Church writers</term> disagree vehemently with each other; from which he claims it is manifest that these men should not be listened to at all. "Since, therefore," he says, "these opinions on the **Nicolaitan** **heresy** are so varied and so discordant among themselves, *it is impossible for more than one to be true, and it is certainly possible that none of them are.*" <note>original: "alterum fieri non potest, ut plus una, alterum profecto potest, ut earum nulla vera sit."</note> I have already sufficiently addressed this point in the **Dissertation** itself. These most learned men imagine a greater discord than actually exists among those ancient writers who mentioned the **Nicolaitans**. I confess, some of them do not sufficiently agree among themselves concerning the founder of this **sect**, whom some affirm was **NICHOLAS**, the **Deacon** <note>Nicholas was one of the seven deacons chosen by the early Church in Jerusalem (Acts 6:5); early writers debated whether he actually founded the sect or if his name was merely used by others</note>, while others deny it; nor do they all attribute the same doctrines to this group. Yet regarding the matter itself—namely, the reality of the **sect**—there is no dispute among them, for they all affirm that it existed; and in this **case**, that is enough. No wise man experienced in human affairs, seeing all writers report that a certain event took place, would conclude that nothing should be believed simply because the consensus of all writers is not unanimous regarding certain minor details that do not touch the heart of the matter itself.

Nothing in these points is difficult to resolve. It would not, however, be clear from this that no such sect ever existed. 

The secondary question is this: Was **NICHOLAS** the father and author of that group called the **Nicolaitans**, or not? There is also no pleasure, in which they imagine they delight. Who is more unhappy: he who labors to persuade himself that everything is filled with fables <note>original: "fabulis"; here referring to myths or unfounded stories</note>, or he who does not doubt that many things are certain? There is something to flying high and mocking the narrow straits in which others labor. But it is safer to stand on the ground. The former must fear a fall; for the latter, a fall is not so easy. It is indeed an insane pleasure to always seek something that opens a place for doubt, to always investigate something to fight against. I would prefer the craftsman’s peace to the soldier’s triumphs, and the rustic's <term>plow-handle</term> <note>original: "stivam"</note> to the sailor's mast. I would call him wiser who looks for where to plant his foot, than him who provides for a state where he can never rest. What delight is there, after long errors and lengthy meditations, to finally achieve this: that you are always wavering? I pass over the losses, I pass over the disasters, which that sort of thing brings upon both literature and human society. I pass over the injuries inflicted on our ancestors, whom they depress to the condition of brute animals. <term>Superstition</term> and credulity are a great evil; yet greater is any rashness in provocation. He sins more lightly who trusts things that are less certain than he who withdraws trust from things that are certain.

--- Page 569 ---
<meta>This page continues the author’s philosophical reflection on historical criticism. Having established that his defense is not of falsehood itself but of careful investigation, he now discusses the difficulty of discerning truth in ancient records and the necessity of intellectual humility.</meta>

<page-num>509</page-num>

We are dealing with matters supported by an enduring reputation, or those which a great age has shrouded in darkness. The more people support the former, the more carefully we must proceed before dismissing them as mere fables. For the latter, the very obscurity that hides them serves as a defense; nothing is harder than proving they are false. Many points can be argued, and many can be refuted. You might easily gather evidence that harms a case; perhaps another will even more easily find evidence that helps it. That ocean of the distant past <note>original: "Oceanus"; here used as a metaphor for the vast and deep nature of ancient history</note> is too vast to be contained by such a narrow mind. What then? We must hold to a middle path. That darkness helps many form educated guesses, but it also gives birth to many errors. It is a foolish voice that says without hesitation: "This is beyond doubt." But it is also dangerous to immediately decree: "This is a lie."

These words represent two extremes: *History and fable, truth and falsehood*. One of them must necessarily prevail. Yet neither should be accepted without long deliberation. Sometimes, a wise person accepts neither. There are many things—perhaps more than most people think—to which that legal phrase, <term>IT IS NOT CLEAR</term> <note>original: "NON LIQVET"; a Roman legal term used by judges when a case was too uncertain to decide</note>, must be applied. In more complicated cases, the *Areopagites* <note>judges of the high court of Athens, famous in the ancient world for their wisdom and impartiality</note> themselves used to refrain from delivering a verdict. If it was not considered a failing for them to do so when a lawsuit involved something as minor as an aqueduct or a shared wall between neighbors, why should we not be praised for doing the same, occupied as we often are with much greater matters?

But a certain terrible lust for penetrating into the most hidden secrets plagues our minds. We are tossed about by the waves, yet we wish to appear as though we are resting safely in the harbor. It is not enough for us to linger at the threshold; we crave to be called "the initiated." For this reason, we do not merely approach a judgment; we rush headlong toward it. This very impulse must be restrained—

Desire <note>original: *cupiditas*; here referring to an uncontrolled longing for discovery or certain answers</note> must be restrained, lest we be carried headlong into trackless wastes and lose the truth while seeking it. Those deeds that are related to the heroic ages <note>The "heroic ages" refers to the legendary period of Greek and Roman antiquity, where history and mythology are intertwined.</note> possess much darkness. But they also enjoy a certain light, which not everyone is able to resist. They both fill our eyes, as it were, and yet escape them. Antiquity is the mother of doubts, but also of veneration. That very simplicity, which presents itself clothed in tradition, stirs up opposing impulses. To some, it offers an occasion for suspicion; others, it carries away into admiration. Few witnesses are present. But perpetual tradition comes to their aid. Whichever way I turn, there will never be a lack of something that either persuades or dissuades. 

Very many people unhappily extricate themselves from these entanglements. According to the variety of their minds, one person selects those things that bear a certain appearance of truth, while another chooses those in which there is some matter for suspicion. This one prefers things to be condemned over those to be praised; that one prefers things to be praised over those to be condemned. From this, innumerable disagreements arise. From this, two "sects," as it were, emerge, which are too troublesome both to themselves and to the study of letters. One side chatters about "Histories," the other about "fables." The former denies nothing; the latter denies everything. 

Both, if you consider the matter rightly, have both something to defend themselves with and something to fear. Neither, however, greatly consults the truth or the sciences. Meanwhile, it is no wonder that both adorn their cause in such a way that it seems superior. There is no fact, I believe, from which something to be disputed cannot be sought, either from its nature or from its witnesses. How much more will these narratives I speak of always provide something that you might either diminish or increase on either side. It is a matter of talent to dispute about obscure things in such a way that they acquire the color of truth. If a certain force of eloquence is added, an <term>Adonis</term> <note>Adonis was a figure in Greek mythology famed for his extraordinary beauty.</note> will be made out of <term>Thersites</term> <note>Thersites was a character in Homer's *Iliad*, described as the ugliest and most foul-mouthed of the Greek soldiers.</note> himself.

Between these two <note>Referring to the two groups mentioned on the previous page: the over-credulous and the over-skeptical.</note>, whoever is superior in argument will also be superior in the fight, until another is found who may overcome him as well.

But I, **MOST DISTINGUISHED SIR** <note>original: *Vir Amplissime*; a formal, respectful address to a person of high status or great learning</note>, judge it to be far removed from the duty of a thoughtful man to align himself with either the former or the latter. I conceive a certain pleasure, but a far greater weariness, whenever I place these struggles before my eyes. The pleasure arises because I perceive that those to whom a certain fertility of intellect <note>original: *foecunditas*; literally "fruitfulness" or "fecundity"</note> has been granted have not entirely died out. The weariness arises because I see that men who are not unlearned achieve nothing despite their greatest effort. May I perish if I can even perceive what it is many people call knowledge <note>original: *scientia*</note>. The true names of things have been lost, and a certain heap of suspicions often passes under this name. For my part, I profess to know nothing except that which becomes most evident. Others think they understand a matter better the further afield they must seek their reasons. There is also a kind of person who thinks they know something if they are simply not ignorant of what others have said. These people certainly strive for learning <note>original: *eruditio*; the process of being "polished" or educated</note>; those others struggle through it. But this is the evil: that almost everyone who strives believes they have already succeeded. There is almost no one who thinks themselves still to be on the journey. *Almost everyone claims to have reached Corinth.* <note>The author quotes a famous proverb: *Non cuivis homini contingit adire Corinthum* ("It does not happen to every man to reach Corinth"). ...history, I call it. As much as others give to subtlety, so much do I usually give to **reason**. If I wished, I could champion this or that opinion. For how much effort is it to sell smoke <note>original: *fumos... vendere*; a Latin idiom meaning to sell empty promises or deceptive words to the gullible.</note> to the ignorant? But it does not please me, since it is foreign to integrity. Reason persuades us that, if it can be done, we should establish the limits between the true and the false. But **prudence** <term>prudentia; in this context, the practical wisdom of knowing one's own intellectual limits</term> commands that we apply moderation to this study, and not try to advance further than is permitted. I do not envy those who strive greatly so that they might be ignorant of nothing. Conversely, no one will envy me if, in the meantime, I work so that I may learn how many things I do not know. This much, however, is certain to me: those who boldly assert that everything is accessible to them are no wiser than I. Both of us suffer from ignorance. The difference is this: they deny it, while I admit it. Which of the sick, truly, is more prudent? The one who shouts that he is well, even though his bed, his complexion, the Physician, and the medicine jars <note>original: *pyxides*; small boxes or vessels used by apothecaries to hold pills or ointments.</note> show the opposite? **Lactantius** <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine the Great.</note> is the authority (*b*) for the story that, while **Licinius** was warring against **Maximinus** <note>Licinius and Maximinus Daza were rival Roman emperors; Licinius defeated Maximinus in 313 AD.</note>, a certain spirit <note>original: *genium*; often a guardian spirit or divine messenger.</note> dictated specific prayers to him in his dreams, which the soldiers were to use to appease God. This is a matter worthy of wonder, but also of doubt! The success that followed the event, and the providence of the divine—which was often witnessed at that time—seem to demand our belief. Yet, the nature of the business itself, the witness, and the cunning of certain emperors cast doubts upon it. Should I believe it? If I do, I shall be guilty of a hollow faith, and I might attribute to divine providence what was perhaps the trickery of a man—one who, like **Sertorius** <note>Quintus Sertorius (c. 126–73 BC), a Roman general who famously claimed a white fawn spoke to him from the goddess Diana to maintain the loyalty of his troops.</note> of old, might have feigned a dream and introduced false religious rites (*c*). Should I deny it? Then I fear I might stain myself with the mark of impiety and cause harm to some. What then? Let another judge; I will not.

Certainly, a similar situation exists for most things in which learned men busy themselves. How many disputes, how many discords have been stirred up—and continue to be stirred up—concerning the events of those earliest times? But I see battles, not triumphs. I admit that quite a few things can be made clearer through our hard work. If those who deliberate on these matters were always free from hatred and favoritism, we would see the truth more clearly. We are more eager for a show of learning than for the truth itself <note>original: *Fuci potius, quam famae studiosi sumus*; literally "we are studious of drones [or pretenses] rather than reputation."</note>. ...would be to our advantage? It is safest that it be neither destroyed nor built up. It now falls to me, lest I seem to have said this in vain, to prove that the arguments you brought against it are not such as to cast it into the category of fables. I have no doubt that this can be done with **YOUR** leave.

Generally speaking, I feel that nothing can be called a fable except that which either conflicts with truth by its very nature, or which relies on no witnesses or clearly incompetent ones. If something occurs that is foreign to human credibility, nothing prevents me from thinking it should be laughed at. Regarding witnesses, we must proceed more cautiously. If contemporary witnesses do not appear—especially those who wrote about the same events—but rather men of a much later age, it is a great sign of a fable. If ancient witnesses are present but are triflers <note>original: *nugatores*; meaning writers of trivial or unreliable gossip.</note>, the matter is doubtful, but not yet a fable. These points, I say, **MOST DISTINGUISHED SIR**, could be raised; however, I shall not raise them. Let us be done with these carping disputes. <note>original: *vitilitigationes*; a rare Latin term for malicious or petty legalistic quarreling.</note> I will acknowledge along WITH YOU that TERTULLIAN is that "Atlas" upon whose shoulders this entire burden uniquely rests. You, in turn, will acknowledge with me that, were there no other reasons for doubt, he would be a sufficiently ancient and suitable witness. For I do not believe your conclusion is this: "Whatever only one person records—no matter who they are—is a fable." There are times when one wise man is to be preferred over a thousand jackdaws. <note>original: *graculis*; jackdaws were often used in classical literature to represent noisy, foolish chatterers in contrast to the quiet wisdom of a single authority.</note>

There are times when the words of a single person outweigh the silence of many. We must now inquire, therefore, what might so weaken his testimony that it should be rejected as if it were full of lies.

There are two things that seem to settle the matter for **YOU**: the fickleness of **TERTULLIAN**, who was prone to believing anything, and the silence of others regarding this matter. Neither of these points should be ignored; yet neither, in my judgment, is of such weight as to prove that this narrative must be regarded as a mere fable. Regarding the first point, many arguments could be raised. He may have been easy to convince at times, but he was also, on occasion, a bit more difficult. I will fight even closer and more boldly: I will concede that he was the most reckless of men, that he accepted every old wives' tale, and that he gave no place to reason. everything is fabricated. Therefore, he who believes everything gives credit not only to fictions, but also to Histories. everything is pleasing. Rarely, if a certain matter becomes a subject of controversy, are its weightier points weighed without emotional disturbances. Generally, I will note two things, neither of which, unless I am mistaken, will be rejected by **YOU, VENERABLE SIR** <note>A formal address to the recipient of this treatise, likely a high-ranking church official or scholar</note>. The first is this: As long as other reasons for the silence of certain later writers can be brought forward—other than a conviction of the falsehood of the matter they omit—the force of this negative argument provides room only for doubt. The reason is plain. Sometimes the effect <term>effectus</term> is seen, while the causes <term>causae</term> remain hidden. Indeed, for a single effect, there can be many causes. And different causes can produce the same effect. This is a fact very well known from Physics and Ethics. Therefore, since the causes are hidden, a wise man neither decides, nor can decide, which one is to be preferred over the other. One may seem more probable than the other; but that is not sufficient for making a pronouncement. And, I ask,

Where are we more easily deceived than in distinguishing between things that are merely probable? Philosophers lament that this branch of the art of reasoning <term>ratiocinandi</term> <note>The systematic process of logical deduction and argumentation, specifically how one weighs evidence</note> has not yet been fully refined. (k) I, for my part, consider those to be wise who are unwilling to run far on this slippery ground. It is a difficult task indeed to establish rules where the sheer variety of things—after infinite discussions—rejects certain laws; where, without long experience, reason alone accomplishes nothing; and where, finally, some indescribable feeling arising from our innermost depths often drags one person here and another there.

Another thing I note is this: the very silence of those who are younger than other witnesses is an indication that there are other reasons for keeping quiet besides a perceived falsehood in the matter. There is, as we all know, a love of truth <term>veritatis amor</term> <note>A foundational concept in Enlightenment philosophy suggesting a natural human inclination toward honesty and factual correctness</note> implanted in our minds, which manifests most easily when we see others caught in an error. We gladly correct what we notice in others that is worthy of correction.

From this, the conclusion is easy: if a later author leaves the accounts of earlier ones completely untouched, it is clear that he either did not know them, had forgotten what he read, or at least doubted whether they contained an error. For it is very probable that he would have removed the fault—lest he lead others into error—if he had believed it to be a fault. I could add other points; but it is not necessary.

I see nothing in these things, **MOST DISTINGUISHED SIR**, that you would not easily admit. However, if we test that argument you used against these points, it is certain that its value is greatly diminished. I shall begin with the last point, which clearly overturns the strength of that argument.

True philosophical reasoning knows nothing of such cycles—yet even the leaders of the learned are driven into them too often, as if onto the Siren rocks. <note>In Greek mythology, the Sirens lured sailors to their destruction on rocky shores with their song; the author uses this to describe attractive but dangerous logical fallacies</note>

For the rest, I could dispute many things concerning the merit of that argument; it cannot be hidden from a wise man that it is surely not as easily applied as many suppose. [Hierony]mus <note>original: "nus." The completion of the name Hieronymus (Jerome) from the previous page.</note> had thought it fitting to meet. The ancients did not inquire into the truth of the things narrated.* <note>The author is quoting his opponent’s counter-argument, which claims that ancient writers weren't critical enough to be used as evidence.</note> Do you not realize that these points actually work remarkably well in my favor? It is truly this: the silence of those who are later in age than other witnesses is proof that they did not regard the matter they omitted as a fable. The reason is this: it is human nature to gladly correct the errors of others. 

I am not so inexperienced in affairs as to be unaware that circumstances can sometimes occur which command silence from men, even if they see errors. Yet, in this specific business, I certainly do not see how such circumstances could be found; and I still contend that, generally speaking, this reasoning <term>ratiocinatio</term> <note>A formal logical process or syllogism.</note> holds true. However, how the story of ***Pope Joan*** <note>original: "Ioanna Papissa." A legendary female pope who supposedly reigned for a few years in the 9th century; by the 18th century, most scholars—Protestant and Catholic alike—regarded it as a myth.</note>—if indeed this is a fable—and many other long-discredited little stories could be defended by the aid of this argument, I certainly do not understand. Let those who are led by a zeal for fables try what they can achieve with its help, and they will realize all too quickly that they have miscalculated their accounts.

He defends his logical framework against the charge that it would force scholars to accept debunked myths like the legend of Pope Joan.</summary>

-># SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT #<-

The reason for the undertaking is explained in § I. Witnesses on behalf of **EBION** <note>The figure traditionally identified by early Church writers as the founder of the Ebionite sect.</note> are cited and defended in § II. The third argument (III), concerning other derivations of the name **EBIONITES** in general, is considered in § V. Specifically, the reasoning of **EUSEBIUS** and **ORIGEN** <note>Both Eusebius and Origen suggested the name "Ebionite" came from the Hebrew word for "poor," suggesting the sect had "poor" or "impoverished" views of Christ.</note> is examined in § VI.
