### § I.

Whether there was a certain **EBION**, who once disseminated perverse opinions in the sacred assembly <note>The "sacred assembly" refers to the early Christian Church.</note>, or not, has long been investigated by learned men. Today, this "good man" <note>The author uses "bonus homo" (good man) ironically here, as Ebion was traditionally considered a heresiarch, or leader of a heresy.</note> is in a state of the utmost peril, and there is almost no one who, after so many weapons have been launched against him by great men, attempts to offer a defense for him. 

But I, after I approached the study of this case with a composed mind, realized that those who stood by the man lacked skill rather than weapons; and that those who desire him to be driven out from the ranks of the leaders of the heretics <note>The author refers to the modern scholarly trend of the time (17th–18th century) to deny that Ebion was a real person, suggesting instead that the name "Ebionite" came from a Hebrew word for poverty.</note> are in no better a position than their adversaries. I shall provide the reasoning for this opinion in this **Dissertation**, in which I will candidly weigh the arguments of both sides. I respect the genius and learning of those who wish **EBION** ill; yet I respect the truth even more. 

It is not my intention, however, to defend the idea that it can be known today with certainty and through exploration that **EBION** truly existed. I only mean that this dispute is one of those which, being very obscure, borrow nearly all their luster from the talent of their advocate: indeed, both sides are fortified with reasons, but neither side possesses those by which the whole matter could be settled after such a long interval of time. Every history has...

They argue that these Fathers heard the name of the **Ebionites**; and from this they conjectured—not unlike they did with other sects—that this group must also have had its own founder, named **EBION**.

Truly, as to whether these arguments have much inherent strength, I strongly doubt. Those [Fathers] might perhaps have contaminated themselves with such an error: but the question remains whether they actually did so. The conjecture would be stronger if more examples of such mistakes committed by them were brought forward: yet none occur to my memory. On the contrary, I see that **TERTULLIAN** refuted the **GNOSTICS** <term>Gnostics: a broad group of early Christian sects emphasizing secret knowledge (gnosis)</term>, yet he did not invent a certain "**GNOSTUS**" as their founder; I understand that others also carefully avoided mistakes of this kind.

Furthermore, those who are accused of ignorance of the Hebrew language were nevertheless very skillful in the history of Christian affairs. This knowledge will easily compensate for that ignorance. Nor indeed was this ignorance common to all of them, but only to some. **JEROME** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was famous for his translation of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate) and was one of the few Western Fathers who mastered Hebrew.</note> had devoted himself to the language of the Jews. **EPIPHANIUS** and others indicate that they themselves were not unaware of what the word **EBION** signifies: yet they do not deny that **EBION** existed. 

To this is added another point: if those whom learned men claim were in error regarding **EBION** had truly been guilty of such a mistake, others would undoubtedly have noted that fault, and those who followed would have changed their minds. But no one ever accused those who admitted the existence of **EBION** of error: no one ever asserted that **TERTULLIAN**, **AUGUSTINE**, and others had introduced a man who was never seen. Since the authority of the testimony has not been weakened in this way, let us now contemplate the remaining arguments which the adversaries of **EBION** believe work in their favor.

->§. III.<-

I willingly confess that the arguments they bring forward are by no means to be despised. For they proceed from men in whom everyone knows there was, and is, the sharpest power of judgment and very great learning. When I compare their arguments with the responses of certain others—which are indeed cold and entirely devoid of wit—I do not wonder that these most distinguished men have begun to judge their own forces more highly because of the very weak defense <note>Literally "lightest armor." The author is saying that poor counter-arguments have made the critics feel more confident in their own position.</note> of their opponents. They begin with the name. They say that *Ebion* is a Hebrew word meaning "poor" <note>Hebrew: *ebyon* (אביון).</note>. I know this, most distinguished sirs; but I deny that it follows from this that a man who held that name never existed. Who does not know that very many of the ancients were accustomed to give names to their children based on actual things? Indeed, the nature of most names that we use today is such that, besides their specific use as a name, they admit a certain common and popular meaning. Truly, he certainly spoke the truth who first said:

->*Names often fit the things they represent.*<-
<note>original: "Conveniunt rebus nomina saepe suis." This was a common Latin proverb used to suggest that a person's name often reflects their character or destiny.</note>

If all those people whose names are also the names of other things were to be excluded from the ranks of teachers, how greatly would their number be reduced?

->§. IV.<-

They proceed to the silence of **IRENAEUS** <term>Irenaeus: A 2nd-century bishop and theologian famous for his work "Against Heresies."</term> and others among the ancients, who, although they frequently mention the *Ebionites*, nevertheless never make mention of **EBION** as if he were their founder. Let learned men see, however, whether those who are silent can be justly used here to oppose those who explicitly affirm his existence.

<meta>This page continues a theological and historical debate regarding whether the "Ebionites" (an early Jewish-Christian sect) were named after a specific founder named "Ebion" or if the name derived from a description of their status or beliefs. If **IRENAEUS** <note>Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202 AD) was an early Church Father known for his writings against heresies.</note> and others denied that *Ebion* ever lived, they could rightly be compared with those who think otherwise. But truly, from the fact that they only take note of the *Ebionites*, and not **EBION** himself, almost nothing can be concluded. To me, certainly, the force of this argument is not clear: "He who only criticizes the *Ebionites* does not believe in **EBION**." There are those who pick at the *Cerinthians* <note>Followers of Cerinthus, a contemporary of the Apostle John who held Gnostic-leaning views.</note>, yet are silent about *Cerinthus*. Is it right to suspect from this that *Cerinthus* was a fictional man? As it pertains specifically to **IRENAEUS**, to whom they appeal above all others, I think it is far more likely that he believed **EBION** was the father of the *Ebionite* sect than anything else. For I do not doubt that if the *Ebionites* had drawn their name from any other source, that pious man would have mentioned it. The fact that he provides no explanation for the term is proof that there is no mystery underlying it, other than that common explanation repeated by him so often: that the name is owed to the founder of the sect. Thus, this silence [of Irenaeus regarding a definition] easily cancels out the force of that other silence [regarding the person of Ebion]. Similarly, regarding the others, silence can be opposed by silence. Many are silent about *Ebion* while speaking of the *Ebionites*. But they are also silent about any "error" made by those who *do* believe in **EBION**. For if they had thought that people were mistaken in this belief, they would without doubt have noted it, and they would have ordered that this man—who they would claim was born only in the imaginations of others—be erased from the record.

Few are unaware that if other witnesses exist who assert the contrary, the authority of such negative arguments is small. Furthermore, I do not understand how much force this argumentation can possess:

Not even the first conclusion is valid, much less the second. We know that some of the Church Fathers derived the names of others too—for example, the **Manichaeans** <note>Followers of Mani, a 3rd-century Persian prophet who founded a dualistic religion.</note>—from somewhere other than from the author of the sect. We must now establish a comparison of witnesses, though its nature is such that it is entirely insufficient for settling any dispute. Let us consider in a few words where the heart of the debate leads, once these points are established.

"**Ebion** did not exist," the learned men contend. But why? Because it is probable that **EUSEBIUS** and **ORIGEN** held that same opinion. What else they could say further, I do not know. If we were now to inquire into the authority of the witnesses—even if they were not superior—the friends of **EBION** <note>Those who argue for his historical existence.</note> would certainly be on equal footing. ### §. VI.

These points, which come to mind when considering the argument under discussion in general terms, clearly strip away all its force. Nevertheless, it is worth examining in more detail the derivations proposed by **ORIGEN** and **EUSEBIUS**, as well as the opinion of the **EBIONITES** themselves. ### §. X.

One point remains upon which I must still offer my opinion—a point which those who challenge the existence of EBION <note>The author is defending the idea that a man named Ebion actually existed, against scholars who claimed the name was just a label.</note> are accustomed to count among their chief arguments. They claim that those Jews who had committed themselves to the name of CHRIST were called "poor" or *Ebionites* by their fellow Jews out of contempt. Even if those who disagree with me were to concede that this had happened, their case would still not be won. For I confess I do not understand how these two propositions are connected: "The Jews called Christians 'poor'; therefore, EBION never existed."

On the contrary, those who embrace this theory tie themselves into an unbreakable knot: how could it be that a Jewish insult, ignored by the circumcised <note>original: "recutitis"—a Latin term for Jews, here used to refer to those who did not convert to Christianity</note>, was adopted by Christians (for whom such poverty was a point of pride) as a way to bring infamy upon their own theological opponents? 

Furthermore, it is by no means proven that the Jews ever branded Christians with this specific name. For anyone searching for the evidence supporting this opinion, they will find only a single passage from ORIGEN <note>A prominent early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) from Alexandria.</note> upon which the entire theory is believed to rest. His words are these: "And those among the Jews who accepted Jesus as the Christ are called Ebionites." <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἐβιωναῖοι χρηματίζουσιν οἱ ἀπὸ Ἰουδαίων, τὸν Ἰησοῦν, ὡς χριστὸν, παραδεξάμενοι."</note> (o)

I am greatly surprised that those who argue against the existence of EBION get stuck on this obstacle, and yet they are unwilling to deny that ORIGEN wrote exactly what their opponents claim. However, those who understand Greek even moderately well can easily see that this is not the actual meaning of ORIGEN’S words. His translator, SIGISMUND GELENIUS <note>A 16th-century scholar known for translating Greek patristic texts into Latin.</note>, deceived many good men when he poorly translated these words as: "*They are called Ebionaeans by the other Jews, who [received] Jesus...*"

But when will such disputes ever come to an end! When, at last, will that so-often-sought conclusion—**EBION** *existed*, or **EBION** *did not exist*—when, I say, will it be placed beyond all doubt? Therefore, let us hold opinions where it is permitted, and let us doubt where reason commands it. Let us state that others have erred if the matter is certain; let us be tolerant where
->the arguments of both sides<-
->rest in uncertainty.<-

->§. I.<-

**T**hose great disturbances in France <note>original: "Gallia"</note> have not yet subsided, which were stirred up in this century by the law passed by **CLEMENT XI**, the Supreme Pontiff <note>Pope Clement XI, reigned 1700–1721.</note>, against the **NEW TESTAMENT OF PASQUIER QUESNEL** <note>Pasquier Quesnel (1634–1719) was a prominent Jansenist theologian; his "Moral Reflections" on the New Testament was the target of papal condemnation.</note>, a Priest and "Father" (as they call him) of the Parisian Oratory. Those who have rejected the Pope's decision and appealed to a general council of the church <note>original: "concilium ecclesiae universae" — a legal maneuver where French clergy claimed a General Council had more authority than the Pope.</note> continue on their path. Although they possess neither strength in numbers nor official favor, they maintain their resolve with constancy. They would rather leave their homeland and the comforts of life than use their votes to approve a decree they judge to be unjust.

I confess that this firmness of spirit deserves much true praise; it should not be considered a small matter when someone prefers the conscience of right actions over all worldly goods. However, if the act itself is examined and compared more carefully with the established rules of those who profess to be members of the Roman assembly <note>The Roman Catholic Church.</note>, it seems to rest not so much on legal right as on the ancient custom of the French <note>Referring to Gallicanism, the French tradition of limiting papal power in favor of national or conciliar authority.</note>. This custom has been confirmed more by the passage of time and an innate love of liberty than by sound reflection.

I do not mean to rebuke the French here for submitting themselves to the judgment of a council, even though it is uniquely fitting for Christians to hear the voice of the Lord, and nowhere in the sacred book <note>The Bible.</note> are we commanded to submit to the judgment of bishops

### §. III.

Very learned men judge, therefore, that JESUS CHRIST conferred the supreme power of settling sacred controversies upon the universal church. They believe the church is represented by those who fulfill the office of bishops and teachers within her. In the same way, a Master General is above individual religious members, even Priors and Provincials, yet he is not above the general congregation, since he must obey it, rather than command it.*

### §. VI.

The disputes concerning the **unity of the church** <term>Latin: *ecclesiae unitas*; the theological concept that the true Church must be a single, undivided body</term> are long and extremely difficult. While everyone professes to believe in this unity, they explain it in such various ways that someone who carefully weighs those great arguments sometimes becomes more uncertain than they were before. The **Ancient Doctors** <note>Also known as the Church Fathers; the influential bishops and scholars of the first few centuries of Christianity.</note> decide the matter boldly enough; they place such a high price on this unity that they establish that no one who violates it can be a partaker of salvation. They state this gravely, and not altogether wrongly. However, they do this very poorly: they nowhere provide a certain and constant definition for the ambiguous word *unity*. Instead, they discourse so perplexely that several different opinions can be attributed to them at once. I point as evidence, among other things, to the small books of **CYPRIAN** and **AUGUSTINE** which they composed concerning the unity of the church. For this reason, very learned men have been led almost to this conclusion: to believe that the Fathers understood too indistinctly the nature of that unity of the church which they preached so much. (l) The most famous man, **JOSEPH BINGHAM**, is not far from this opinion, and no one would accuse him of holding the Fathers in contempt. (m) Among more recent authors, that which the Fathers...

### §. XI.

It is therefore certain that IGNATIUS already had a certain unity of the church in mind, the ultimate goal of which was the bishop; but of what nature that unity was, I do not dare to determine in every respect. There will perhaps be those who think that even this eminent man himself, if he had been asked by someone, would not have explained the feelings of his mind without digression and confusion of matters; there will be those who suspect that *union* <note>original Greek: ἕνωσιν (enōsin), often implying a moral or social harmony</note>, or *concord*, was distinguished by him with too little care from *unity* <note>original Greek: ἑνότητι (henotēti), implying a more essential or structural oneness</note>; but for now, I neither agree nor disagree. I see two things placed clearly in the open: first, that IGNATIUS wished to signify something more majestic than a mere moral unity or harmony; second, that he gave instructions regarding the unity of individual churches, but not at all regarding the association of the entire Christian community with some "chief bishop" <note>The author is arguing that Ignatius promoted the authority of local bishops, not a global Papacy.</note>. That age was not yet so discerning as to adapt the images and notions of civil government to sacred affairs. And for this very reason, I judge the letters of IGNATIUS to be of the greatest antiquity, since I find rarer traces of this ancient simplicity in subsequent writers.

### §. XIII.

Whatever the case may be, those who in this manner corrupted the dogma of the church's unity in the second and third centuries conceived of a certain **physical unity**, beyond a mere agreement of minds and opinions. Unless I am greatly mistaken, their opinion essentially comes down to this: that the Apostles, endowed with the Holy Spirit, bestowed their gifts upon those whom they had placed in charge of the churches; that from these disciples, those same gifts flowed into the teachers of subsequent times who were placed over the same congregations; and that from the bishops, that heavenly grace is derived down into the priests <term>presbyters</term> and the rest of the multitude of the saints. Just as all the sap is diffused from the root into the branches of the entire tree, or as the whole abundance of rivers and the fertility of the fields proceeds from a single ultimate spring, so too does every abundance of heavenly virtue flow down from the Apostles and their successors. For this reason, anyone severed from them can be a partaker neither of the Holy Spirit nor of the truth. Either **IRENAEUS** and **CYPRIAN** mean nothing in the words which I will immediately subjoin, or they mean exactly what I have said. Thus, the former <note>Irenaeus</note> writes: (i) *For this gift of God has been entrusted to the Church...* <note>original: "Hoc enim ecclesiae creditum est Dei munus."</note>

Having previously argued that a body cannot function without its head, the author now addresses the specific legal and theological distinctions used by French scholars to justify their semi-independence from Rome.</meta>

->۞ ( 612 ) ۞<-

They establish that there is a Pope of the **sacred empire** <term>sacred empire: A term used here to describe the Church as a spiritual kingdom or "Christendom."</term>, to whom the remaining parts of this vast body must therefore be related. And, to tell the truth, this kind of unity seems to please the **Gauls** <note>The "Gauls" refers to the French (Gallican) theologians who argued for national church autonomy.</note> more than others. Although they disagree with others concerning the nature of this sacred empire, they still do not dare to deny that the **Pontiff** <note>The Pope</note> holds great power and jurisdiction over all the provinces of the kingdom of **CHRIST**. However, they frequently express their views on the true nature of Papal rule in such a way that they themselves do not seem to understand its character. 

*The Pope,* says **EDMUND RICHER**, (t) *is only the ministerial, not the essential head of the church.* <note>original: "ministeriale, non essentiale caput ecclesiae." Richer (1559–1631) was a famous Gallican who argued that the Pope was an executive servant (ministerial) of the Church, rather than the source of its being (essential).</note> The **Gauls**, according to **PAOLO SARPI**, (u) say that *the Pontiff has the authority to feed and rule all the churches, but not the universal church.* 

I admire the cleverness of these most learned men, if they can freely declare these ideas and successfully follow them with their intellect. The rest of us find it more difficult to grasp these and similar notions. I can guess what an *essential head* might be, but I do not entirely follow what a *ministerial* one is in every respect. Moreover, as for their claim that the Pope presides over all or individual churches, but not over the universal church, this seems to me just as "clever" as if someone were to assert that the limbs are indeed ruled by the head, but not the body which is made of those limbs; or that all the cities, villas, and estates of a province are subject to the King, but not the very [province] itself which is contained by these.

Among the **Venetians** <note>The Republic of Venice was a common historical example used in early modern political theory to discuss shared power.</note>, majesty—the source and unity of the state—rests not in the **Doge** <note>original: "Duce." Therefore, if a certain visible association flourishes in the church, but the council is of higher standing than the Pontiff, then the core of civil harmony must be placed in the council, not in the Roman **prelate** <note>original: "antistite." A high-ranking clergyman; here referring to the Pope as the Bishop of Rome.</note>, whose decrees can be subjected to the council’s debate.

For what, I ask, does it mean to withdraw from civil unity with the Prince and head...

# SUMMARY.

Section I. *Johannes Amandus, the first overseer <note>original: "antistes," a high-ranking cleric or chief pastor</note> of the people of Goslar, already fell under the suspicion of <term>Zwinglianism</term> <note>The teachings of Huldrych Zwingli, who viewed the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper as symbols rather than the literal body and blood of Christ.</note> §. I. Later, Heinrich Knigge caused even greater disturbances: as he was teaching wrongly in public regarding the **Holy Supper** <note>The Eucharist or Communion</note> and its benefit, he was first refuted by Nikolaus von Amsdorf <note>A close ally of Martin Luther and a strict defender of his doctrine.</note>; afterward, when he refused to yield, he was expelled from the city along with his colleague Johannes Grauert. §. II. After their expulsion, a law was passed in Goslar against the Zwinglians. §. III.*

Section II. Theological matters. The division of the subject. §. I. The first question. The state of the controversy. On the one side, the Zwinglians taught that Christ is not present in the bread and wine which are distributed in the **Holy Supper**. §. II. The <term>Orthodox</term> <note>In this context, "Orthodox" refers to the Lutheran party, who maintained the "Real Presence" of Christ in the sacrament.</note>, on the contrary, affirmed that the body and blood of Christ are distributed together with the bread and wine in the **Holy Supper**. §. III. Arguments by which the Orthodox confirmed their own opinion. §. IV. The arguments of the Zwinglians weighed and examined. §. V. VI. VII. The second question: Whether Judas received the **Holy Supper**, or was made a partaker of the body and blood of Christ? §. VIII. Which the Orthodox affirmed against the Zwinglians. §. IX. The third question: concerning the benefit <note>original: "fructu"</note> of the **Holy Supper**. The Zwinglians denied that there is forgiveness of sins in the **Holy Supper**; the Orthodox affirmed it. §. X. Whose opinion is explained and defended. §. XI. XII. Amsdorf seems to have been excessively vehement <note>Amsdorf was known for his uncompromising and sometimes harsh polemical style.</note> in this cause. §. XIII. There was some departure from the original principle in this controversy, and it was argued with some ambiguity. §. XIV.*

-># PREFACE.<-

*Perhaps no one will find fault with a more careful examination of churches that are confined to specific regions or cities, and the events that took place within them, except for those who think nothing is right unless they have done it themselves. Not to mention that it is customary—unless we are enemies of literature—to read with singular pleasure the deeds of our very own ancestors; the path to constructing a universal history must be prepared through the development of specific, local histories. Thus, since I have obtained certain documents from my blessed father and ancestors which I believed could be usefully applied to public use, I wished this* **Specimen** <note>A "specimen" in this context refers to a sample or inaugural piece of scholarship presented to the public.</note> *of my future labors regarding the first* **sacramentarian** <term>Sacramentarian</term> <note>A term used, often pejoratively by Lutherans, to describe reformers like Zwingli who viewed the bread and wine of the Eucharist as symbols rather than the literal body and blood of Christ.</note> *disturbances in* **Goslar** <note>An important imperial city in Lower Saxony, Germany, which became a center of Reformation conflict.</note> *to be published: both because the order of time assigns them the first place, and because the venerable Valentin Ernst Löscher mentioned them in Part I of his* **History of the Movements** <note>original Latin: "Hist. Mot." referring to Löscher's "Historia Motuum," a famous history of the Lutheran-Reformed controversies</note> *on page 205 of the first edition, and page 191 of the later edition, based on H. W. Triumph’s* **Church History of Goslar** <note>original German: "Goslarischer Kirchen-Historie"</note>; *I wished therefore to reveal a fuller account of these matters. If these works are not displeasing, the later sacramentarian disturbances will follow in due time—the acts involving* **Bunting, Triller** <note>Local figures or theologians involved in the continuing religious disputes in the region.</note> *and certain other matters—though in such a way that I will be more concise in rendering judgment than in this specimen, which had to be simultaneously adapted to the nature of a* **Theological Disputation** <note>A formal academic debate or thesis defended at a university.</note>. *In the meantime, look with favor upon these things, kind reader, and expect from me a more expanded version of the aforementioned* **Ecclesiastical History of Goslar** <note>original: "H. E. Goslar."</note> *by Triumph, given a* **favorable opportunity** <note>original Greek: "εὐκαιρίᾳ"</note>.

# SECTION I.
## HISTORY
### §. I.

Dr. John $(a)$ AMANDUS, the first Superintendent of the people of **Goslar** <note>An important Imperial City in Lower Saxony that joined the Reformation early on.</note> since the church was purified by **Luther** <note>Referring to the Protestant Reformation initiated by Martin Luther.</note>, had already fallen under suspicion of **Zwinglianism** $(b)$ <term>Zwinglianism</term> <note>The theological system of Huldrych Zwingli, which differed from Luther’s primarily regarding the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist.</note> even before the erroneous views of Master HENRY KNIGGIUS—whom at that time not yet in sacred [orders]...

---

$(a)$ He is wrongly called *Peter* by Hartknoch and Seckendorf, according to JOH. MICH. HEINECCIUS in *Antiquities of Goslar, p. 448.* For, to pass over other matters, Amandus himself undoubtedly must be said to have given himself the name *John*, as is clear from a monument which I am pleased to describe in the words of SIMON STRUBIUS: "In honor of Peter Kilhorn (Minister of the Goslar Church from 1572 to 1591; see my uncle Henr. Wilh. Trumphius’s **Church History of Goslar**, *p. 77*), in the house he purchased from St. James Church, he [Amandus] had a coat of arms in the window with these words beneath: *John Amandus, Bearer of the Word of Jesus Christ.*" <note>original German: "In Ehrn Petri Kilhorns... Iohannes Amandus Wortholder JESU Christi."</note> From a manuscript treatise titled *Saint James*, written by SIMON STRUBIUS, my great-great-grandfather, who was Deacon and later Pastor of St. James in Goslar from 1578 to 1616 (see *H. W. Trumphius, as cited above, pp. 77–78*). In this work, he covered the affairs of the Goslar churches of his own time and the period immediately preceding, and I do not deny that we owe a great deal of what we shall say to this source, as will be clear from the citations. These notes were recorded around the year 1531.

$(b)$ HEINECCIUS briefly describes his life in *Antiquities.*

Goslar, p. 448. Those things which can be added to this will be reserved for the new edition of the *Ecclesiastical History of Goslar*.

$(c)$ Kniggius was among the first after Luther’s reformation to teach Christian doctrine in its pure form in Brunswick <note>Latin: "Brunsvigae"</note>, according to HAMELMANN’S *Historical Genealogical Works on the Reborn Gospel in Illustrious Brunswick, p. 907, 909.* Afterward, near the end of the year 1528, he was expelled from there because of <term>Sacramentarianism</term> <note>The theological view, contrary to Luther's, that the bread and wine of the Eucharist are merely symbolic of Christ's body and blood.</note>, as noted by HAMELMANN in the cited work, p. 909, 912; see also **Rehtmeyer’s Church History of Brunswick**, Part III, ch. 5, p. 73 ff. and 80 ff. For we rightly marvel at the knowledge of most unique events concerning the reborn Gospel shown by HAMELMANN in various places, but he is mistaken <note>Latin: "Hallucinari," literally 'is hallucinating' or dreaming.</note> when he asserts that Corvinus succeeded Knigge in the *Historical Genealogical Works*, Part II, p. 871, in the section on the reborn Gospel in the city of Goslar. Both these local documents show the truth, and Heineccius observed it from Corvinus’s own treatise (which I will cite in a moment) in *Antiquities of Goslar, p. 450.* Chytraeus, in *Saxonia* for the year 1531, p. 333, makes the same error as Hamelmann.

$(d)$ Preacher at the Market Church <note>Latin: "aedem forensem"</note>, as they call it; see note $(d)$ to §. II. Mention of him during the actual disturbances is not as frequent as that of Kniggius—whether by chance, or because Kniggius was the “torch and trumpet” <note>Meaning the primary instigator and spokesperson.</note> while Gravert was merely Kniggius’s follower.

$(e)$ Corvinus was the first Evangelical Pastor appointed to St. Stephen’s in Goslar in 1528. I tell you, that is exactly how it happens: whenever there is now a poor fellow whom people would like to trample underfoot, a snare must be laid for him with such lies. Had these two sects of Zwingli and Müntzer <note>Thomas Müntzer, a radical reformer and leader in the Peasants' War, often grouped with Zwingli by their detractors as "fanatics."</note> not arisen, with what would Satan drive poor fellows out of the Lord’s vineyard! Not that I wish to defend the <term>Tropists</term> <note>From the word "trope"; a derogatory term for those who interpreted "This is my body" as a figure of speech or metaphor.</note>, but rather that it vexes me that those who are innocent of this matter should suffer because of it. He is so friendly toward me that even if he kept it secret [from others], he would have confessed it to me. Now he does not keep it secret, nor has he ever taught it publicly, as all of Goslar must admit; yet he must be labeled a <term>Schwärmer</term> <note>A German term meaning "fanatic" or "enthusiast," used by Luther and his followers to dismiss radical reformers who claimed direct inspiration from the Holy Spirit.</note>.

### §. II.

These whisperings were the preludes to the battles that were soon to give rise to even greater disturbances, (b) of which you may receive this
->summary<-
from the manuscript letters (i) of **HELMBOLD POPPIUS**, a colleague of *Knigge*:

---

(b) Around the end of the year 1529 and the following year. <note>See Hamelmann in the place cited, note c, §. I.</note>

(i) Regarding POPPIUS, STRUBIUS says in the place cited for the year 1528: <note>original German: "Um diese Zeit ist auch Ehr Helmboldus Poppius, der ein fein gelehrter Münch zu Rittershausen gewesen war / zu St. Stephan gewesen."</note> "Around this time, the honorable Helmbold Poppius, who had been a fine, learned monk at Rittershausen, was at Saint Stephen’s." He wrote letters of great value to a friend about the disturbances caused by Knigge; because he was Knigge's colleague, he could not have been better informed about these matters. Nor can it be proven by any evidence that he indulged in wicked biases; on the contrary, it appears from his gentle manner of writing about his adversary—contrary to the customs of those times—that he was a fair witness. Strubius preserved these letters in the place cited for the year 1537, prefaced by these words: <note>original German: "Wie es sich darinn verhält / (dimissionem Kniggii indigitat) hat Ehr Helmboldus Poppius, Capplan zu St. Stephan und des Kniggen Collega zu der Zeit an einen seiner guten Freunde geschrieben"</note> "How the matter stands therein (referring to Knigge's dismissal), the honorable Helmbold Poppius, chaplain at Saint Stephen’s and Knigge's colleague at that time, wrote to one of his good friends." We are not reluctant to record these letters here, for to us, reviewing the doctrine of those times is of more value than the mere history:
> Grace and peace be with you. Receive briefly the cause of the banishment of Master Henricus Knigge. In almost all his sermons, he drummed these two arguments especially into the people: "Christ sits at the right hand of the Father, therefore <note>The letter uses "E." as an abbreviation for the Latin *ergo*.</note> he is not in the bread." Even though he later stated to his listeners that "Christ is not in the bread or the sacrament of the altar corporally," he did so in such a way that you would believe him a Proteus <note>A figure from Greek myth who could change his shape; Poppius implies Knigge was being slippery or evasive in his definitions.</note>; for he neither affirmed that Christ was present corporally in the Supper, nor did he deny it. Nevertheless, he contended with all his strength and energy that they should not treat this article of faith—"Christ sits at the right hand of the Father"—as something childish, as if it were something they had learned from their mother in the cradle, but rather that they should look more deeply into the matter—

...ment <note>original: "men"; likely the conclusion of a word such as "certamen" (struggle) or "nomen" (name) from the previous page</note>. Knigge seemed to deny, in his public sermons, the real [presence] of the body and blood

and that they should diligently weigh what it means that Christ, a true and natural man and the son of Mary, was taken up into heaven with body and blood, bones and nerves. Likewise, [they should weigh] what it means when He says: *The poor you will always have, but me you will not always have* <note>Matthew 26:11</note>. And again: *I am no longer in the world* <note>John 17:11</note>. And that word of the Apostle: *Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer* <note>2 Corinthians 5:16</note>. He proposed these things as if they were in conflict with one another, and from them he wished to infer that Christ is indeed in heaven in his body, but not bodily in the sacrament of the Eucharist <note>The Lord's Supper</note>, despite the word of Christ: *This is my body* <note>Matthew 26:26</note>; rather, [he argued Christ is present] only sacramentally and as a sign. Finally, he always asserted that it was against the Christian faith if anyone said at the same time that Christ was bodily in heaven and also bodily in the sacrament of the altar. 

Another thing which he never failed to preach was that the <term>forgiveness of sins</term> <note>original: <term>remissio peccatorum</term></note> by no means happens to those who receive the sacrament of Christ's body and blood. Instead, he argued that they must already have the forgiveness of sins beforehand, and that the sacrament is only an external sign by which a believer is distinguished from an unbeliever.

Since he was teaching these things openly and rumors about him were growing daily, he was warned by the other brothers who announce the word of Christ here, lest he produce sects or divisions. [They told him] that it is by no means against Scripture that Christ is bodily in heaven and in the bread; indeed, it is consistent with Scripture, which hands down both: *Christ sits at the right hand of the Father*, and *Take and eat, this is my body*. And although it is unknown to us how it happens that the same body is in heaven and in the sacrament, yet here the word of Christ must be grasped by faith, for He cannot lie, nor is it right to make God a liar in His own word. 

Furthermore, [they argued] it is by no means against the Christian faith if one says they will receive the forgiveness of sins in the sacrament: not indeed because of the physical <term>eating</term> <note>original: <term>manducatio</term></note>, but because of the word of Christ. ...the presence of Christ in the Holy Supper <note>original: *S. coena*, or the Eucharist</note>. Then also concerning [the fact that it is not only a badge to] distinguish Christians, but also a sign of grace, which certainly reminds us to believe that we have the forgiveness of sins through the death of Christ, which was indeed achieved once on the cross, but is distributed daily through His Sacrament and His word. 

But this reminder moved him not at all; instead, it irritated him more and more, so that a grave contention arose among us preachers, not without great danger to the souls of the people. Finally, the matter was brought before the Senate <note>the city council of Goslar</note>. The Senate requested that both parties remain quiet until our Consul, Christian Baller, returned from the imperial assembly <note>original: *comitiis*; likely referring to the Diet of Augsburg</note>—for at that time he was staying in Augsburg. He promised he would do his utmost to ensure this dispute was settled by learned men; in the meantime, we were to remain silent about the sacraments so that disagreements and riots would not arise. 

But Henry <note>Henricus Knigge</note> did not obey this order either. Instead, even more than before, he took great pains to lecture at length on the sacraments, with the result that the people were split into two factions. A large part sided with the Pastor of St. Stephen’s, to the point that some did not fear to say publicly that only bread and wine are present in the Lord’s Supper, and not the body and blood of Christ. 

Conversely, the other side affirmed that the true body and blood of Christ are there, and that one receives the forgiveness of sins through the sacraments, provided they are received with faith. To be brief: Dr. Nicolaus Amsdorf was summoned here, as he was the first Bishop of our city who first laid the foundations of the Gospel truth here. 

When he ascended the pulpit, he publicly refuted these aforementioned arguments as heretical (you may see this sermon, which was already printed at that time, in Heineccius, *Antiquities of Goslar, p. 456 and following*). Then, on the third day, with the entire Senate present, a public debate was held between Dr. Nicolaus Amsdorf and Henry Knigge. 

First, Dr. Amsdorf began by saying: Christ is not to be sought in heaven according to Henry’s doctrine, nor at the right hand of the Father. He is indeed in heaven at the right hand of the Father according to the universal <note>original: *catholicam*, referring to the historic creeds of the church</note> faith, but there [he said] by no means...

<meta>This page continues the theological debate between Nicolaus von Amsdorf and the local preachers Henry Knigge and John in Goslar. The previous page established that tensions had risen over the nature of the Eucharist, leading to Amsdorf's arrival to resolve the dispute.</meta>

# ### ...that they had taught incorrectly concerning the fruit of this sacrament, saying— ###

---

[Christ] is to be sought, but here in the sacrament and in the word, according to that saying of the Apostle: *Do not say in your heart, "Who shall ascend into heaven?" The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.* <note>original: "Ne dixeris in corde tuo, quis ascendet in coelum, prope est verbum in ore tuo & in corde tuo" — Romans 10:6-8. Amsdorf argues that Christ's presence is accessible through the Church's rituals rather than being a distant celestial mystery.</note> 

But Henry <note>Henricus Knigge</note> contended the opposite: that Christ is to be sought above in heaven, according to the same Apostle: *If you have risen together with Christ, seek those things which are above,* etc. <note>original: "Si simul surrexistis cum Christo, quae sursum sunt, quaerite" — Colossians 3:1. This reflects the "Sacramentarian" or Reformed view that Christ's body is physically located in heaven and not on the altar.</note> 

Amsdorf replied: "This passage of Paul does not forbid seeking Christ in the sacrament, but rather intends that Christians should live not according to the desires of the flesh, but according to the spirit of Christ." From which it follows: *Mortify your members,* etc. <note>original: "Mortificate membra vestra" — Colossians 3:5</note> Henry replied that he did not deny that Christ must also be sought in the sacrament and in His word.

Secondly, Amsdorf questioned Henry whether he believed that Judas had eaten the body of the Lord with the other Apostles. <note>This was a classic "litmus test" in Reformation theology: if the bread literally *is* Christ, then even the wicked eat it. If it is only a symbol, the wicked receive nothing but bread.</note> 

Henry replied that he had doubts about this; it seemed incredible to him, since Judas, as Christ testified, was a devil. And Christ said: *Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.* <note>John 6:54</note> From this it would follow that Christ would have two bodies—one for believers and another for unbelievers. *What fellowship has Christ with Belial <note>a name for the devil</note>, or what part has a believer with an unbeliever?* <note>2 Corinthians 6:15</note> 

Amsdorf replied: "Eating Christ is understood in two ways: 
1) Christ is eaten **spiritually**, which is what John discusses. In this manner, only believers eat the body of Christ. Therefore, the entire sixth chapter of John—even by the testimony of the Sacramentarians <note>A term used by Lutherans for those who denied the Real Presence, such as followers of Zwingli</note> themselves—pertains only to spiritual eating. 
2) The body of Christ is eaten **sacramentally**; in this way, not only believers but also unbelievers eat the body of Christ, according to the Apostolic word: *Whoever eats unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.*" <note>1 Corinthians 11:27</note> 

Finally, they came to the last point: "You," said Amsdorf, "Henry and John, both of you have taught openly that there is no forgiveness of sins in the sacrament; what do you say to this?" Both replied that this was indeed so.

To this, Dr. [Amsdorf] began...

# SECTION II.
## JUDGMENT
### §. I.

Proceeding now to the second section of our dissertation, both concerning the status of the controversy and—

---

...[for]eigners, not men. <note>The sentence fragment suggests a distinction between those who are truly part of the community and those considered outsiders or "not human" in their behavior.</note> Who has ever heard or read that this saying—*he who eats my bread, treads me under his feet*—belongs to the Sacrament? Christ speaks thus in **John 13**: *I do not speak of you all; I know whom I have chosen; but that the Scripture may be fulfilled, He who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me.* <note>original: "der mein Brod isset/ der trit mich mit füssen"</note> Christ laments here that His friend, who daily ate and drank with Him, would betray Him, as **Psalm 41** clearly indicates, from which this saying is taken; there it is written: *But my friend, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, treads me under his feet*, as if Christ wanted to say: a stranger or my enemy will not betray me, but my friend, who is constantly with me at my table, he will betray me. Thus, this saying does not contain a single letter about the Sacrament and pertains to the Sacrament as much as the sayings about the five loaves and the breaking of bread at **Emmaus**, etc. <note>original: *mox* (presently); used here to indicate a skip in the quoted source material.</note> Therefore, they should be ashamed in their hearts that they dare to come before the people with these and similar **Zwinglian** <note>Followers of Huldrych Zwingli, whom the author accuses of reducing the Eucharist to a mere symbol.</note> sayings, which they do not understand, nor do they know where they belong, and yet they want to boast and fight with them against the divine truth. Similarly, they acted shamelessly regarding **Abraham** and **Cornelius** <note>A reference to the Roman centurion in Acts 10; the debate likely concerned whether one can be justified by faith/spirit before receiving external rites.</note> and dared to say to my face (which both the old and new Council along with the congregation heard) that they were justified without the external Word. <note>The "external Word" refers to the audible preaching of the Gospel and the physical administration of Sacraments, which Lutherans insisted were the necessary means of grace.</note> What that means (praise be to **God**) I understand well. These are **Zwinglian** arguments by which everything that was externally ordained and established by Christ is rejected.

...[me]n, Amsdorf prepared a defense in a printed letter. (r)

<margin>(r) Strubius in the place cited, for the year 1531.</margin> In that same [15]31st year—after the expelled **Zwinglian** preachers <note>Followers of the Swiss reformer Huldrych Zwingli, who taught that the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper were symbolic rather than the literal body and blood of Christ.</note> sent out all sorts of defamatory pamphlets <note>original: *Schmäh-Karten*</note> to justify their cause—Licentiate Nicolaus von Amsdorf had a letter printed. In it, he explains the reasons why the two preachers, Master Johann Grawert and Master Heinrich Knigge, were driven out of Goslar. They had preached **Zwinglian** arguments and subject matter and hammered it into the people, yet they nonetheless claimed they were not Zwinglians. <note>Amsdorf is accusing them of "crypto-Zwinglianism"—secretly holding views they publicly denied.</note> On page A. iii. b. [he writes]: Now they are public liars, in that they publicly denied the Zwinglian teaching while being crude, unlearned, and shameless heads who know and can do nothing. Finally, they are poisoned by Zwinglian error and devilish heresy, entirely drowned and hardened in it, as they prove with this verse from **John 13**: *He who eats my bread treads me under his feet.* <note>original: "Wer mein Brod isset / der tritt mich mit Füssen." This refers to John 13:18.</note> 

They threw this verse at me and asked me what Christ meant by it; for shortly before, in the pulpit where he had cited that same verse, he had bellowed and screamed—as those crude ass-heads are wont to do—"Do you see? Here it says bread, bread, bread! Judas ate bread, not the body of Christ!" Previously, they publicly lied, saying they were not Zwinglian and had never used his arguments nor preached them; yet now, with this verse, they trap themselves, showing they are Zwinglian through and through. For he [the preacher] expected me to answer just as he had preached and now publicly confessed before the whole Council and the friends of the community: that Judas had eaten mere bread and not the body of Christ, because Christ says: *he who eats my bread treads me under his feet.* Therefore, he could not believe that Judas had eaten the body of Christ. Such things they teach, such things they preach, such things they confess, and yet they claim not to be Zwinglian and dare to say they have not preached Zwinglian arguments. Out with the liars! But is it not a pity that such unlearned asses dare to undertake preaching? They should preach to sows and dogs... <note>The text cuts off here as the author transitions to the next page.</note>

both Word and sign, which is a damned heresy <note>The "heresy" Amsdorf refers to is the idea that one can have a relationship with God through "spirit" alone, bypassing the physical church, Bible, or sacraments.</note>; for one must and shall come to the Spirit and faith through the external Word and sign, and not otherwise. **God** has so ordered and commanded it. It is also a lie that both <term>Abraham</term> and <term>Cornelius</term> <note>Amsdorf’s opponents likely cited these biblical figures to prove that God grants the Spirit directly without rituals. Cornelius (Acts 10) was a Gentile who received the Holy Spirit before being baptized.</note> were made righteous without an external Word: Abraham’s words are expressed in the Scripture in Genesis 12, which Abraham believed and thereby became righteous, as in Romans 4. Regarding Cornelius, it is written in Acts 10 thus: "He was godly and God-fearing with his whole house." If he was God-fearing, he must have known **God** through faith; how else could he have feared Him? If he believed in **God**, then he must indeed have had a Word that he believed, for faith cannot exist without the Word, as in Romans 10: "But how shall they believe in Him of whom they have not heard?" If he wanted to say, "Should they believe, they must hear." Since Cornelius feared and knew **God** through faith, he must have heard a Word from **God**.

Therefore these are rascally tricks they deal in, that they falsify the Scripture and open the mouths of the poor common man with their shouting and thus falsely mislead them. Therefore, because I myself have seen and heard all this—namely, that they cannot tolerate that we seek **Christ** in the **Word** and **Sacrament** and there obtain forgiveness of sins, and furthermore they publicly deny what they have preached, and yet reveal and betray themselves as <term>Zwinglian</term> <note>original: *Zwickglische*. A reference to the Swiss reformer Huldrych Zwingli. Lutherans like Amsdorf were often in bitter conflict with Zwinglians over the nature of the Lord’s Supper.</note> heretics, as heard; also that they are so unlearned and ignorant in the Scripture, and finally, that they regard the **Sacrament** as mere bread and wine—so I would and should not tolerate them as preachers any longer, since an <term>Honorable Council</term> <note>original: *Erbar Radt*. The governing body of the city of Goslar.</note> and the community have entrusted and commanded this office to me. For one cannot and should not tolerate in Christendom that **Christ's** Word and ordinance should be despised, changed, and manipulated; rather, every Christian shall [hold] **Christ's** Word and ordinance, however minor and external [they may seem]...

The state of the controversy primarily turns on this matter: that our local *Zwinglians* <note>Followers of the Swiss Reformer Huldrych Zwingli, who argued that the bread and wine in the Lord's Supper were symbols rather than the literal body and blood of Christ.</note> have asserted that Christ is not in the bread and wine distributed in the Holy Supper, that is, in

[...if they were] destroyed by emptiness. The sheep would flourish and increase if wolves were set over them as shepherds. Finally, they attached this question to their <term>libelous pamphlet</term> <note>original: *Schmee-Büchlein*. A polemical, often anonymous publication intended to mock an opponent.</note> with these words: "A simple question for the laity. Tell me if you know it: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; Flesh, Blood, Bread, and Wine. Can all that truly be one God?" 

This question is not the question of a simple layman, but of a godless, unbelieving villain, who believes neither in God, Christ, nor His Word; who mocks and most highly blasphemes and defiles Christ with His works, order, and Word. A simple layman believes the word of Christ, "This is my body, this is my blood," and remains there with a simple heart. But unbelieving <term>reason</term> <note>original: *Vernunfft*. In this context, it refers to human logic that refuses to accept divine mysteries that it cannot physically explain.</note>, since it can neither grasp nor understand God’s work and word, falls away from it, blasphemes and defiles God’s word, mocks His work, and wants to be wiser and do it better than God. 

This is just as the heathens despised and mocked the Christians for holding and worshiping a crucified man as God, according to the sound of divine scripture and divine words. So also do these <term>desecrators of the Sacrament</term> <note>original: *Sacrament Schender*. A common Lutheran term for those who denied the Real Presence of Christ's body and blood in the bread and wine.</note> act; they laugh at us, mock, defile, and blaspheme us because we believe, according to the sound of the words of Christ, that the bread is the true body of Christ. 

Therefore, we will let them go with their human wisdom as if they were <term>Heathens and Turks</term> <note>A common 16th-century rhetorical grouping to denote those outside the Christian faith.</note>, and we shall hold the words of Christ dear and worthy along with all the angels, and believe firmly from the whole heart, however foolish they may sound to reason. May our dear Lord Jesus Christ help us all in this, Amen.

It can be proven that the <term>minor premise</term> <note>In a logical argument (syllogism), the minor premise is the second statement that applies the general rule of the major premise to a specific case.</note> stands on firm ground in the following way. God willed that humans be instructed in the knowledge of spiritual things through Holy Scripture (2 Timothy 3:15–17, etc.). Therefore, it is necessary that the words of Holy Scripture pour out a certain and distinct meaning, or produce certain and clear concepts in those reading attentively, so that they might know from it that this is the nature of spiritual things, and not another: in this consists true knowledge.

Therefore, the words of Holy Scripture signify that which they ordinarily and properly signify in other writings by human custom and designation; or, if they must signify something else, then it is necessary that certain marks exist by which the first and ordinary mode of signifying is redirected to another. For if this were denied, a certain concept of spiritual things could not be obtained from Holy Scripture.

But Holy Scripture uses such words regarding the Holy Supper which, according to their customary meaning, produce this sense of the substantial presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Holy Supper. For when Christ says in Matthew 26:26, while offering the bread: "Take, eat, this is my body" <note>original Greek: λάβετε, φάγετε, τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμά μου</note>; these words, according to the common use of speech and the nature of <term>exhibitive propositions</term> <note>A statement where an object is not just described, but actually presented or "exhibited" to the recipient through the speaking of the words.</note>, signify nothing other than that Christ offered, and the disciples consequently received and ate, the substantial body of Christ.

### §. VI.

The following passage, from 2 Corinthians 5:16, which [our opponents] have fought with, is no more of an obstacle: *even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer.* (h) <note>original: "etsi cognovimus secundum carnem Christum, sed nunc iam non novimus"</note> First, no one will deny that this saying is somewhat obscure; sound reason in the practice of interpretation dictates that an obscure passage should not be used to destroy the proper and ordinary meaning of a clear and transparent declaration. Second, if we were to grant that the phrase *according to the flesh* should be understood as meaning *we no longer know the body and person of Christ on earth*, that knowledge would still only be denied in the same sense it was asserted in the first half of the verse. Since it is said there that *we have known Christ according to the flesh*, it cannot be denied—even by our adversaries—that this should be understood as having looked upon Christ with the physical eyes. That this ocular <term>ocular: relating to physical sight or the eyes</term> knowledge has been removed, and is not restored through the <term>substantial presence: the doctrine that the actual substance of Christ's body and blood are present in the bread and wine</term> substantial presence of Christ’s Body and Blood in the Sacred Supper <note>The "Sacred Supper" refers to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, is something that no adherent of the <term>Augsburg Confession: the primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church, delivered in 1530</term> Augsburg Confession has ever denied.

However, consider this exposition of the passage drawn from the mouth of the most venerable Lord Presiding Official: In verse 15, it says *we must live for Christ*; the hinge of the Christian life turns on this. In verse 16, it says *therefore we know no one according to the flesh*, which means we grant no one a special privilege because of their birth from Abraham or other external factors. *Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh*—that is, even if we Jews are joined to Christ by the closeness of our race—nevertheless, *now and henceforth* [we no longer regard him merely in that way].

Furthermore, Holy Scripture explains that <term>session</term><note>The "Session of Christ" is the theological term for Christ's state of dignity and power after his Ascension, traditionally described as "sitting" at God's right hand.</note> (which is to be understood metaphorically) in no other way than through the <term>communication</term><note>In this context, "communication" refers to the sharing of divine attributes (like power and omnipresence) with Christ's human nature.</note> of the full use of divine power and majesty granted to the human nature of Christ, as is clear from Ephesians 1:20–22: *[God] seated [Christ] at his right hand in the heavens, far above all rule and authority, etc.* 1 Corinthians 15:25: *He [Christ] must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet.* Compare Psalm 110:1: <note>The text cites Ps. CXI (111), but the quote is from the famous Messianic Psalm 110.</note> *Jehovah said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.* This explanation is perfectly consistent with the meaning of the word "right hand" when it is used to represent power. See Exodus 15:6: *Your right hand, O Jehovah, shatters the enemy.* Psalm 118:16: *The right hand of Jehovah is exalted; the right hand of Jehovah acts mightily.* It is clear from this that: 1. Our opponents have not proven their own explanation of the "sitting" at the right hand of God. 2. There is another explanation that is far truer, which makes it clear that this "sitting" in no way contradicts Christ’s substantial presence in the Holy Supper.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether the "fruit" or benefit of the Lord's Supper includes the actual forgiveness of sins, specifically examining the views of the Zwinglians and the Lutheran theologian Nikolaus von Amsdorf.</meta>

<page-num>652</page-num>

Our local Zwinglians <note>Followers of the Swiss reformer Huldrych Zwingli, who generally viewed the sacraments as signs or memorials rather than direct means of grace.</note> maintain: *in this sacrament there is no remission of sins* <note>original: "in sacramento isthoc non est remissio peccatorum"</note>. This can be understood in two ways: either that the sacramental action—whether you consider the roles of the humans using and administering it, or the roles of God and Christ—is not the very action by which sins are forgiven; or in this way: that the sacramental action is not an action through which those using it, even if they have faith, are reminded that their sins have been forgiven, and thus the remission of sins is confirmed for them.

Since, therefore, they denied the remission of sins itself, but *not the confirmation of that remission*; and since they maintained that for those communicating worthily, sins must have been forgiven beforehand (an assertion with which the actual remission of sins, and not the confirmation of remission, is in conflict), the former sense of their proposition—concerning the denial of remission itself—seems thus far to be attributed to them. But what they add—namely, that *the Holy Supper is only an external sign by which the believer is distinguished from the unbeliever*—finally brings it about that we seem to be able to attribute to them, without injustice, the denial of the confirmation of the remission of sins as well.

It is not much easier to clarify what was in the mind of *Amsdorf* <note>Nikolaus von Amsdorf (1483–1565), a close friend of Luther and a strict "Gnesio-Lutheran" who often took polarizing stances.</note> <note>[x] in the place cited.</note>; yet we believe his view was this: that not the remission of sins itself, but its confirmation, is obtained from the Holy Supper, and he wished to defend this very point. This is suggested by the fairness <term>equity</term> <note>A principle of interpretation that seeks to read an author's words in the most favorable and reasonable light.</note> we owe to great men, which commands us to exempt them, where possible, from the fault of error or of a less accurately established dispute. It is also suggested by the fact that *Amsdorf represents the Holy Supper as a sign of divine grace*, and describes it, like the Word of God, as [a means of] remission—

...that the certainty of the remission of sins might be acknowledged, we do not doubt that it can be proven by the following arguments.

### §. XII.

1. A benefit <term>Beneficium</term> is when one person presents something to another who does not deserve it, by which—with the giver's knowledge and will—the other person's happiness can be promoted.
2. We know something "with probability" <term>Verisimiliter</term> <note>The author is using logical terminology here to distinguish between absolute necessity and a reliable, frequent occurrence.</note> when we see its reason, from which that which we know follows quite often, though not always or necessarily. 
3. In this context, we define Love <term>Amor</term> as occurring when someone is so inclined toward another that they desire to promote their happiness. 
4. Therefore, we recognize one who presents a benefit to another as someone who is likely driven by love toward them. For experience itself and the nature of things teach that benefits most often proceed from those who love—indeed, they are presented as a token <term>tesseram</term> <note>original: "tesseram" — a sign, token, or password used to recognize a friend or ally.</note> of love. 
5. Faithfulness <term>Fidelitas</term> is when someone exhibits signs through words or deeds toward another, from which it can likely be known that they are well-inclined toward the other, and in truth, they *are* so inclined. Everyone holds this concept of faithfulness. Since a deceitful and hypocritical mind is the opposite of this, everyone admits that he is devoid of faithfulness who, through words and deeds staged to appear like love, hides a latent bitterness of mind or at least a lack of love. 
6. God is abundant in faithfulness. *1 Corinthians 1:9: God is faithful. 1 Thessalonians 5:24: Faithful is he who called you, who also will do it.* 
7. The Holy Supper <term>s. coena</term> <note>original: "s. coena" — an abbreviation for *sacra coena*, the Sacred Supper or Eucharist.</note> is a benefit from God (see point 1). For God has prepared it for people who use it—though they are undeserving—and who are to be more strongly moved by sensible signs <note>Physical elements like bread and wine.</note>, for the explanation of Himself. *1 Corinthians 11:28.* [It is] an exercise of faith.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the theological disputes involving Friedrich Knigge and the followers of Zwingli. ...principles, <note>original: "la"; likely completing the word "regula" (rule or principle) from the previous page.</note> which teach what must be done or what must be avoided, usually recommend themselves by their own clarity. They should be reinforced frequently rather than proven at great length, lest they slip from the mind, or lest we neglect to obey them when the opportunity arises. First, therefore—unless clear evidence of a change of heart exists—those who have participated in false doctrine in other places should not be easily admitted to public office. We are taught this by the example of *Knigge* <note>Friedrich Knigge (1549–1611) was a controversial theologian whose shifting views on the nature of the Eucharist caused significant friction within Lutheran territories.</note>, who was expelled from *Brunswick* <note>original: "Brunswiga"; referring to the city or Duchy of Braunschweig.</note> due to *Zwinglian* errors <margin>(k) See the place cited, Section 1, c, page 4.</margin> and who was found to be promoting those same errors again in *Goslar*. This is supported by many other examples: it is not easy for a vice to be cast out once the mind has been imbued with it. This same *Knigge*, while suppressing his error, nevertheless taught things from which, by logical consequence, others were infected. <margin>(l) See the place cited, Section 2, b, page 7.</margin> This warns us to be cautious whenever we notice those who are like *Knigge*. Indeed, one should not immediately attribute an error to a person if their speech does not contain it expressly, but merely suggests it through logical consequences; nevertheless, unless other factors prevent it, we are rightly made anxious that such a person might be infected by that error.

At the same time, it is beyond doubt that the same power of the purer religion which we profess through divine favor was present in the early days of the Christian religion itself, when it was first spread throughout the world by the <term>Savior</term> <note>original: "Servatore"; referring to Jesus Christ.</note> and his friends. For this reason, the work of the **Reformation**, as it is called, was not brought to completion by human effort or strategy, but was undertaken and carried out by the will and help of God. 

But one may also hope for other benefits from this work. The sycophants of the <term>Roman Court</term> <note>original: "aulae Romanae"; referring to the papal administration in Rome and its hangers-on.</note> will blush when these things are known—if, indeed, any sense of shame or religion remains in them. They will come to curse the cruelty of their ancestors toward innocent men who were stained by no other vice than their steadfastness in defending the truth they had clearly seen. 

Furthermore, our own people, upon seeing and reading these illustrious examples, will find an opportunity—should they choose—to praise the divine kindness by which we have been delivered into freedom from the brutality of our enemies. Likewise, they may find occasion to acknowledge and correct their own laziness and sluggishness, with which—alas! <note>original: "prob dolor!"; a Latin exclamation expressing grief or "to our shame."</note>—we struggle all too much today.

Influenced by these reasons, I have allowed myself to spend several of those hours left free from my duties—whenever the responsibilities I hold by God's will keep me away from home—on the translation of this **Spanish Martyrology**...

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

Emperor Charles V <note>Charles V (1500–1558) was the Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain; he was a central figure in the European religious conflicts of the 16th century.</note> and his son Philip sent theologians of exceptional reputation and learning from Spain into Germany, England, and the Netherlands <note>original: "Belgium", which at this time referred to the Low Countries, encompassing modern-day Netherlands and Belgium.</note> to bring the Protestants in these provinces back to the obedience of the Roman Church. However, once these men had read the books of those who had set out to restore religion, and after they had held conversations and debates with them, they renounced <note>original: "nuntium miserunt", literally "sent a message," a Latin idiom meaning to formally break off a relationship or renounce a tradition.</note> the very sacred rites they had received as tradition from their ancestors. Filled with fervor and a desire to spread the holy religion they had embraced among their own fellow citizens, they returned home. 

They lacked nothing that is necessary for a man undertaking such a holy and difficult work: for they shone with incomparable piety and were equipped with a great abundance of learning. And so, their plan and effort succeeded so well that I have no doubt they would have purged the entire kingdom of Spain of Roman superstitions in an even shorter space of time than occurred in other provinces, had not the cruelty and harshness of the *Inquisition*, as they call it, early and forcefully intervened against their pious labors. For it can hardly be said how much the heavenly doctrine, through such excellent men...

# MARTYROLOGY
## OF THOSE WHO MET DEATH IN SPAIN FOR THE RELIGION OF THE PROTESTANTS.

Around the Year of Christ 1440, a great multitude of people, by the command and instigation of the Inquisitors, were forced by royal soldiers to travel from the mountainous parts of the province of *Durango* <note>original: *Duringo*; a town in the Basque Country of northern Spain</note>, which is part of *Biscay*, to *Valladolid* <note>original: *Vallisoletum*</note> and to the *shrine of Santo Domingo de la Calzada* <note>original: *fanum Dominici de Calcadar*; a significant stop on the pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela</note>. In these cities, they were put to death by the flames because they refused to renounce several doctrines which are held as *heretical* by the Roman Popes.

What kind of doctrines these were, the profession of which brought death and destruction to so many people, is nowhere found recorded in the historical record. However, it is most likely that they were the same as those of the *Waldensians* <note>A Christian movement originating in the 12th century that sought a return to the poverty and simplicity of the early Church; they were frequently targeted by the Inquisition and often sought refuge in remote mountain ranges</note>, who inhabit the Alpine valleys. For the doctrine of the early Christians was preserved pure and unstained in certain mountainous regions—to which access is very difficult—up until this time, because neither the Monks devoted to the Roman Pope nor the Inquisitors had reached those places to either corrupt the religion itself or to execute its faithful and noble professors.

### AGUSTÍN CAZALLA

In the year of our Lord 1558, **AGUSTÍN CAZALLA**, a Canon of the church at Salamanca—who for several years had served as chaplain <note>original: *a sacris*</note> to Emperor **CHARLES V** while he was staying in Germany—was apprehended and thrown into prison by the Inquisition located at Valladolid. This was because he had shown himself to be devoted to the "purer religion" <note>A common contemporary term for the Protestant Reformation</note>. The same fate befell his mother, **ELEONORA de VIVERA**, in whose house those who had abandoned Roman superstitions were accustomed to hold their sacred meetings. Likewise, his three brothers and two sisters, as well as their male and female servants, were all arrested; **CAZALLA** had persuaded them all to embrace the Catholic religion. I believe the doctrine of the Protestants should be called by this name "Catholic," because it does not differ from that religion which all Christian assemblies professed at the time when the Creeds <note>original: *Symbola* — referring to the foundational statements of faith like the Apostles' or Nicene Creed</note>, in which this name is found, were first established. **PARAMUS** <note>Luis de Páramo, a famous Spanish Inquisitor and historian of the office</note>, one of the Inquisitors, describes this most holy and

## PEREZ. <note>original: "PEREZIUS"; referring to Francisco de Pérez, a Spanish Protestant martyr</note>

PEREZ, a priest from those whom they call secular <term>secular|A priest who lives in the world rather than in a monastery or religious order</term>, a man second to none in piety and erudition, and a most eloquent orator, was drawn out from the prisons of the Inquisition and publicly burned together with those I have mentioned. ### ELEONORA de CISNEROS.

ELEONORA de CISNEROS had as her husband the most blessed martyr, HERREZUELO <note>Antonio Herrezuelo, mentioned on the previous page</note>; after she had lain in the prisons of the Inquisition of Valladolid for several years, she was condemned to death and publicly consumed by flames. She endured this cruel and horrible punishment with such constancy that, if she did not surpass her husband in strength of mind, she certainly equaled him. *The writer of the Pontifical History relates that these holy spouses and* CHARLES de SESO *bore the violence of the flames so courageously as if they were made of stone, rather than composed of flesh and blood.*

**JUAN GIL** <note>original: "Iohannes Aegidivs," often referred to in Spanish as Doctor Egidio</note> first performed the duties of Rector at the University of Alcalá <note>original: "Academia Complutensi"</note>. From there he was transferred to Sigüenza <note>original: "Liquensam"</note>, where he taught public Theology for a certain time. However, he did not hold this provincial post for long. Indeed, the Dean and the Chapter of the Cathedral Church of Seville <note>original: "Hispalensis"</note> claimed him for themselves, honoring him with the office of sacred orator and, at the same time, the dignity of a Canon. He administered all these offices, especially the last one, so faithfully and diligently that everyone to whom he was known both loved and looked up to his remarkable piety, admirable learning, and greatest modesty of spirit.

Moreover, he was hardly dearer to anyone than to the Emperor **CHARLES V**, who, we have heard, was accustomed to call him "his own preacher." And here, in the year 1550, so that he might testify to the goodwill with which he embraced him, the Emperor designated him Bishop of the city of **Tortosa**; this prefecture is among the most profitable in all of Spain. 

But before this great and holy man could be initiated into this new office by the sacred rite, the Inquisition of Seville ordered him to be seized and led away as a captive, because he favored the new religion of the Protestants and passed it on to others. At what time and by what kind of death he passed away in the prison of the Inquisition is not clear. However, we do know this: that several years after he had been sent into custody, his bones were brought out and publicly burned in a certain *Act of Faith* <term>Act of Faith|An Auto-da-fé, the public ritual of sentencing and execution performed by the Inquisition</term> celebrated in Seville, as if [he were a heretic].

## JUAN PONCE de LEÓN

In the year 1559, on the fourteenth day of September, JUAN PONCE de LEÓN, son of **RODRIGO**, Count of Bailén <note>original: "Comitis Baylensis"</note>, was put to death by fire in Seville <note>original: "Hispali"</note> along with several others on account of his adoption of the Protestant religion. That learned martyr of whom I spoke a little earlier, Doctor AEGIDIUS, was the leader and the influence behind these holy witnesses of truth turning away from the superstitions of their ancestors. And in their lives and deeds, no less than in their glorious deaths, they showed themselves to be worthy sons of such a spiritual father. The doctrines on account of which they were condemned to death are as follows:

(I) That the public worship prescribed by the Roman Church is tainted by the crime of idolatry.

## DOCTOR CONSTANTINE PONCE DE LA FUENTE <note>original: "Constantinus Pontius"</note>.

Constantine Ponce, court preacher to the Emperor Charles V <note>Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain (1500–1558)</note> and, as some writers add, his confessor, was a Canon and preacher at the cathedral in Seville <note>original: "Hispalensi"</note>. After the Emperor had abdicated his power and retired to Spain, Constantine was seized by the Seville Inquisitors and thrown into chains as a heretic corrupted by Protestant doctrine. He met his final day in prison; whether by disease or by some other means, only the Inquisitors know. His body, along with several handwritten books he had composed, was dragged out from custody into the light and burned in the flames. Among these books destroyed by fire, one was titled *The Image of a True Christian*; in it, he argued that no such person could exist except one devoted to a purer form of worship. Another title was *On the Anti-Christian Church*; he maintained that this was the Roman Church. Also present among these books was a unique argument against the fire of purgatory and Indulgences <note>The practice of granting remission for temporal punishment of sins</note>, as well as another in which he attacked what is called *Transubstantiation* <note>The doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the literal body and blood of Christ</note>. Finally, there was a commentary opposed to the error of those who think they can appease God with their own good works.

The Emperor had ordered this most learned man to accompany his son, Philip <note>Philip II of Spain</note>, into Belgi-

Therefore, in order to strip all power from these great examples, they saw to it that the professors of a purer religion were either strangled with a noose before they were burned—falsely claiming that they had returned to the communion of the Roman Church while on the pyre itself—or they would murder them in prison and then cast effigies <note>images or statues representing the person</note> of the slain into the flames.

Only when it was time to eat was freedom restored to his mouth
