## CHRISTOPHER LOSADA.

**Christopher Losada**, a physician of exceptional learning, was burned at the same time as the man mentioned above <note>meaning John de Leon</note> because he had rejected the dogmas of the Pope. He endured death with the same fortitude and steadfastness as the others, showing such joy and peace of mind in his final hour that all the spectators who were present were struck with amazement.

I suspect that the unfortunate **MICHAEL SERVETUS** <note>Michael Servetus (1511–1553) was a Spanish polymath and physician whose radical views, particularly his rejection of the Trinity, led to his execution in Geneva. The author here attempts to distance mainstream Spanish Protestant martyrs from Servetus’s more radical "errors."</note>, who was the most outstanding physician of his age, was one of those who went into voluntary exile at that time to escape the hands of the Inquisitors. However, wherever this wretched man may have learned those errors for which he was later put to death in Geneva, it is certain that he did not carry away from Spain the disgraceful doctrines of which he was convicted. For none of those who were put to death in Spain for their love of the reformed religion <note>original: "emendatae religionis"; literally "amended" or "improved" religion, a common term for the Protestant Reformation</note> were ever accused by the enemies of truth of the specific errors that brought about the death of **SERVETUS**.

# CHRISTOPHER AURELIUS.

Christopher Aurelius held a position of no small importance among the doctors known as the <term>Scholastics</term> <note>Scholasticism was a medieval school of philosophy and theology that emphasized logic and the authority of the Church Fathers; Aurelius was a trained academic within this system.</note>. However, through his diligent reading of the holy books, he reached a point where he perceived the falsity of the Roman religion. Consequently, he was burned at the stake by order of the Inquisitors at the same time as Losada <note>Christopher Losada was a physician and prominent member of the secret Protestant community in Seville.</note>. This punishment was so far from breaking his spirit that he instead triumphed over death in the midst of the flames, as if over a defeated enemy.

# GARCIA ARIAS.

Garcia Arias, a monk from the order of Saint Isidore <note>Specifically the Hieronymite monastery of San Isidoro del Campo near Seville.</note> whom the common people used to call **Doctor BLANCO** <note>original: "Doctor BLANCO"; the name means "White" in Spanish, likely referring to the color of his hair or habit.</note>, turned from being a most grievous enemy of the purer religion into its most steadfast protector and patron, much like Saint Paul. This zeal of his for spreading the truth earned him the penalty of fire. He endured this at Seville with such a spirit that he celebrated God with great joy, for God had judged him worthy to suffer death for so noble a cause. The Monastery of Saint Isidore, where this holy man lived, was in those times a virtual seat and home of the reformed religion. Indeed, five monks were dragged from that place and burned by order of the Inquisitors; twelve others, however, fled from there and reached Geneva safe and unharmed.

When she refused to obey this command, the use of her tongue was taken away from the maiden by a gag <note>literally: "a knot thrown into her mouth"</note> placed in her mouth as she climbed the pile of wood. For this reason, when she was already bound with chains on the pyre, they suddenly shouted: *“She has converted, and desires, before she dies, to return to grace with the Roman Church,”* and they proclaimed the absolution of her sins. Once this was done, her throat was immediately broken with a noose <note>The "garrote," a method of strangulation used to kill the condemned before the fire was lit, often granted as a "mercy" to those who purportedly recanted.</note>, and her body was consumed by the flames.

At that same time, several other women, some of whom were of very high birth, were publicly burned both in Valladolid <note>Latin: "Vallisoleti"</note> and in Seville <note>Latin: "Hispali"</note> on account of having accepted the purer religion <note>Latin: "religionem puriorem"; a common contemporary term for Protestantism, emphasizing a return to biblical basics.</note>. Because these women were all highly skilled in the Sacred Scriptures, they were very troublesome to the Inquisitors. For this class of men <note>the Inquisitors</note>, being utterly unrefined and lacking knowledge of the divine oracles <note>the Bible</note>, was not at all able to debate with them concerning the truths and dogmas delivered therein. Because of this, Páramo <note>Luis de Páramo (c. 1545–1629), a Spanish Inquisitor and author of a famous history of the Inquisition.</note>, a Spanish Inquisitor second to none in his fury, takes the opportunity in a vehement and incited oration to generally—

## HEARTFELT GREETINGS <note>original: "S. P." abbreviated from "Salutem Plurimam," a standard Latin greeting meaning "very much health" or "most hearty greetings."</note>

# MAGNIFICENT
# LORD PRORECTOR!

## MOST REVEREND, MOST LEARNED,
## DISTINGUISHED, MOST EXPERIENCED,

### FATHERS OF THE ACADEMY,

I fear that I might not only lack the skill to fulfill the role that duty <note>original: *pietas* — A Latin term describing a deep sense of social and religious obligation toward one’s family, mentors, and country.</note> imposes on me today, but that I may actually struggle to bear it at all. ...of Germany, the most illustrious. If I thought that I could equal the gifts and virtue of this Man in my speaking, or if I believed anything could be produced by me that would match the remarkable devotion of everyone toward him, I would rightly be seen by wise men as frivolous—lacking not only in judgment of all things, but even in knowledge of myself. It is difficult, **LISTENERS**, it is difficult and almost full of peril, to attempt the praises of a Man whom nature itself almost shaped for immortality, whom no prudent person ever criticized, whom so many great men looked up to and admired, and whom finally an incredible strength of character and incomparable diligence <note>original: *industria* — This refers to Schmidt's prolific output as a historian and theologian.</note> placed in the sight and light not only of our own and these lands, nor of Germany alone, but of the entire literate world.

The sorrow we have felt from the death of this most longed-for Man has something singular and exceptional about it, and it should be measured not only by its magnitude, but especially by its long duration. Six years and more have passed since we saw our **SCHMIDT** lying down and struggling with his imminent fate; for just as many years, we have followed his most bitter misfortune—whose lamentable end we feared daily—with pain and tears. So much time...

But the matter turned out far differently than many had anticipated in their minds. For as soon as that mournful news reached our ears—that our SCHMIDT had finally succumbed to illness and passed over to the dwellings of the blessed spirits—such a great grief suddenly seized the minds of all, as is accustomed to arise in those whom a very brief moment robs of the greatest opportunities. 

How, I ask you, could I be equal to expressing such great and persistent grief? I, who have never been able to gather any superior ability in speaking because of the thinness of my own talent, and who can only with difficulty force myself to turn my eyes and mind away from the funeral of him whom I cherished and loved like a father?

If any comfort remains for me, constricted as I am by such great obstacles, it must all be drawn from the same source where the disturbance was born. I appeal indeed first to YOU, **REVERED OLD MAN**, to whom we pay our final duty today; and then to You, **LISTENERS**, who have gathered here in such great numbers. 

Indeed, **BLESSED OLD MAN**, your virtue and merits placed you long ago in such a position that nothing so dry or worn out can be said about YOU that it does not make YOUR name splendid and magnificent. Thus, what neither the talent nor the abundance and eloquence of the speaker can provide, the subject itself will procure as honor for my speech. ...I feel <note>The text begins with the suffix "-am," likely completing a word like *sentiam* (I may feel) from the previous page.</note>, as will certainly happen, that you notice I do not even moderately reflect the abundance of your grief, you will understand by that very fact how great a man he was whom we have lost, and how worthy he was of the devotion of everyone. Support, therefore, support my weakness with your love; do not consider what I ought to have said, but rather what could proceed from a troubled and meager talent.

No place, **LISTENERS**, absolutely no place will be given by me to the vain "colors" <note>technical term for rhetorical ornaments or flourishes</note> of rhetoricians, nor to the common arts of orators, while I am occupied in demonstrating how great a loss we have suffered in the death of this one man. Allow me, **LISTENERS**, to explain this memorable matter without pretense or ambiguity.

Those who are called **Theologians** <term>Theology|In the 17th and 18th centuries, the study of God and religious doctrine was the "Queen of the Sciences," but it was also a field fraught with intense political and personal conflict</term> find themselves on very slippery and treacherous ground in this most suspicious age of ours—especially those whom either the kindness of fame or a particular abundance of talent has raised above the rest. For since they are commanded to ensure that the "holy city" <note>A common metaphor for the Church or the community of the faithful</note> suffers no harm, and to throw themselves against the incursions of enemies, very few of the more celebrated men are able to fulfill this duty in such a way that they spend their lives in peace, free from many calamities, offenses, snares, and accusations. 

Suppose they step forward into the battle line: immediately they are heard by many to be "slaves of brawls and contentions"; and even if they are circumspect and most modest, they are bound by insults and slanders and handed over to public hatred. Suppose they remain silent: immediately someone is there to accuse them of abandoning their post, of violating their faith, and of betraying the **Church**. Such a critic brings them to a judgment not merely of the "head" <note>A reference to capital punishment or civil status</note>—which might be bearable—but a judgment of the soul and of eternal salvation! Suppose they apply their talent and labor to calming the minds of their brothers and settling internal wars: then the entire crowd from every side, "Trojan or Rutulian" <note>original: "Tros Rutulusve" — a reference to Virgil's *Aeneid*, meaning "no matter which side one is on." It implies that in a heated conflict, a peacemaker is attacked by both factions</note>, flies at the man as if he were a villain.

...slanders. They cry out that he is trying to invade the very citadel of sacred truth by digging tunnels <note>original: "cuniculis" — a military metaphor referring to the practice of mining or tunneling under a fortification’s walls to cause them to collapse</note> and that, through an ill-timed zeal for peace, he is betraying the defenses of the Christian community to its enemies. No matter what they desire or set in place, an adversary is always standing behind them, threatening a grim struggle and battle. How fortunate you are! You who preside over either the administration of the law or the healing of bodies; your conflicts, though they are often bitter, are not joined with such great envy, nor do they end, in the end, in eternal fire! <note>The speaker suggests that while lawyers and doctors have difficult jobs, they do not face the same risk of religious persecution or the threat of damnation ("eternal fire") for their professional disagreements.</note> We theologians rarely descend into the grave without bloodshed and wars; indeed, the common crowd of theologians doubts the salvation of no group more sharply than they doubt the salvation of other theologians.

Though our friend was among that rank of **Theologians** <term>Theologian|A scholar of divinity; in this period, the role often involved defending orthodoxy against perceived heresies</term> which everyone desires but few ever reach, and though he spared no error that he understood to be deadly and harmful, he nevertheless enjoyed this unusual good fortune: that he was never branded with the mark of infamy by any wise person. Instead, he was pleasing and welcome to all—even to those he had opposed—and has now passed from these turmoils into eternal peace. He publicly defeated almost all the sects <term>Sects|Religious groups or denominations that diverged from the established church doctrines</term> that reject our sacred rites. He spoke his mind candidly concerning the civil disagreements of the church; he did not always follow the judgments of the common crowd, but quite often followed his own judgment. Yet, he never received a heavy blow from anyone, nor did he incur the censure of any sensible man. Believe me, **LISTENERS**, out of all the virtues in which our **SCHMID** <note>Johann Andreas Schmidt (1652–1726), the subject of this funeral oration</note> excelled, this is the one thing I claim for myself above the rest; this I wish for, this I seek with every prayer: that, having conducted the work of **JESUS CHRIST** well and successfully, and without any announcement of curses...

...[from life] I may be settled, and that I might carry away from here the praise not so much of an "erudite" man—a title won only with great toil—but of a wise, modest, and peace-loving **Theologian** <term>Theologian|A scholar who studies the nature of the divine; here, the speaker emphasizes Schmidt’s desire for peace over academic vanity</term>. Happy are they—indeed, three and four times happy <note>original: "terque quaterque felices" — a classical Latin idiom, famously used by Virgil, to express extreme good fortune</note>—who detest every kind of victory that does not bear the fruit of knowing the truth; those who are allowed to plead the cause of God without giving offense to anyone; and those, finally, who have no need, so to speak, of any "un-cursing" by the Eumolpidae after their deaths. <note>original: "Eumolpidarum... resecrationibus" — The Eumolpidae were a family of priests in ancient Athens who held the power to curse or excommunicate individuals. With what zeal, with what fire our **Venerable Old Man** <note>A respectful reference to the deceased, Johann Andreas Schmidt</note> was engaged in the study of all history, especially sacred history—this escapes no one, except those whom everything escapes. Although he ventured into almost every branch of learning, his industry was so uniquely focused on this genre that he seemed to have surpassed even himself in many ways. Posterity will praise him as one of the chief pillars of **Ecclesiastical History** <term>Ecclesiastical History|The study of the history of the Christian Church; at this time, it was a field often mired in sectarian bias</term> that **Germany** has produced. Future generations will remember that it was by this one man's sleepless vigils that this branch of study was liberated from infinite filth, and thus became pleasing to many for whom it previously seemed too gloomy and full of conflict.

On this point, **LISTENERS**, lest I repeat things too well known or sin against your fairness, I must omit many things for which memory is deservedly due. Therefore, I remain silent on how, with immense labor, he devoured historical records of every kind—sacred and secular, ancient and recent—and recorded into his notebooks those things which seemed to be of use. I say nothing of the ease with which he drank deeply into his mind not only ancient history, but also medieval and more recent history—subjects so vast that one of them alone is scarcely enough for a single man. I pass over the expenses, which certainly...

...made you seek out no small number of books and **records** <term>records|Original: "monumenta" — This refers to physical evidence, inscriptions, and primary source documents rather than just later histories</term>. I leave aside the fact—which is well known—that his diligence served only the most select arguments, every one of which he examined in all its aspects and strengthened with sound reasoning and authorities. Finally, I pass over that very skill which he applied, in no common or vulgar way, to dispelling the **darkness of antiquity** <note>original: "vetustatis tenebris" — a common metaphor for the obscurity or lack of information regarding the distant past</note>. I shall consider it sufficient for his praise if I merely demonstrate how providently and circumspectly he managed this entire province of study.

Those who apply themselves to these studies often bring a mind choked by **superstition** <note>original: "superstitione faucium" — literally "superstition of the throat," implying a person swallowed by or gasping under the weight of irrational belief</note>; by its force, they are driven to embrace everything that an ancient writer, in a hoarse voice, commanded them to believe. In this way, not just handfuls but whole armies of fables are constructed; the **nightly trifles of old women** <note>original: "anicularum lucubratiunculae" — "old wives' tales." The term "lucubratiunculae" refers to works produced by candlelight or at night, often implying they are trivial or nonsensical</note> veil their own shame under the title of "venerable antiquity," and certain little stories, overgrown by the rot of long ages, are substituted in place of the truth. It is incredible to say how much disgrace and infamy redounds upon our most holy religion from this practice.

Yet others, sharper than these, hold whatever is ancient under suspicion of falsehood. They are never more "ingenious" than when they desire to persuade the people that nothing should be believed concerning the early Christians. **A noble deed indeed!** <note>original: "Praeclarum vero facinus!" — This is heavy sarcasm. The author argues that skeptics treat the early Church as if it were even less reliable than ancient myths.</note>. There are some who, though free from these vices, yet with difficulty...

...nevertheless they pass judgments in History, and yet they do not wish for the deeds of the ancients to be judged, but only to be recounted. They are not unlike those men who would contend that the statues of **Praxiteles** <note>original: "Praxitelis" — Praxiteles was one of the most famous Greek sculptors of the 4th century BCE, known for introducing a more human, graceful style to statues of gods</note> were set up solely for display and ornament, rather than for critical evaluation. Opposed to these are many who always have the art of **Criticism** <term>Criticism|Original: "Criticam artem" — Here referring to the scholarly discipline of analyzing ancient texts to determine their authenticity and original meaning</term> on their lips, and they demand that everything they read or hear be subjected to its strict laws and rules.

Our friend, **LISTENERS**, having entered this difficult province of study, tempered the practices of all these people with a particular sharpness of mind. He approved nothing rashly; he rejected nothing rashly. He did not allow fables to deceive him, but neither did he go hunting for fables with excessive zeal. He did not keep silent about the **blemishes of the Fathers** <note>original: "naevos Patrum" — This refers to the errors or flaws found in the writings of the early Church Fathers</note>, as they are called, but he also proclaimed their virtues. Where there was a need, he called the Critics to his aid; where there was no need, he ordered them to remain quiet. A great and wise man, **LISTENERS**! If he finds many imitators—as we hope he shall—we will much more quickly rout the profane forces and, raised above dull quibbles, with **Christ as our leader** <note>original: "Christo duce"</note> and piety and reason as our companions, we shall triumph.

But I remember that I am here to praise a Theologian. Since it is only right that such a person be a man of piety and integrity, reason itself has long called me to this point: to speak briefly about **Schmidt’s piety** <note>original: "Schmidiana pietate" — referring to the personal devotion of Johann Andreas Schmidt</note>. To be frank, **LISTENERS**, this entire topic is not difficult for an orator—provided he is not completely dull—to decorate with fine words, but it is a very laborious task to make it truly persuasive. Alas! The ignorant eloquence of many, having overstepped all shame, has long made this kind of praise—than which nothing is more excellent—seem common and cheap, having...

...[pro]gressed, men laden with vices have been raised to the heavens with wordy little phrases and antitheses. ...sign and testimony of carefully cultivated <term>Piety|Original: "pietatis" — In this context, it refers to both religious devotion and the fulfillment of duty toward God and man</term>. I refer to that fatal disease and most heavy misfortune which, more than six years ago <note>Johann Andreas Schmidt suffered a debilitating stroke in 1720, which left him partially paralyzed until his death in 1726</note>, attacked this great man and finally overwhelmed him.

Most of us know with what constancy, what faith, what fortitude, and what equanimity of mind he endured for so many years that wretched calamity, which was beyond what anyone could imagine. Robbed for the most part of the use of his limbs, almost excluded from human society, forced away from those most pleasant labors and meditations in which he alone found delight, and finally besieged by a multitude of afflictions, he never uttered a word that indicated a mind anything less than composed and serene. As soon as he returned to himself after receiving that deathly blow, and realized that he had been cast into such a lamentable state, he complained of nothing greatly; nor did he, in the common manner of men, testify to his own innocence <note>That is, he did not protest that he was "too good" to deserve such a fate</note>. Instead, he turned himself entirely to God, professing with an unconquered spirit that he ought to live according to God's will, not his own. Nor could he ever be moved from this greatness of mind and tranquility. Through this spirit, he most happily overcame pains, inconveniences, the desires implanted by nature, the fear of death, and finally fate itself and his final hour. I remember, and no doubt many of you remember, that when he was greeted by those performing their social duties, he said nothing of his miseries and hardships except piously and moderately; nothing of death except with constancy and without fear; nothing of the dwelling place of holy and blessed souls except with confidence and joy; and nothing of God except reverently and most lovingly.

<meta>catchword: manner</meta>

If there was anything he bore with a lack of moderation, it was only this: that he could no longer serve the needs of others with the same speed and vigor as he had done before. For he valued his <term>health|Original: "valetudinem"</term> and his life primarily by this standard: his ability to be useful to his fellow man. What a truly holy sorrow! This quality alone serves as an excellent proof of the point I have undertaken to explain.

Now I ask you to consider: would all these qualities—this <term>steadfastness|Original: "firmitas"</term> of mind amidst the most adverse circumstances and agonizing illnesses, this hope and confidence in a better life, this joy, this <term>disregard|Original: "contemtio"</term> for worldly affairs, this disdain for death (which he watched approaching with slow steps), and this serenity during terrible pains—would all these have been present in our friend if he had not been united with God long before? If he had not, through an ardent love for the <term>Savior|Original: "Servatoris"</term>, strengthened his soul against every assault of misfortune and the hardships of human life? Or do you perhaps think that when the mind is failing, the body is prostrate, strength is broken, and the final hour is pressing, the principles of the greatest virtues could suddenly slip into a soul as soft and wayward as that of most mortals? Do you think they could suddenly reveal the kind of immense strength required by the events I have just described? Do you believe that <term>holiness|Original: "sanctimoniam"</term> can grow to maturity in the space of a single hour—and a miserable, frantic hour at that—and then proceed to radiate such brilliant light through a long period of the most grievous suffering? For my part, if there are any people so bold as to think such things are possible, I consider them ignorant of human nature and character. My conclusion is this: Just as...

In the same way as sailors—who, when winds suddenly disturb the waters and a storm unexpectedly arises, keep an undaunted spirit and show no shadow of fear in their expression or gestures because they have, long before, while sitting securely at anchor, meditated on the instability of the sea and the uncertainty of fate—so too, no mortal can face the sudden arrows of fortune with an open heart. Nor can they maintain the highest cheerfulness without any distress amidst the frequent and long-lasting attacks of the most bitter suffering until their very last breath, unless they have long ago joined themselves in close friendship with the <term>Supreme Divinity|Original: "supremi Numinis"</term> through faith.

&emsp;&emsp;How great a man we have lost, then, members of this audience! What an exceptional safeguard he was for both sacred and worldly matters! If we do not merely groan at his funeral but are profoundly moved, it is all the more justified because we are mourning a disaster and calamity that belongs not just to us, but to the entire University—which has lost a truly distinguished teacher—and the entire province—which has lost a most wise guardian and advisor. We mourn for the whole Church, which has lost a theologian of proven faith and virtue, and for the entire <term>Republic of Letters|Original: "reipublicae litteratae" — the international community of scholars and intellectuals</term>, which has lost a great champion of its honor and fame. He has indeed been welcomed among the citizens of the heavenly homeland; from his high place, he looks down upon the fleeting and fragile concerns of mortals, nourishing his holy soul with eternal joys.

Let us entrust this concern to their wisdom <note>referring to the Princes mentioned on the previous page</note>, and meanwhile, let us not—lest we be ungrateful—begrudge this Old Man, who has remarkably deserved so well of us all, the rest he has earned through so many labors.

# OF WRITINGS,
### WHICH ARE CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME.

I. A Commentary on the Date of the <term>Apologeticus<note>original: "Apologetici". This refers to the "Apology," a famous defense of Christianity written by the North African theologian Tertullian around 197 AD.</note></term> of <term>Tertullian<note>A prolific early Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) known as the "father of Latin Christianity."</note></term>, and the beginning of the persecution of Christians under <term>Severus<note>The Roman Emperor Septimius Severus, whose reign (193–211 AD) was marked by various localized persecutions of the early Church.</note></term>. p. 1.

II. A Commentary on the <term>Church<note>original: "Ecclesia"</note></term> being disturbed by the more recent <term>Platonists<note>original: "Platonicos". This likely refers to the Neoplatonists, philosophers whose ideas often competed with or deeply influenced early Christian doctrine.</note></term>. p. 85.

III. A Dissertation on the Causes of <term>forged books<note>original: "suppositorum librorum". These are "pseudepigrapha," or writings falsely attributed to apostles or other famous figures to gain authority.</note></term> among Christians of the first and second Centuries. p. 217.

IV. A Dissertation on the true Date of the <term>Apology<note>original: "Apologetici". A formal defense of the Christian faith against pagan accusations.</note></term> which <term>Athenagoras<note>A 2nd-century Christian philosopher from Athens who wrote an influential "Plea for the Christians" to the Emperor Marcus Aurelius.</note></term> wrote on behalf of the Christians. p. 269.

V. A Dissertation on the Zeal of the <term>Pagans<note>original: "Ethnicorum". Literally "the nations," used by Christian writers to refer to non-Jewish, non-Christian polytheists.</note></term> for imitating Christians. p. 321.

VI. A Demonstration concerning the Sect of the <term>Nicolaitans<note>An early Christian group mentioned in the Book of Revelation, often accused by early Church fathers of heresy and immoral practices.</note></term> against its most learned Opponents. p. 389.

VII. A Supplement to the Dissertation on the Nicolaitans. p. 457.

VIII. A Letter to <term>Christoph August Heumann<note>A prominent 18th-century German theologian and scholar (1681–1764) known for his work on the history of literature and theology.</note></term> regarding <term>John being cast into boiling oil<note>A traditional legend that the Apostle John was miraculously unharmed after being thrown into a vat of boiling oil at the Latin Gate in Rome.</note></term>. p. 497.

IX. A Letter in Response to Christoph August Heumann. p. 535.

X. A Dissertation, in which it is shown: That it cannot be certainly and definitively determined today whether a certain <term>Ebion<note>The traditionally cited founder of the Ebionites, a Jewish-Christian sect. Many scholars argue that "Ebion" was a fictional person invented by early historians to explain the name "Ebionite," which actually stems from the Hebrew word for "the poor."</note></term> once existed as the author of a new sect among Christians or not? p. 547.

XI. A Dissertation on the appeals of the <term>French<note>original: "Gallorum". This refers to Gallicanism, a movement in the French Catholic Church that sought to limit papal power in favor of the authority of the state and general church councils.</note></term> to a <term>General Council<note>original: "Concilium universae Ecclesiae". A meeting of the whole church's leadership to settle major disputes; appealing to such a council was often a way to bypass the Pope's authority.</note></term> of the Church, which undermine the visible unity of the Church. p. 577.

XII. A sample of a treatise to be published concerning the sacred disturbances in the Church of <term>Goslar<note>A historic town in Lower Saxony, Germany, which experienced significant religious upheaval during the Reformation.</note></term> since the time of the Reformation, presenting the first <term>Sacramentarian<note>original: "Sacramentarias". This refers to bitter disputes over the nature of the Eucharist (the Sacrament), specifically whether Christ was physically or only spiritually present.</note></term> disturbances led by <term>Knigge and Gravert<note>Friedrich Knigge and Brandan Gravert, local ecclesiastical figures in Goslar involved in these 16th-century theological conflicts.</note></term>. p. 621.

XIII. <term>Michael Geddes's<note>Michael Geddes (c. 1650–1713) was a Scottish historian and Anglican clergyman who wrote extensively on the history of the Spanish and Portuguese inquisitions.</note></term> Martyrology of those who, in Spain, were executed with the <term>supreme penalty<note>original: "supremo supplicio". A formal Latin term for the death penalty.</note></term> because of their profession of the Protestant Religion, translated from English into Latin. p. 663.

### XIV. A Funeral Oration for <term>Johannes Andreas Schmidt<note>A distinguished German Lutheran theologian and historian (1652–1726). He was a prolific writer and professor at the University of Helmstedt, known for his work in church history and antiquities.</note></term>, Abbot of <term>Marienthal<note>original: "vallis Mariae." Marienthal was a former Cistercian monastery near Helmstedt; following the Reformation, it served as a Lutheran administrative title and educational center held by high-ranking clergy like Schmidt.</note></term>, p. 699.

->**To God Alone the Glory**<note>original: "S. D. G." (Soli Deo Gloria). This was a common closing dedication used by authors and composers of the era—most famously J.S. Bach—to signify that their work was intended for the honor of God rather than personal fame.</note><-
